items.title: Terraform Learning Notes
items.text:
Personal notes and a from-scratch book on learning Terraform (and its open-source fork OpenTofu) — Infrastructure as Code done properly.

Start with the Learning Path: a topic-by-topic route from zero to platform-engineering-grade Terraform, with a resource plan and milestone for each topic.

As each topic is finished, a synthesized chapter lands in the Book.

items.title: Learning Path: Terraform (and OpenTofu)
items.text:
Current stable versions: Terraform CLI 1.16.0 (released 2026-08-26, BSL 1.1) · OpenTofu 1.12.6 (2026-08-19; 1.12.0 released 2026-05-14, MPL 2.0) Next releases: Terraform main carries 1.17 alphas. OpenTofu 1.13 is at beta1 (2026-08-27), so treat 1.13 rows as provisional.

⚠️ 1.16 rows are no longer provisional. Through 2026-08-26 this path treated every 1.16 claim as release-candidate material. v1.16.0 is now tagged and this page's 1.16 rows are current. Anything still labelled 1.16-rc1 in these notes is a stale label, not a provisional fact: the CHANGELOG delta from v1.16.0-rc1 to v1.16.0 is one line (release-feature-map).

⚠️ Do not run 1.15.8 or OpenTofu 1.12.5 or earlier. Both carry published security advisories. Terraform 1.15.9 (2026-08-19) mitigates CVE-2026-14978 in go-slug, where Unicode normalisation could stop files being excluded by .terraformignore when uploading to HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise. OpenTofu 1.12.6 (2026-08-19) fixes credentials for one origin being resent to the target of an HTTP redirect when installing from OCI registries, plus CPU/memory exhaustion in tofu init resolving crafted relative URLs. Details in version-facts. Local stack: Terraform CLI + a cloud account (AWS recommended for cert alignment); OpenTofu optional as a drop-in.

How to read this page. Topics are the primary unit. Each topic has a "How to learn it" section that recommends a multi-modal path — video first, then hands-on, then depth reading, then reference docs. Resources serve the topics; they are not the organizing structure. Terraform and OpenTofu share HCL, providers, and state format — learn either; differences are called out where they matter (see E3).

Status markers. ⬜ not started · ✅ done, chapter written · 🔄 revisit — the chapter exists but later research changed or contradicted what it says, so it needs a re-read before the topic counts as done again. A 🔄 topic always names what changed and why, so the revisit is actionable rather than a vague doubt. Checkpoints still count a 🔄 topic as written.

📌 TUR targets Terraform ~1.1

TUR targets Terraform ~1.1 (3rd ed., first release 2022-09-19). Core concepts (modules, state, testing philosophy) are still the best treatment available, but verify newer syntax (terraform test, import/removed blocks, Stacks) against current HCDocs.

Chapters 2 onward build an ASG on aws_launch_configuration, and AWS has closed that path: no EC2 instance type released after 2023-01-01 works in one, and accounts created on or after 2024-10-01 cannot create one by any method (launch-configurations-eol). Substitute aws_launch_template. The teaching is unaffected — none of TUR's module, state or testing arguments depend on the resource — but budget for the swap before typing anything into a terminal. Reading notes are under Books › Terraform: Up & Running.

Cert Provider Level Topics tested Fee Format When to attempt Terraform Associate (004) HashiCorp Intermediate exit IaC concepts · fundamentals (providers/state) · core workflow · HCL config language · modules (use + author) · state management · infrastructure maintenance · HCP Terraform $70.50 USD (+ local taxes; free retake not included) Online proctored, multiple choice, 1 hr, credential valid 2 yrs; tests Terraform 1.12 After Intermediate Terraform Authoring & Operations Professional HashiCorp Advanced exit resource lifecycle · dynamic config & troubleshooting · collaborative workflows · modules · providers · HCP Terraform $295 USD (+ local taxes; free retake included) Online proctored, lab-based and multiple choice, 4 hrs incl. a 15-min break, US QWERTY keyboard only, valid 2 yrs; tests Terraform 1.6, AWS provider (Azure variant expected late 2026) After Advanced

004 replaces 003 — and here is exactly what 004 added

004 replaces 003 (retired 2026-01-08). If you see 003 study material, the content is ~90% the same but use 004 resources where possible. HashiCorp publishes the delta, so study these four objectives specifically when working from an older course:

  • 4f — depends_on and create_before_destroy lifecycle rules (path: I1, I2)
  • 4g — validate configuration using custom conditions (path: A2)
  • 4h — ephemeral values and write-only arguments (path: A6)
  • 8c — organize and use HCP Terraform workspaces and projects (path: A4)

Plus: the exam now tests Terraform 1.12 and includes HCP Terraform content throughout. The Pro exam assumes deep HCL + CLI fluency and real cloud experience.

HashiCorp does not publish a question count for 004

This path used to state "~57 multiple-choice". The official exam-details table gives assessment type, format, duration, price, language and expiry — no question count. The 57 figure is the size of ExamPro's free practice exam, which circulates widely enough to get mistaken for the real thing. Plan against the 1 hour limit, not a question count. Verified against the certifications page, 2026-08-15.

items.title: Beginner
items.text: Goal: Write, plan, and apply a real Terraform configuration against a cloud provider, and understand what state is. Estimated time: ~30 hrs

items.title: ✅ B1 — Infrastructure as Code & where Terraform fits
items.text:
What it is: The idea of provisioning infrastructure from declarative, version-controlled files, and how Terraform (declarative, cloud-agnostic, provider-based) compares to OpenTofu, Pulumi, CloudFormation, and Ansible.

Why you need it: Without the mental model of declarative + desired state + plan/apply, every later command looks like magic; you also need to know when Terraform is the right tool vs config management.

How to learn it:

  1. Video — TF2026 "Core Terraform Concepts" (00:00, ~40 min) — watch the "what is IaC / why Terraform" opening; build the mental picture before touching syntax.
  2. Book chapter — TID Ch 1 (~1 hr) — read the IaC framing and the Terraform-vs-OpenTofu positioning (this book covers both). (Captured notes: 01-brief-overview; the cross-source synthesis of this whole topic — HCDocs, TID Ch 1 and TUR Ch 1 read against each other — is iac-fundamentals.)
  3. Reference — HCDocs "Intro / Use Cases" (~20 min) — skim the official framing; note the declarative vs imperative distinction. (Captured notes: terraform-intro, terraform-use-cases.)
  4. Book chapter — TUR Ch 1 (~1 hr) — the argumentative version of this topic, and the one that makes the milestone easy. Captured: 01-why-terraform. Two things it has that nothing else here does: the five-category taxonomy (ad hoc scripts → configuration management → server templating → orchestration → provisioning) that shows most "Ansible or Terraform?" arguments are cross-category, and the 10 → 15 servers example that demonstrates declarative rather than asserting it — the Ansible edit gives you 25 servers, the Terraform edit gives you Plan: 5 to add. ⚠️ Its comparison tables are June 2022 and its "Source: Open" row for Terraform predates the BSL relicensing and OpenTofu; the note's Version reckoning section carries the corrections.

🧪 Labs (KK)

None — KodeKloud's IaC intro (Challenges with Traditional IT / Types of IaC Tools / Why Terraform?) is lecture-only. First KodeKloud lab is HCL Basics (→ B2/B4).

Milestone: You can explain in two sentences why Terraform is declarative and how it differs from Ansible and from CloudFormation.

items.title: ✅ B2 — Install, providers & your first project
items.text:
What it is: Installing the Terraform (or OpenTofu) CLI, wiring cloud credentials, declaring a required_providers + provider block, and laying out a first working directory.

Why you need it: Nothing runs until the CLI, a provider plugin, and credentials are in place; project layout mistakes here cause pain forever.

How to learn it:

  1. Interactive — HCTut "Install Terraform" + "Create infrastructure" (~1 hr) — follow the AWS (or Docker) quick-start end to end in your own account. (Captured notes: tf-install-cli, tf-aws-create.)
  2. Reference — HCDocs "Provider Requirements" (~20 min) — understand required_providers, source addresses, and version pinning. (Install) (Captured notes: provider-requirements; the version-constraint operator syntax used for pinning — ~>, >=, ranges — is in tf-expr-version-constraints.)
  3. Book chapter — TID Ch 2 (~1 hr) — first-project walkthrough; note the .terraform/ and lock-file layout.
  4. Book chapter — TUR Ch 2 (~1 hr) — the same ground as a single narrative that runs init/plan/apply repeatedly on one growing configuration, ending at a load-balanced ASG. Captured as 02-getting-started. ⚠️ Read the account-setup section for shape only: it creates an IAM user with long-lived access keys and AdministratorAccess, which is now against AWS's own guidance, and the console step it describes no longer exists. Use IAM Identity Center or the emulator below. It also writes no required_providers block anywhere, which is exactly what step 2 above exists to correct.

📌 You do not need an AWS account to do any of this

Every topic from here on can run against a local AWS emulator in Docker instead of a real account, and the book's 🧪 Lab sections all target it. The setup lives in Book Ch 1; the path just points at it, because "wire cloud credentials" is the step that stalls people at B2.

All the candidates serve the LocalStack API on port 4566, so they are interchangeable and the tflocal wrapper drives any of them. Floci is the book's default — MIT, no account, no token (floci-facts). MiniStack is the other no-signup option (ministack-facts). LocalStack is the most documented but now needs a free account and LOCALSTACK_AUTH_TOKEN (localstack-facts). Robotocore was evaluated for IAM enforcement and rejected — see robotocore-facts before reaching for it.

Know the boundary: an emulator answers API calls, it does not reproduce a cloud. Fidelity gaps are real and show up as phantom diffs — Floci dropped aws_s3_bucket creation tags up to 1.5.34, which made one lab replan the same tag forever until the fix shipped in 1.6.0. Use it to learn the Terraform half; use a real account when the question is about the provider half. Pin the image tag rather than tracking latest, and re-verify the recorded gaps when the pin moves.

Two things worth knowing before trusting a lab to it, both read from the source rather than the marketing (see floci-facts). Floci CI-tests Terraform and OpenTofu against itself — compatibility-tests/ holds compat-terraform, compat-opentofu and compat-cdk alongside five SDK suites, running real clients with no mocks, and the Terraform case exercises an S3 remote backend with a DynamoDB lock table. So the backend work in I6 is a tested path here, not a lucky one. And IAM policy evaluation can be turned on with FLOCI_SERVICES_IAM_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED=true, which makes explicit-deny-beats-allow demonstrable locally — with the caveat that it enforces authorization, not authentication, so a wrong secret key is still accepted.

🧪 Labs

  • KL: Lab 01 — getting started · Lab 02 — create your first resource. Free, runs in Codespaces.
  • KK: KodeKloud free labs — HCL Basics (first init→plan→apply run) · Version Constraints (provider pinning + the .terraform.lock.hcl file).

Milestone: You can stand up a fresh directory, terraform init it, and provision one real resource (an S3 bucket or a Docker container) from scratch.

items.title: ✅ B3 — The core workflow: init / plan / apply / destroy
items.text:
What it is: The four-command loop — init (download providers, set up backend), plan (compute a diff), apply (execute), destroy (tear down) — plus the dependency lock file.

Why you need it: This loop is the heartbeat of Terraform; the Associate exam tests it heavily and every workflow is built on it.

How to learn it:

  1. Interactive — HCTut "Manage infrastructure" + "Destroy infrastructure" (~45 min) — run a full modify-then-destroy cycle; read the plan output symbols (+, -, ~, -/+). (The init/validate/apply half of this loop is captured in tf-aws-create; the modify half — in-place ~ update vs -/+ replacement, the -out warning, and dependency-graph ordering — is captured in tf-aws-manage; the teardown half — remove-from-config vs terraform destroy, the - symbol, and reverse-dependency destroy order — is captured in tf-aws-destroy.) The language reference's own destroy page is tf-destroy-resource, which separates the three ways an object leaves your infrastructure: deleting the block, terraform destroy, and the removed block that stops managing without destroying (→ I7).
  2. Video — Krausen "Terraform Associate 004 Exam Prep" (core-workflow section) (~40 min) — walks the plan/apply lifecycle with cert framing. Free substitutes in the callout below.
  3. Reference — HCDocs "Dependency Lock File" (~25 min) — the fourth thing init does. Captured as tf-dependency-lock: the lock file records providers only (module versions are never locked — pin them with an exact constraint), init re-selects the locked version unless -upgrade forces re-resolution, and checksum verification follows a trust-on-first-use model. Learn to read the four kinds of lock-file diff (new provider · upgraded version · new checksums · removed provider), and know why zh: and h1: hashes coexist.
  4. Reference — HCDocs CLI commands (~20 min) — bookmark plan / apply flags (-out, -target, -auto-approve). This index is the complete command surface — the path teaches the four-command loop, but a complete operator also knows the everyday utilities: terraform fmt (canonical formatting), terraform validate (config-only checks), terraform show (render state/plan, -json for tooling), terraform output (read outputs, -json for scripts), terraform graph (emit the dependency graph as Graphviz — see tf-cmd-graph; full treatment in E5), terraform get, terraform providers, terraform version. The global terraform -chdir=DIR <cmd> option runs any command as if launched in DIR — cleaner than cd-ing around in scripts. The whole surface is captured as a one-row-per-command reference in tf-cli-commands; enable shell completion once with terraform -install-autocomplete. Five of those utilities — graph, output, show, state list, state show — are grouped by the docs as Inspecting Infrastructure, captured in tf-cli-inspect — all five now captured individually (tf-cmd-graph, tf-cmd-output, tf-cmd-show, tf-cmd-state-list, tf-cmd-state-show). Two flags worth memorizing: state list -id=<cloud-id> answers "which resource owns this object?", and show -json is the only supported machine format — state show output is explicitly human-only: read-only commands whose stated purpose is to "integrate other tools with Terraform's infrastructure data", which is the same reason tf-state names the -json forms as the supported parse targets rather than the state file.

💰 Free alternatives to the Krausen paid course (step 2)

Any one substitutes for step 2's paid Krausen course.

  • KL — Krausen's own free labs repo (cloned locally at C:\opt\learn\terraform\repos\terraform-associate-labs). Lab 01 (getting started) + Lab 05 (state/data/CLI) cover this loop. Best free match — it's the paid course's hands-on content, open-sourced. ⚠️ Its README says to create a Codespace from that repo and promises a pre-configured container, but the repo has no .devcontainer — the badge points at a separate btkrausen/terraform-codespaces repository. Expect to install Terraform yourself, or use the local clone. (krausen-labs-facts)
  • HCTut Get Started (step 1 above) is the official free 1:1 — it is the init→plan→apply→destroy walkthrough.
  • KK — KodeKloud free labs / Coursera "Terraform for the Absolute Beginner" run the loop in-browser with no cloud account. B3-relevant labs: HCL Basics (first init→plan→apply→destroy) + Terraform Commands (fmt/validate/show/output surface); the Update and Destroy Infrastructure lesson pairs with HCL Basics.
  • FCC — freeCodeCamp's full Terraform Associate course on YouTube (free lecture+lab video).
  • CLX — Collabnix Terraform Hands-on Labs (free, open, init-plan-apply).

📌 Force a rebuild with -replace

To force one resource to be destroyed and recreated, use terraform apply -replace=ADDRESS (exactly 0.15.2). This supersedes terraform taint / untaint — which date to 0.4.0, April 2015, and mutated state out-of-band; -replace shows the recreation in the plan first, so you review it before it happens. Six years separate the two, which is why so much older material still teaches taint. (See feature-history, release-feature-map.)

📌 Two reference pages for “when did this land?”

feature-history and opentofu-feature-history give the headline feature per release and are what the callouts in this path cite. When you need the exhaustive answer, release-feature-map (Terraform 0.1.0 → 1.16.0) and opentofu-release-feature-map (1.6 → 1.13) are built from every version branch's CHANGELOG.md, plus a schema diff across release tags for things the changelog never announced.

Why the precision matters here: features routinely land in patch releases, and dating one to its minor is a common way to be wrong. for_each on resources is 0.12.6, not 0.12.0. try/can are 0.12.20. terraform login is 0.12.21. The locals block is 0.10.3. Provider network mirrors are 0.13.2, output -raw is 0.14.3, -replace is 0.15.2, and -refresh-only is 0.15.4. If a required_version constraint has to be exact, check there rather than assuming the x.y.0.

📌 Lock-file checksums across platforms

The lock file records provider checksums. Use terraform providers lock to record hashes for all platforms (not just yours) so CI on Linux and a dev laptop on macOS agree. OpenTofu 1.12 does this automatically at tofu init (full cross-platform zh:+h1: set). Cross-platform mismatches are a classic "works on my machine" init failure. (See feature-history, opentofu-feature-history.)

Two ways to land in that failure, per tf-dependency-lock. Installing a provider for the first time from a filesystem or network mirror means Terraform can only verify checksums for the platform it ran on, so it records only those — the config is then unusable elsewhere. Installing from an origin registry with signed checksums avoids this, because Terraform accepts the whole signed set and records every platform's hashes at once. The h1: entries that keep appearing in your diffs afterwards are Terraform migrating from the legacy zh: (zip-archive hash) to h1: (package-contents hash) as it sees the provider on new platforms.

📌 Already captured — core-workflow

The cross-source synthesis of this topic, HCDocs read against TID Ch 1 §1.4 and Ch 5. The useful disagreement it records: HCDocs names the loop Write → Plan → Apply, while TID expands it to five boxes — change desired → init → plan → review → apply — because init is a separately observable phase that the three-word version folds into "Write". It also breaks plan into the subphases the docs gloss: Refresh (read real state and data sources) → Compare (diff against configuration) → Plan (build the DAG of actions), and notes that circular dependencies break the DAG model and need manual workarounds, which the intro-level docs never mention.

📖 Deep-dive: how the plan is actually computed

The four-command loop is the what; the how is the plan engine. TID Ch 5 ("The Terraform plan") is the definitive treatment — captured as 05-terraform-plan: the resource graph (DAG) Terraform builds and walks, the plan-output symbols (+/-/~/-/+, (known after apply), read bottom-up), the three planning modes (default / destroy / refresh-only, each starting with a refresh), the two apply paths (own-plan vs saved-plan file), -replace vs deprecated taint, -target (an antipattern), and the graph-born pitfalls (cycles, cascading replacements, hidden deps). Cross-book synthesis in The dependency graph and Core workflow.

Milestone: You can read a terraform plan and correctly predict what each +/~/-/+ line will do before running apply.

items.title: ✅ B4 — HCL language basics
items.text:
What it is: HashiCorp Configuration Language — blocks, arguments, primitive/collection types, comments, and the top-level block kinds (terraform, provider, resource, variable, output, locals, data, module).

Why you need it: Every .tf file is HCL; fluency here is the difference between copying snippets and writing configuration.

How to learn it:

  1. Reference — HCDocs "Configuration Syntax" (~40 min) — read blocks/arguments/expressions; this is short and canonical. Captured as tf-config-syntax (arguments vs blocks, labels, identifiers, comments, UTF-8/line-endings). Pair it with the official Style Guide for idiomatic naming, file layout, and formatting conventions (guidance, not a feature — but it's what "writing it right" means), captured as tf-style-guide (formatting/fmt, naming, param order, file layout, .gitignore, version pinning, module/repo structure, secrets, testing, policy). The official guide tells you the rules; for the toolchain that enforces them, see code-styling from Anton Babenko's community book — pre-commit + terraform_fmt, .editorconfig, and terraform-docs, none of which HashiCorp's page mentions.

  2. Book chapter — TID Ch 2 §2.2 "Block syntax" (~1.5 hrs) — the language deep-dive (block types, labels/subtypes, arguments vs subblocks, attributes, ordering, style); work the examples in an editor. (Captured notes: 02-hcl-components.)

  3. Interactive — rewrite your B2 project (~1 hr) — split it into main.tf / variables.tf / outputs.tf by convention.
  4. Reference — the language's own spec, when the docs are vague (~20 min, as needed) — HCL is specified in spec.md (the syntax-agnostic information model) and hclsyntax/spec.md (the native syntax), both in hashicorp/hcl and cloned at C:\opt\learn\terraform\repos\hcl. Reach for them when a docs page paraphrases rather than defines — identifier grammar, what <<- actually strips, which templates get backslash escapes, why a strip marker doesn't trim an interpolated value. Facts already extracted, plus the fact that Terraform and OpenTofu build against different HCL code, in hcl-library-facts.

📌 Style is enforced by tooling, not by discipline

terraform fmt is "intentionally opinionated and non-configurable", which is the point — a uniform format lets reviewers argue about substance instead of layout. But fmt only runs when someone runs it. Three pieces close that gap, and none are in HashiCorp's style guide (code-styling):

  • pre-commit with the terraform_fmt hook from antonbabenko/pre-commit-terraform, so formatting happens before the commit rather than in review. Pin the rev: and expect it to age.
  • terraform fmt -check in CI — exits 0 when everything is formatted and non-zero with the offending filenames otherwise, which is what makes it a gate rather than a suggestion. Wired into the pipeline in A3.
  • .editorconfig — the layer fmt cannot reach. fmt never touches non-.tf files, so a repo with a Makefile still needs something to stop an editor writing spaces where tabs are required.

One convention worth knowing is not HashiCorp's: delimiting section headers in code with # ----- or ######. Both sources agree on # over // and block comments, but the header style is the community book's own, and nothing in the toolchain enforces it.

fmt is also a parser, which makes it a cheaper first gate than its name suggests. It cannot rewrite what it cannot read, so on a broken configuration it reports the files it did reformat and then prints ordinary HCL diagnostics for the ones it could not — Error: Invalid character / Error: Invalid expression, with line numbers (tut-troubleshooting-workflow). The boundary against validate is the page's own: "terraform fmt only parses your HCL for interpolation errors or malformed resource definitions, which is why you should use terraform validate after formatting your configuration to check your configuration in the context of the providers' expectations." That context is provider schemas, which is why validate needs init first and fmt does not.

TID Ch 7 assembles all three pieces into one arrangement, and adds the convention that makes them coherent: every tool gets a pair of makefile targets, one that changes files (fmt, terraform-docs) and one that only checks (fmt -check, terraform-docs --output-check) and exits non-zero. The check form is the gate; the change form is the convenience — and because CI invokes the same target name, "runs locally" and "passes CI" stop being separate claims. The .editorconfig point above is literally this chapter's first footgun: Make requires a tab to indent commands, and spaces are an error. Full toolchain in A3.

📌 JSON-equivalent syntax

HCL has a JSON-equivalent syntax — *.tf.json and *.tfvars.json are parsed the same as .tf/.tfvars. You rarely hand-write it, but it's the format machine-generated configs (codegen, other tools) emit, so recognize it. (See feature-history.) Full treatment in TID Ch11 §11.2: one JSON object per file with block labels becoming nesting, the list form for blocks that may repeat under one name (provider with aliases), every expression written as a string template — which is the real constraint, since generated logic can then only produce strings — and a "//" key accepted in any object, worth using for a do-not-edit header and per-object provenance.

📌 Override files

A file named override.tf or ending _override.tf (HCDocs) is loaded last and merges its blocks into matching ones, replacing set arguments. Handy for local/temporary tweaks; use sparingly since it hides config from the primary files.

🧪 Labs (KK)

KodeKloud — Terraform HCL free lab — the dedicated HCL blocks/arguments lab, the exact B4 topic. (Krausen's KL labs have no B4 lab — lab 01 is setup, lab 02 jumps straight to a first resource; they skip pure syntax.)

Milestone: You can author a multi-file HCL configuration by hand, using the correct block type for each purpose, without copy-paste.

items.title: ✅ B5 — Providers & resources
items.text:
What it is: How the provider plugin model works, resource blocks, resource addresses, arguments vs attributes, and the resource dependency graph Terraform builds implicitly.

Why you need it: Resources are the unit of everything Terraform manages; understanding implicit dependencies (via attribute references) is essential to avoid ordering bugs.

How to learn it:

  1. Video — TF2026 "Lifecycle & Providers" → "Resources" (43:15, ~45 min) — see how a provider's resources map to real cloud APIs.
  2. Reference — a real provider's docs (e.g. AWS provider) (~ongoing) — learn to navigate the registry docs for arguments/attributes. See aws-provider and google-provider for captured overviews (example usage, credential precedence, key provider arguments) — and the Providers topic page for an AWS-vs-GCP config/auth comparison. For the resource block how-to (address, timeouts, meta-arg map, built-in/local-only resources) see tf-configure-resource. (Resources — captured as tf-resources, dependencies) The section overview is captured as tf-providers — provider tiers on the Registry (official / partner / community), the plugin cache, .netrc credentials for private registries, and where provider documentation lives versus where the plugin comes from. See tf-aws-create for the resource-address / type-name / implicit-reference walkthrough on a real aws_instance, and tut-resource (Configuration Language tutorial) for the explicit arguments vs attributes vs meta-arguments taxonomy plus a random_pet + aws_security_group build (vpc_security_group_ids as a list, reading the Registry argument reference).
  3. Book chapter — TID Ch 2 §2.4–2.5 + §2.7.3, and Ch 5 §5.1–5.2 (~1 hr) — providers and resources, then implicit vs explicit dependencies and how the graph is derived (Ch 5 is the DAG chapter). An attribute reference is the dependency edge; see dependency-graph for the two inputs the DAG is built from, and why nothing warns when one is missing.

🧪 Labs

  • KL: Lab 03 — variables & outputs · Lab 04 — managing multiple resources.
  • KK: KodeKloud free labs — Terraform Providers · Multiple Providers · Resource Attributes · Resource Dependencies.

Milestone: You can chain three resources where each references the previous one's attributes, and explain the resulting apply order without depends_on.

items.title: ✅ B6 — Input variables, outputs & locals
items.text:
What it is: Parameterizing configs with variable (types, defaults, .tfvars, env vars, precedence), exposing values with output, and computing intermediates with locals.

Why you need it: Hard-coded configs can't be reused across environments; variables/outputs are how modules and pipelines pass data.

How to learn it:

  1. Interactive — HCTut "Manage infrastructure" (input variables + outputs) (~1 hr) — work the variables + outputs sections; try all variable-passing methods. (Captured in tf-aws-manage — variables.tf/outputs.tf split, -var on the CLI, terraform output.) For a deeper variables-only hands-on covering every type (string/number/bool/list/map + structural), .tfvars files, multiple validation blocks, and live terraform console debugging, see tut-variables (Configuration Language collection).
  2. Reference — HCDocs "Input Variables" precedence table (~20 min) — memorize the override order (CLI > env > .tfvars > default). (Captured in tf-input-variables — full precedence table, sensitive/ephemeral, validation, undeclared-variable behavior, and the const attribute for init-time evaluation. The argument-level spec — every variable argument, reserved names, type/validation/nullable/deprecated — is in tf-block-variable.) (outputs — captured in tf-outputs: the four purposes, module.<child>.<output> access, and sensitive/ephemeral outputs — with the full argument spec (type, precondition, depends_on, deprecated) in tf-block-output, and the hands-on terraform output / -raw / -json workflow in tut-outputs; locals — captured in tf-locals: locals block vs singular local. reference, module-only scope, and the readability tradeoff; hands-on in tut-locals — the merge(var.tags, local.required_tags) minimum-tags pattern and the locals-can-be-dynamic-but-variables-must-be-literal contrast; the block-level spec — multiple locals blocks per module, identifier rules, and the singular-local.-vs-plural-locals split — is in tf-block-locals)
  3. Book chapter — TID Ch 3 (variables/outputs/locals) (~45 min) — when to use locals vs variable.
  4. Book chapter — TUR Ch 2 (variables and outputs sections) (~20 min) — the shortest honest motivation for variables in any source here: a port number written twice, once in a security group and once in a boot script. Captured as 02-getting-started. Also the clearest statement of the output depends_on case (an IP that is useless until a firewall rule exists, with no reference linking them) and the scripting loop apply → terraform output → curl. ⚠️ Its variable argument list predates nullable, ephemeral, const and deprecated, and it writes bare list/map, which are compatibility shorthand for list(any)/map(any) — step 2 above is the current list.

📌 Output type (Terraform 1.15)

Terraform 1.15 added a type attribute to output blocks — outputs can now carry the same type constraints (and documentation value) variables always have. Prefer typing the outputs of any module others consume: the constraint is checked, and it documents the interface. There is a second-order effect worth knowing but not worth overselling: a fully-typed output set makes module.<NAME> a real list/map under count/for_each instead of a tuple/object (GetModule branches on "does the module fully define all output types"; verified 1.15.8, Ch 7 §3). Callers almost never notice, because a tuple splats, converts, and satisfies a list(object(...)) constraint just as a list does — the gain is exactness and clearer errors, not new capability. Resources have no such switch, always structural (Ch 7 §3). OpenTofu has no typed outputs (TF-only as of OT 1.12.4). Evidence: conditional-branch-evaluation. (See tf115-ot112-features; the full output argument spec is in tf-block-output.)

📌 nullable variable argument (TF 1.1)

The nullable variable argument (TF 1.1) controls whether a caller may pass null. Set nullable = false to forbid it (and fall back to the default when null is supplied) — useful for required-but-defaulted inputs. (See feature-history.)

🧪 Labs

  • KL: Lab 03 — variables & outputs · Lab 07 — local values.
  • KK: KodeKloud free labs — Variables · Using Variables in Terraform · Output Variables.

Milestone: You can parameterize your project so the same config deploys to two environments by swapping only a .tfvars file.

items.title: ✅ B7 — Expressions, operators & built-in functions
items.text:
What it is: HCL expressions — references, conditionals (? :), for expressions, splat, string templates — and the built-in function library (for_each helpers, lookup, merge, try, coalesce, templatefile, etc.).

Why you need it: Dynamic, DRY configuration is impossible without expressions; the exam and real modules lean on them constantly.

How to learn it:

  1. Interactive — terraform console (~1 hr) — open the REPL and experiment with for, merge, try, string templates against live values. tut-variables shows the console workflow concretely (list indexing, slice(), map key lookup) plus regexall() in validation and ${} string interpolation. (Gotcha: the console loads config only at startup — restart to pick up edits. And it takes the state lock, so no plan or apply can run while a session is open — a forgotten console in another terminal is a plausible cause of a lock error. For a guided hands-on rather than free experimentation, HCTut "Develop configuration with the console" (~13 min, AWS, not free-tier) uses the REPL to author rather than to look things up — captured as tut-console, with the JSON pattern below.)
  2. Reference — HCDocs "Functions" + "Expressions" (~40 min) — skim the function categories; bookmark for lookup. The conditional (ternary) cond ? a : b is captured in tf-conditionals — both result values must share a type (else auto-convert; prefer explicit tostring()), plus the condition-building cookbook (contains, length(...) != 0 over == [], for + alltrue/anytrue, and can() to turn an error-throwing expression into a bool). This page is the exhaustive function list, captured as tf-functions — the full built-in catalogue linked by category (numeric, string, collection, encoding, filesystem, date/time, hash/crypto, IP, type conversion, provider-defined provider::terraform::*), each row marking whether Stacks config (.tfcomponent.hcl/.tfdeploy.hcl) supports it, plus the terraform console experimentation note. The path teaches the skill of using functions, not each of the ~150 individually; treat tf-functions + feature-history as the complete catalogue (e.g. strcontains/plantimestamp landed in 1.5, templatestring in 1.9). terraform metadata functions -json (TF 1.4+) dumps every function's signature machine-readably — mostly for editor/language-server tooling. The Expressions section is captured page-by-page, mirroring the HCDocs sidebar: tf-expressions (section overview — the expression kinds and terraform console), tf-expr-types (types & values, null, auto-conversion), tf-expr-strings (string literals, heredocs, ${}/%{} template interpolation & directives, whitespace stripping), tf-expr-references (referencing resources/vars/locals/path.*/terraform.workspace, plus unknown/sensitive values), tf-expr-operators (arithmetic/equality/comparison/logical + order of operations — note the var.list == [] tuple([]) gotcha), tf-expr-function-calls (call syntax, ... argument expansion, sensitive-argument propagation, plan-time vs apply-time file/timestamp/uuid), tf-expr-for (for transforms, if filtering, grouping mode with ..., element ordering), and tf-expr-splat (the [*] splat shorthand for for, single-value-as-list for optional null inputs in dynamic for_each, and the legacy .* form to avoid).
  3. Book chapter — TID Ch 4 (Expressions and iterations) (~1.5 hrs) — TID's dedicated expressions/functions/iteration chapter: operators, standard-library + provider-defined functions, string templates, regex, type conversion, try/can, and for/splat. Captured as 04-expressions-iterations. (A B7-adjacent pitfall — the plan-time-known limit on computed values in count/for_each — is captured from the plan side in 05-terraform-plan §5.7 Calculated values and iterations; it belongs mostly to I1.)

🔧 Decode to author, encode to submit — the JSON pattern for policy documents

Every cloud's IAM policies arrive as JSON, and the provider wants them back as a JSON string. Hand-editing that string forfeits everything HCL gives you. tut-console's round trip keeps it:

echo 'jsondecode(file("bucket_policy.json"))' | terraform console

That prints the vendor's JSON as HCL. Paste it into a jsonencode({ … }) in the resource and replace the placeholders with real references — "<BUCKET_ARN>/*" becomes "${aws_s3_bucket.data.arn}/*", which is a genuine dependency edge a string literal could never be. jsondecode once at authoring time; jsonencode on every plan.

The payoff shows up in the diff. Terraform special-cases jsonencode in the plan renderer and expands the structure — + Action = [ + "s3:GetObject", … ] line by line — where a here-doc string would diff as one unreadable blob.

Do not carry the same trick into outputs. After using jsonencode in the console to verify the shape, the tutorial defines the output as a plain map and reaches for terraform output -json instead, because "when you include the -json flag […] Terraform converts maps and lists to the equivalent JSON data structures." Encoding inside the output would yield a JSON string nested inside JSON — doubly escaped and useless downstream. The machine-readable form belongs on the command, not in the configuration (tf-cmd-output, tf-cli-inspect).

📌 The console is the cheapest type checker you have

Printing a resource address in the console renders values with their cty types attached — tolist([]), toset([…]), tomap(null) /* of string */, tostring(null), null /* object */. terraform show does not do this, and an empty list and an empty set are otherwise indistinguishable in output while behaving differently under contains() and indexing.

Worth reaching for whenever a type error is the suspected cause. tut-troubleshooting-workflow's central exercise — a splat expression feeding for_each, which needs a map or set of strings and got a list — is a question the console answers in one line. (See tut-console, tf-expr-type-constraints.)

📌 convert() (Terraform 1.15 — Terraform-only)

Terraform 1.15 added the convert(value, type) function for precise inline type conversion — cleaner than the old tolist/tomap/toset juggling in tricky spots. Terraform-only — OpenTofu has no convert() (request opentofu #2630, filed 2025-03-25, closed completed 2026-08-13 — convert is now in OpenTofu main via opentofu#4449 and lands in 1.13.0, but git tag --contains on the introducing commit returns nothing and the newest tag is v1.12.5, so it is in no released version; the statement holds for every installable OpenTofu today and expires when 1.13 ships). What OpenTofu lacks is the function, not the capability: convert() is an inline shortcut for the machinery every type = constraint already runs, so a typed variable (root or module input) performs the identical coercion, extra object attributes discarded and all (verified on OpenTofu 1.12.4). The toType casters cover primitives and collections in both tools, but they cannot express an object/tuple schema — so the portable answer there is a declared boundary, not a caster. OpenTofu has no typed output either (that's TF 1.15+), so a variable is the boundary you get. Evidence: conditional-branch-evaluation. (See tf115-ot112-features.)

📌 The type system — collection vs structural, and why only two types have a literal

The two families are defined by HCL's own spec, not by Terraform docs convention: collection types (list/map/set) "combine together an arbitrary number of values of some other single type"; structural types (tuple/object) are "constructed by combining other types", each position or key carrying its own type. Everything else follows. Brackets always build a tuple, braces always build an object — there is no list, set, or map literal anywhere in the language. A collection needs one shared element type the syntax never states, so it needs unification, which needs a target type to aim at: a type = constraint, a provider schema, or an explicit to* call. Hence there is no totuple()/toobject() — the three collection casters exist precisely because those are the three types you can't write down. The spec's type-identity rules are the root of the var.list == [] gotcha (a list(string) and a tuple([]) are simply different types) and of a tuple's length being part of its type. Ch 7 §2 covers the value side; the constraint side (type =, optional()) is I3. Evidence: conditional-branch-evaluation.

📌 Provider-defined functions (TF 1.8)

Beyond the built-ins, provider-defined functions (TF 1.8) let a provider ship its own functions, called as provider::<name>::<fn>(...) — e.g. provider::aws::arn_parse(...). Available in the AWS, Google, and Kubernetes providers among others. Authoring them is E1. (See feature-coverage-matrix.)

📌 templatestring() (Terraform 1.9)

Terraform 1.9 added templatestring(ref, vars) — like templatefile(), but renders a template string obtained at runtime (e.g. from a data source) instead of a file on disk. (See feature-history.)

📌 Short-circuit && / || (OpenTofu 1.10, Terraform 1.12)

Logical operators now short-circuit (&&/|| stop evaluating once the result is decided), so guards like var.x != null && var.x.enabled no longer error on the null case. OpenTofu shipped it first in 1.10; Terraform followed in 1.12. Boolean-only — the ternary ? : still type-checks both branches. (See feature-history.)

📌 Built-in named values

Learn the built-in named values you can reference anywhere: path.module / path.root / path.cwd (filesystem paths, e.g. for templatefile), terraform.workspace (current CLI workspace name), count.index, each.key / each.value (inside count/for_each), self (inside provisioners), and terraform.applying (ephemeral bool, true during apply; TF 1.10). (HCDocs references)

🧪 Labs (KK)

None in the Basics course — KodeKloud covers functions/conditional expressions in a later section with no standalone lab; practice in terraform console (step 1) instead.

Milestone: You can transform a list of maps into a keyed map with a for expression and use it to drive resource creation.

items.title: ✅ B8 — Data sources
items.text:
What it is: data blocks that read existing infrastructure or provider info (AMI IDs, availability zones, existing VPCs) without managing it.

Why you need it: Real configs must reference things Terraform doesn't own; data sources are how you look them up at plan time.

How to learn it:

  1. Reference — HCDocs "Data Sources" (~20 min) — the block syntax and when data is read (plan vs apply). Notes: tf-data-sources — the plan-vs-apply deferral rules, custom conditions, count/for_each on data blocks, aliased providers; tf-block-data — the argument catalog (which meta-arguments a data block takes, lifecycle limited to pre/postcondition).
  2. Interactive — HCDocs "Query data sources" tutorial (~45 min) — the official hands-on: replace hard-coded region/AZ/AMI with aws_availability_zones / aws_region / aws_ami lookups, and wire a two-workspace VPC→app stack together with terraform_remote_state. Notes: tut-data-sources. The data "aws_ami" filter pattern also appears in tf-aws-create.
  3. Book chapter — TID Ch 2 §2.6 "Data sources" (~30 min) — dependency implications of data reads. (Captured notes: 02-hcl-components.)
  4. Book chapter — TUR Ch 2 (the ASG subnets section) (~15 min) — data sources arriving as the answer to a concrete problem: an Auto Scaling Group needs subnet IDs, and hardcoding them "won't be maintainable or portable". Captured as 02-getting-started. Two framings worth keeping — the arguments are search filters, not settings, and data. is simply a prefix on the resource reference grammar you already know. ⚠️ Read it against the chapter's own hardcoded, region-locked AMI ID, which is the textbook case for an aws_ami data source and which the chapter never converts.

📌 List resources + terraform query (TF 1.14)

Beyond point lookups, Terraform 1.14 added list resources (defined in *.tfquery.hcl files) and the terraform query command — you can enumerate and filter existing infrastructure a provider knows about, not just read one known object like a data source does. Useful for discovery/inventory ahead of an import. Newer than both books and the 004 exam; verify against the CHANGELOG. (See feature-history.)

🧪 Labs

  • KL: Lab 05 — state, data sources & CLI (data-source section).
  • KK: KodeKloud free labs — Datasources.

Milestone: You can look up a resource you didn't create (e.g. the latest AMI or default VPC) and wire it into a managed resource.

items.title: 🔄 B9 — State fundamentals
items.text:
What it is: What terraform.tfstate is, why Terraform needs it (mapping config → real resources), what's in it, and why it must be protected and never hand-edited.

Why you need it: State is Terraform's source of truth; almost every advanced problem (drift, imports, backends, locking) is a state problem.

How to learn it:

  1. Video — Krausen "Terraform Associate 004 Exam Prep" (state section) (~30 min) — why state exists and what breaks without it. The written version of the same argument is HCDocs "Purpose of Terraform State", captured in tf-state-purpose: real-world mapping (and the abandoned AWS-tag prototype), retained dependencies for destroy ordering (the reason TID Ch6 §6.1 omits), the attribute cache as the explicitly optional part, and syncing/locking.
  2. Reference — HCDocs "State" overview + "Sensitive Data in State" (~30 min) — note that state can hold secrets in plaintext. Overview captured in tf-state: bindings between remote objects and resource instances as state's primary purpose, the one-to-one mapping rule and the two operations that break it (terraform import, terraform state rm), the no-version-control warning, and terraform output -json / terraform show -json as the supported way for external software to read a snapshot.
  3. Book chapter — TID Ch 6 (state) (~1 hr) — anatomy of the state file; read but don't edit it.
  4. Book chapter — TUR Ch 3 (~1 hr) — the same topic argued from consequences rather than anatomy: state exists, therefore it must be shared, therefore locked, therefore isolated, therefore your repository has a shape. Captured as 03-manage-state. The definition to keep is that a plan is "a diff between the code on your computer and the infrastructure deployed in the real world, as discovered via IDs in the state file". ⚠️ Its locking setup is obsolete on both engines — see the use_lockfile callout under I6 — and its sensitive-plus-TF_VAR_ secret handling still writes the password to state in plaintext. Cross-source synthesis: State.

🧪 Labs

  • KL: Lab 05 — state, data sources & CLI (state + CLI sections).
  • KK: KodeKloud free labs — Terraform State (purpose of state, state considerations).

Milestone: You can open a state file, explain how a resource address maps to a real cloud object, and articulate three reasons never to edit it by hand.

🔄 Chapter written 2026-07-30, one claim superseded 2026-08-28

Ch 9: State fundamentals — Terraform 1.16 added -json to terraform state show, which undercuts the chapter's “explicitly not a machine interface” framing. The chapter now carries a dated revisit box; the surrounding distinction between rendered and specified output still holds, and nothing else in it is affected. Flip back to ✅ once the section is rewritten rather than annotated.

✅ Chapter written — Ch 9: State fundamentals (2026-07-30)

Blends tf-state, tf-state-purpose, 06-state-management §6.1–6.3/§6.6, tf-manage-sensitive-data, and the inspection-command notes (tf-cmd-state-list, tf-cmd-state-show, tf-cmd-show, tf-cmd-output, tf-cmd-refresh). Lab verified end-to-end on TF 1.15.8 against the emulator: a no-op apply still bumping serial, the sensitive output stored in plaintext and readable with a flagless named query, and state list -id= resolving a bucket name back to its address. Re-audited 2026-07-31 on TF 1.15.8 and OpenTofu 1.12.4: the old resources + 1 rule for serial was wrong and is gone — the count is timing-dependent (identical runs landed on 1, 1, 1, 4), and OpenTofu writes once where Terraform writes several.

items.title: ✅ Beginner Checkpoint
items.text: You are ready to advance when you can: - Provision, modify, and destroy a multi-resource config against a real cloud provider from a clean directory. - Parameterize that config with variables/outputs so it deploys to two environments. - Read a plan accurately and explain what state is and why it matters.

items.title: Intermediate
items.text: Goal: Build reusable modules, manage remote state safely, and handle real-world state operations — the level the Associate 004 exam validates. Estimated time: ~45 hrs

items.title: ✅ I1 — Meta-arguments: count, for_each, depends_on
items.text:
What it is: Creating multiple instances with count and for_each, addressing them ([0] vs ["key"]), and forcing ordering with explicit depends_on.

Why you need it: Real infra needs N-of-a-thing; choosing count vs for_each correctly prevents the classic "changing the list re-creates everything" bug.

How to learn it:

  1. Video — TF2026 "Loops & Dynamic Infrastructure" (3:06:31, ~40 min) — see why for_each is safer than count for keyed resources.
  2. Reference — HCDocs "Meta-arguments" index (~10 min) — what the class is (core-defined, not provider-defined) and the six members. Notes: tf-meta-arguments.
  3. Reference — HCDocs "count" + "for_each" + depends_on (~30 min) — the addressing rules and when each is legal. Notes: tf-meta-count, tf-meta-for-each, tf-meta-depends-on. From the for_each page, memorize: each.key / each.value, identical for a set; keys must be known, cannot come from impure functions (uuid, bcrypt, timestamp), and cannot be sensitive — an error, because keys are always disclosed in UI output; lists and tuples are not implicitly converted, so toset() is mandatory and is lossy (drops order, dedupes); and a for_each resource can be chained into another's for_each, which couples their instance keys structurally rather than coincidentally. From the count page, memorize: count.index is zero-based; the block address (aws_instance.server) and the instance address (aws_instance.server[0]) are different things, and a block with no count/for_each needs no index at all; self inside provisioner/connection is the instance; count must be known before any remote operation, so it can never depend on a post-apply attribute. Read its silences too — it never warns that count keys by position, and never says the block reference is a tuple, not a list.
  4. Interactive — HCTut "Manage similar resources with count" (~10 min, also served at /tutorials/0-13/count) — refactor two hard-coded EC2 instances into one count block sized by var.instances_per_subnet * length(module.vpc.private_subnets), placed round-robin with count.index % length(...), then wired into a load balancer via a splat. Notes: tut-count. Two things to take from it beyond the syntax: the rename app_a → app costs "8 added, 0 changed, 4 destroyed" because a resource address is its state identity — a moved block (TF 1.1+) is the fix, and the tutorial never mentions one; and its aws_instance.app.*.id is the legacy splat, which you should write as [*] (tf-expr-splat). ⚠️ Pins are years stale (AWS provider ~> 4.22, vpc module 3.14.2) and the page's own elb_http snippet references this_security_group_id, an output name dropped in security-group module v4.0 — its example repo is correct, the rendered snippet is not.
  5. Interactive — HCTut "Manage similar resources with for_each" (~15 min) — continues the previous tutorial's config, refactoring one project into many by iterating a map(any) of project records. Notes: tut-for-each. The thing to take from it: count and for_each are illegal in the same block, so move the count resource into a module and put for_each on the module block — the only documented way to multiply on two axes, and neither reference page mentions it. With it comes a constraint: a module using count/for_each cannot declare a provider block and must inherit from its caller, so this buys multiplication but not multi-provider fan-out. ⚠️ Two of its statements are wrong — "the for_each argument also supports lists" (lists and tuples are rejected outright) and "each.key is the index of the item" for sets (it is the member string; each.key == each.value); both re-verified on TF 1.15.8. Its own Note also warns against using for_each for independently-lifecycled environments, which is exactly what its example does.
  6. Interactive — HCTut "Create resource dependencies" (~10 min) — the depends_on lab: an Elastic IP implicitly ordered behind one EC2 instance while a second instance runs in parallel, then an explicit depends_on on both a resource and a module block. Notes: tut-dependencies — read the apply and destroy logs, not just the config. Interleaved Creating... lines mean Terraform thinks those nodes are independent, so the log is a free dependency check. It also names the second cost of depends_on that the reference page omits: longer apply wall-clock time from serialized work, on top of the degraded plan. ⚠️ The example config pins AWS provider ~> 4.17.1 and writes vpc = true on aws_eip; that argument was removed in provider v6.0.0 — use domain = "vpc" in anything you write yourself.
  7. Practice — inspect the DAG (~20 min) — run terraform graph on a config with one implicit edge and one depends_on, then delete the depends_on and watch the edge vanish while validate still passes. Notes: dependency-graph, tf-cmd-graph.
  8. Book chapter — TID Ch 4 §4.8 "count and for_each" (~1 hr) — the re-creation/reindex pitfall and how for_each keys avoid it; depends_on is Ch 2 §2.7.3. (Captured notes: 04-expressions-iterations. The plan-side angle — the plan-time-known constraint (§5.7) and the resource graph the meta-args expand into (§5.2) — is in 05-terraform-plan.)
  9. Book chapter — TUR Ch 5 (the Loops half, ~1 hr) — captured as 05-tips-and-tricks. The same reindex pitfall, but shown as a plan: drop the middle of a three-item list and Terraform renames one IAM user and destroys another, because index is identity. It also carries the rule that inverts the usual advice — for_each for copies, count for conditionals, since a count that is only ever 0 or 1 has no middle to remove — and the one(concat(a[*], b[*])) idiom for reading an attribute off whichever of two count-gated resources exists.

📌 for_each accepts a map, an object, or a set of strings — the error message and the docs omit the object

Both the "must be a map, or set of strings" error and HashiCorp's for_each page list only maps and sets of strings. The implementation checks three kinds — map, set, and object — and accepts all of them (internal/terraform/eval_for_each.go:361, verified on TF 1.15.8). OpenTofu's docs get this right (ot-provider-for-each: "must be a map, object, or set of strings"). It matters because braces build an object, not a map, so for_each = { a = "1", b = "2" } works with no tomap(). It also converts nothing: a list(string) and a bare ["p","q"] tuple are both rejected outright (the docs are explicit that lists/tuples are not implicitly converted to sets), which is why toset(...) is mandatory. Finally, "of strings" binds only to the set — only keys become instance addresses, so a map/object may hold values of any type (for_each = { a = 1, b = "x" } plans fine). Evidence: conditional-branch-evaluation.

count and for_each are mutually exclusive

You cannot use both in the same resource or module block. Choose by shape: count for nearly identical instances derived from an integer index, for_each when some instance arguments need distinct values an index can't produce.

Both are legal on data blocks. The meta-arguments index page omits data from its count list, but the count reference page names data, ephemeral, module, resource, and list (query configs). Trust the per-argument reference. (See tf-meta-arguments.)

Nothing warns you about a missing depends_on

The DAG is built from expression references plus the depends_on you write. A dependency Terraform can't see does not exist to it, so plan, validate, and the provider all stay silent. Verified on v1.15.6: deleting a depends_on drops the edge from terraform graph while validate still reports success.

The failure lands at apply, usually as a race — passes locally, fails in CI, or fails once and succeeds on rerun. Worst case it "succeeds" and the object is semantically broken (the docs' EC2-instance-can't-reach-S3 example).

Counterweight: depends_on is a last resort, not a safety blanket. It forces more values to (known after apply) and replaces more resources than necessary, especially on module blocks. Prefer an attribute reference wherever one exists. (See dependency-graph, tf-meta-depends-on.)

Counterweight to the counterweight — know the case it is for. In the fixed S3 module of tut-module-create, aws_s3_bucket_acl must be applied after aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls and aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, but it consumes no attribute from either, so there is nothing to reference. Ordering with no data flow between the two resources is precisely where depends_on earns its place; "prefer an attribute reference" presumes one exists.

📌 OpenTofu — enabled (1.11)

OpenTofu 1.11 adds enabled, a first-class on/off switch for a resource, cleaner than the count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0 idiom (which forces [0] addressing and index churn). OpenTofu-only; in Terraform you still use the count trick.

It is an argument inside the lifecycle block, not a seventh top-level meta-argument — earlier notes here said otherwise. At the resource top level OpenTofu errors with "An argument named enabled is not expected here." A disabled resource evaluates to null, not an empty collection, and the address never gains an index. Verified empirically on OpenTofu 1.12.4: opentofu-enabled-argument.

🧪 Labs (KL)

Lab 04 — managing multiple resources · Lab 08 — deploying multiple resources with for_each.

Milestone: You can convert a count-based set of resources to for_each and explain why removing a middle element no longer destroys unrelated resources.

items.title: ✅ I2 — The lifecycle meta-argument
items.text:
What it is: lifecycle blocks — create_before_destroy, prevent_destroy, ignore_changes, replace_triggered_by, plus the two condition rules (precondition/postcondition → A2) and action_trigger (→ A1) — and how each alters the plan.

Why you need it: Zero-downtime replacements, protecting stateful resources, and ignoring externally-managed drift all depend on lifecycle rules.

How to learn it:

  1. Reference — HCDocs "lifecycle" meta-argument (~30 min) — each option and its plan effect. Notes: tf-meta-lifecycle — the state semantics (only create_before_destroy is recorded), CBD propagating to dependencies and silently overriding any attempt to switch it back off, ignore_changes being honored on create and ignored only on update, the three replace_triggered_by trigger conditions, and the precondition/postcondition ordering guarantees.
  2. Interactive — HCTut "Manage resource lifecycle" (~8 min stated, budget ~45 with AWS) — one exercise per rule on an EC2 instance plus security group. Notes: tut-resource-lifecycle. What it gives that the reference cannot: the prevent_destroy rejection text (an error with no override flag, and -target as the sanctioned escape), the plan symbol flip from -/+ to +/- create replacement and then destroy, the deposed object line in the apply log, and drift manufactured with aws ec2 create-tags so ignore_changes can be seen refreshing state to the drifted value. ⚠️ Written against Terraform 0.14 and AWS provider 3.26.0 — the rules are unchanged but two output formats have moved on, and one code block typos drift_example as Drift_example.
  3. Interactive — experiment (~30 min) — extend the tutorial's config: confirm CBD propagated to the security group without being written there, then force the security group to be replaced rather than updated in-place and watch the name collision that propagation causes.
  4. Book chapter — TID Ch 2 §2.7.2 "Lifecycle" (~30 min) — the lifecycle meta-argument itself, real use cases and gotchas (Captured notes: 02-hcl-components). ignore_changes as the fix for cascading # forces replacement is Ch 5 §5.7 Cascading changes (05-terraform-plan).
  5. Book chapter — TUR Ch 2 (the ASG section) (~10 min) — create_before_destroy introduced not as an availability option but as the only exit from a deadlock: an immutable resource must be replaced, the default order destroys first, and something else holds a reference so the destroy cannot happen. Captured as 02-getting-started. The shape recurs on any immutable resource with a dependent; the AWS specifics have expired, since launch configurations cannot be created in accounts opened on or after 2024-10-01 (launch-configurations-eol).
  6. Book chapter — TUR Ch 5 (Zero-Downtime Deployment, ~30 min) — captured as 05-tips-and-tricks. Builds the classic ASG zero-downtime deploy on create_before_destroy plus min_elb_capacity, then argues against its own technique: it resets the ASG to min_size after every deployment, breaking scheduled scaling, and it is glue rather than a mechanism. The replacement is AWS's native instance_refresh, and the generalisation is the keeper — prefer the platform's own rollout primitive over a Terraform-shaped workaround. ⚠️ On aws_launch_template, instance_refresh never starts if version = "$Latest"; point it at the template's latest_version attribute.

📌 lifecycle has seven rules, and takes no references at all

Beyond the classic four, lifecycle also holds precondition / postcondition (→ A2) and action_trigger (→ A1). Full list in tf-block-resource.

Why literals only: "Configurations defined in the lifecycle block affect how Terraform constructs and traverses the dependency graph. You can only use literal values … because Terraform processes them before it evaluates arbitrary expressions." The block is an input to graph construction. (See meta-arguments-lifecycle.)

Measured on 1.15.8 while writing Ch 11: "literal" is the wrong word for the boundary. prevent_destroy = true && true and !false are valid, while local.protect is rejected with Error: Variables not allowed and alltrue([true]) with Error: Function calls not allowed. Operators over constants are fine; every reference fails, even a local. The rule is no references, not no expressions.

Also note prevent_destroy "doesn't prevent Terraform from destroying the resource if you remove the resource configuration" — the guard dies with the block it guards.

📌 Lifecycle rules are not in state — except create_before_destroy (added 2026-08-03)

The reference page states it plainly: "Except for create_before_destroy, Terraform does not explicitly record a resource's lifecycle rule to state." That is the mechanism behind the prevent_destroy caveat above, not a separate fact — the guard exists only in the config, so deleting the block deletes the guard. Use a removed block with destroy = false instead (I7).

create_before_destroy is exempt because it decides destroy ordering, which must still work once the config is gone; state v4 stores it per instance. It also propagates: enabling it on A enables it on everything A depends on, written to state, and an attempt to override it back to false on those resources is silently ignored rather than rejected (no error, no warning; only TF_LOG=trace shows ForcedCBDTransformer: forcing create_before_destroy on for …). Measured on 1.15.8 and OpenTofu 1.12.4 in labs/chapter11/lab2. So one create_before_destroy = true can change the replacement strategy of resources you never edited — and CBD is only safe where old and new objects can coexist. Both verified against Terraform v1.15.8 source. (See tf-meta-lifecycle, meta-arguments-lifecycle.)

📌 OpenTofu — dynamic prevent_destroy (1.12)

OpenTofu 1.12 adds dynamic prevent_destroy (bind it to a variable); Terraform still requires a literal. See E3.

Milestone: You can configure a resource for zero-downtime replacement and protect a database from accidental destroy.

Chapter written: Ch 11 — The lifecycle meta-argument (2026-08-03).

items.title: ✅ I3 — Dynamic blocks & complex types
items.text:
What it is: Generating repeated nested blocks with dynamic, and modeling data with object/map/list/set/tuple and optional attributes.

Why you need it: Flexible modules need to emit variable numbers of nested blocks (ingress rules, tags) from typed input variables.

How to learn it:

  1. Reference — HCDocs "dynamic blocks" + "Type Constraints" (~40 min) — syntax and when dynamic is worth the readability cost. The dynamic-blocks page is captured as tf-expr-dynamic-blocks — full anatomy (for_each/iterator/labels/content, the key/value iterator attributes and the set-key caveat), the meta-argument-block limitation (can't generate lifecycle/provisioner), multi-level nesting with a distinct iterator per level, flatten/setproduct to shape for_each, and the "write blocks literally where possible" best practice. The Type Constraints page is captured as tf-expr-type-constraints — keywords vs constructors, primitive/collection (list/map/set)/structural (object/tuple) types, the similar-kinds conversion rules (lossy map → object → map, set ordering), why any is rarely right (only for opaque pass-through like jsonencode), and optional(type, default) attributes with top-down default application and the ? :-with-null idiom to leave one unset.
  2. Interactive — build a security-group module (~1 hr) — drive ingress rules from a list-of-objects variable via dynamic. HashiCorp's own version of this exercise is the CORS half of HCTut "Customize modules with object attributes" — notes: tut-module-object-attributes — which stacks the two mechanisms cleanly: count = length(var.cors_rules) > 0 ? 1 : 0 as a zero-or-one guard on the resource, dynamic for the nested blocks inside it. Its design rule is the transferable part — make the module's type constraint mirror the wrapped resource's own required/optional split, or you reject valid configurations and defer errors to apply. It also shows why optional() pays off in a dynamic body: since omitted attributes arrive as null and a null argument reads as unset, the content block assigns all five attributes unconditionally instead of carrying five conditionals.
  3. Book chapters — TID Ch 3 (type constraints & optional()) + Ch 4 §4.10 (dynamic blocks) (~30 min) — the complex-type system (object/map/list/set/tuple, optional()) is in Ch3; dynamic blocks are in Ch4, captured as 04-expressions-iterations. Measured behaviour for this topic — what was tested locally rather than read — is in dynamic-blocks-facts.
  4. Book chapter — TUR Ch 5 (the dynamic material, ~20 min) — captured as 05-tips-and-tricks. Supplies the motivation the reference pages assume: count cannot loop over inline blocks at all, so ASG tag blocks are the case dynamic exists for. It also shows conditional inline blocks as a nested for that filters the for_each collection, rather than as a separate mechanism.

📌 dynamic block anatomy — content, the label iterator, and iterator

Inside a dynamic "X" block the iterator variable defaults to the label (X.value / X.key) and the body must sit in a content {} sub-block. Rename the iterator with the optional iterator = <name> argument — an unquoted name, not a string — which is needed when nested dynamic blocks share a label so the inner one doesn't shadow the outer's keyword. Toggle a whole block on/off with for_each = cond ? ["x"] : []. Stable in Terraform and OpenTofu (the only recent change is OpenTofu 1.12 allowing provider-defined functions in a dynamic for_each, opentofu#3429). Full treatment: TID Ch4 §4.10.

📌 An object(...) constraint silently deletes undeclared attributes (added 2026-08-05)

The Type Constraints page says it in passing: "values with additional attributes are also acceptable, but the extra attributes are discarded during type conversion." The consequence is that a caller's typo becomes a no-op. Pass enable_https to a module that declared enabled_https and the attribute is dropped, the module reads its default, and terraform validate prints Success!. Measured at a module boundary on 1.15.8.

OpenTofu 1.12.4 warns and Terraform never does — Warning: Object attribute is ignored. The boundary is narrower than it looks: OpenTofu warns for module calls and variable defaults, and stays silent when the same extra key arrives from a .tfvars file. Values are identical in both tools; only the diagnostic differs. Measured in labs/chapter12/lab4.

📌 optional() and a variable default disagree about null (added 2026-08-05)

Same word, two mechanisms. A variable default covers absence only, so an explicit null from the caller is kept (nullable defaults to true). An optional() attribute default covers absence and an explicit null, always, with no opt-out — it behaves like nullable = false. That is why a non-null optional() default is "guaranteed to never have the value null within the receiving module" and a variable default carries no such promise. The one-argument optional(string) has no guarantee either. Measured on 1.15.8.

📌 The meta-argument limit gives you a typo's error message (added 2026-08-05)

dynamic "lifecycle" and dynamic "nonexistent" produce the identical diagnostic on 1.15.8 and OpenTofu 1.12.4: Blocks of type "…" are not expected here. Nothing says the block type exists but may never be generated, so the reader goes hunting for a misspelling that isn't there.

🧪 Lab — KL has no dynamic block lab (corrected 2026-08-15)

This slot previously cited KL's Lab 06 — making code dynamic & reusable as a "dynamic-blocks section". It has none. A grep of that repository returns zero dynamic "…" blocks in any file; the lab's title uses dynamic in the plain-English sense, and its steps are variables, data sources and string interpolation. Use it for parameterizing hardcoded values, not for this topic. Evidence and the rest of the inventory in krausen-labs-facts.

Milestone: You can write a module that accepts a list of rule objects and emits one nested block per rule with a dynamic block.

Chapter written: Ch 12 — Dynamic blocks & complex types (2026-08-05).

items.title: ✅ I4 — Using modules
items.text:
What it is: Consuming modules — the registry, source addresses (registry/git/local), version constraints, passing inputs, and reading module outputs.

Why you need it: Almost no production config is flat; you compose from modules, and the exam tests module sourcing/versioning.

How to learn it:

  1. Interactive — HCTut "Modules overview" (~7 min) — the conceptual opener to the Modules collection; no code. Notes: tut-module. Take three things from it: the definition is broad enough that every configuration is already a module (the directory you run commands in is the root module, one called by a module block is a child module), the strongest argument for modules is a security one rather than a tidiness one (encode the correct S3/GCS settings once, since misconfigured object storage is a recurring incident class), and Terraform reads only one directory's files — a module block is the only thing that makes it read another. ⚠️ Its best-practices list says "Name your provider terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>" — that convention names a module repository; providers use terraform-provider-<NAME> (verified against Publishing Modules, 2026-08-08).
  2. Interactive — HCTut "Use registry modules in configuration" (~12 min) — consume the AWS vpc and ec2-instance registry modules to stand up a VPC plus two EC2 instances. Notes: tut-module-use. (A first taste is also in tf-aws-manage — the terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws module block, module.<name>.<output> references, re-init to install it, and module.vpc.* state addressing.) Four things to take from it beyond the syntax: 22 resources come out of two module blocks, which is the encapsulation benefit and the review problem in one number; module outputs are not inherited — a child's outputs are readable in config but invisible at the CLI until the root module re-exports them; count is legal on a module block (the mechanism tut-for-each uses to multiply on two axes); and local modules are referenced in place, so edits to them take effect with no re-init and no terraform get. (The page says "symlinked"; measured on 1.15.8, .terraform/modules/ holds only modules.json and its Dir points back at the relative source path — no symlink, no copy. The edit-loop consequence is unchanged, and both callers of a shared local directory move together. Book Ch 13 §7, labs/chapter13/lab1.) The page also states the negative case for variables well — "if your organization requires NAT gateway enabled for all VPCs, you should not use a variable to set the enable_nat_gateway argument" — a variable is a permission to vary, and declaring one hands the decision to the caller. (Its own config then does exactly that.) ⚠️ Every pin is years stale (provider ~> 4.49.0, vpc 3.18.1, ec2-instance 4.3.0) and the ami is a hardcoded region-locked ID — but every argument and output it uses still exists at vpc 6.6.1 and ec2-instance 6.4.0 (verified 2026-08-08), so the pins are a version exercise, not a rewrite. The rendered page and its example repo also disagree on name; here the page is the better one (my-ec2-cluster-${count.index} vs. the repo's un-indexed name, which tags both instances identically).
  3. Reference — HCDocs "Modules" section index (~10 min) — read this first for orientation; it is short. Notes: tf-modules. It gives the Develop → Distribute → Provision split the whole docs section is organized around, and a definition that complements the tutorials': a module is "a collection of resources that Terraform manages together" (semantic) where tut-module says "a set of Terraform configuration files in a single directory" (structural). The second makes "every configuration is already a module" true; the first is what makes the scoping question in I5 answerable at all.
  4. Reference — HCDocs "Use modules in your configuration" (~30 min) — the consumer-side reference, and the one that covers what tut-module-use leaves out. Notes: tf-modules-configuration. Git sources default to whatever HEAD points at today unless you add ?ref=, which takes a branch, tag, or SHA; ?depth=1 makes a shallow clone. The const = true requirement on variables feeding source/version is a timing argument, not a safety one — modules install at init, before plan-time evaluation exists — and the constraint is on the whole dependency chain, so a local composed from const variables is legal in the source position. Two operational facts worth holding: init honours what is already installed while -upgrade re-resolves the constraint, which with no module lock file is exactly where an untested version arrives; and -replace takes individual instance addresses only, including full nested paths like module.example.module.from-child2.aws_instance.child2-inst, with no module-wide form and no wildcards. ⚠️ Its removal section is garbled — a version note stranded mid-paragraph, a stray "And", an unclosed backtick, and a closing link to the moved block reference at the end of a section about removed.
  5. Reference — HCDocs "module block reference" (~35 min) — the argument spec, and the exhaustive source catalogue (local, registry, GitHub, Git, BitBucket, Mercurial, HTTP, S3, GCS). Captured as tf-block-module. Things that live only here: // marks a sub-directory within a package, with query parameters after it (<package>//<subdir>?ref=<x>), and because Terraform extracts the whole package to disk, sibling modules inside it can reference each other by local path — which is what makes A8's module-split shim resolve. Same source, different labels is legal and is the multi-region workaround forced by the static provider association in I8. Absolute local paths are copied into the module cache and are discouraged for coupling a config to one machine's filesystem. localterraform.com/<NS>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER> resolves against whichever HCP/TFE instance runs the config — portable where a hard-coded hostname is not. HCP Terraform can authenticate to Git sources only with SSH keys, stated four times but never prominently. And ignore_nested_deprecations (1.15) is the consumer's opt-out from a module author's deprecated warnings (I5). ⚠️ The page contradicts itself on source ten lines apart — "must specify a literal string… does not support… arbitrary expressions" against "can reference constant input variables and local values"; the second is current, the first is stale pre-1.15 text. Its depth "default is 1" also cannot be right, since that would make every Git source a shallow clone and break the SHA refs the same page documents.
  6. Reference — HCDocs "Module Sources" + version constraint syntax (~30 min) — ~>, git refs, local paths. The version-constraints page is captured as tf-expr-version-constraints — the operators (=/!=/>/>=/</<=/~>, with the ~> right-most-increment rule), that constraints apply to modules, provider requirements, and required_version, the "newest installed that qualifies, else download" resolution, pre-release matching only via =, and the reusable-module (min-only >=) vs root-module (~> upper+lower bound) best-practice split.
  7. Book chapter — TUR Ch 4 (~1.5 hrs) — the classic module treatment; still the best explanation of inputs/outputs/composition. Captured: 04-reusable-modules. Read it for why each feature exists — it arrives at inputs, locals and outputs because its running example broke without them, which no reference page can do. Three lines worth memorizing: "the input variables are the API of the module"; a variable is permission to change a value, which is why the port/protocol constants became locals (callers could otherwise override them accidentally); and prefer separate resources to inline blocks in a module, because a separate resource "can be added anywhere" while an inline block can only be added by the module that owns it. It is also the only source here that walks the promotion workflow end to end — tag v0.0.2, point staging at it, leave production on v0.0.1, roll forward once proven. ⚠️ Its aws_launch_configuration example is unrunnable in a recent AWS account, its aws_security_group_rule advice now points at a superseded resource (aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule is current), and its "Git tags are as stable as a commit" needs the correction in the callout below — tags move.

📌 Already captured — modules

The cross-source synthesis, blending HCDocs, TID Ch 2 §2.8 and Ch 3, TUR Ch 4 and the AWS get-started tutorial, and it splits along the same seam this path does: consuming modules is I4, authoring them is I5. Three framings worth having before the reference reading.
