A module behaves like a function — variable blocks are the parameters, output blocks the return values, and locals are internal-only, so from outside you can set inputs and read outputs and nothing else. A module is not a provider: it is pure HCL with no Go plugin, it cannot define new resource types, and it can mix resources from several providers, which is why modules abstract systems rather than objects. And the three flavours matter for where a provider block is legal — only in a root module, the directory you actually run init in.

📌 Dynamic module sources (Terraform 1.15)

Terraform 1.15 added dynamic module sources: source and version can now be variables, not just string literals — so one module block can point different environments at different registries/pins instead of duplicating the block. Any variable feeding a module source must be marked const = true (module sources resolve at terraform init). OpenTofu offered this earlier; this is one of the 1.15 gap-closers. Note the exam (004, Terraform 1.12) still assumes literal sources. (See tf115-ot112-features.)

📌 terraform modules (TF 1.10)

terraform modules (TF 1.10+) prints every module declared in the config — key, source, and version — for the whole tree. Use it to audit what you depend on and to drive policy on module consumption. (See feature-history.)

📌 Governing module versions — no lock file to lean on

.terraform.lock.hcl records providers only. Module selections live in uncommitted .terraform/modules/modules.json, so a fresh clone or a clean CI runner re-resolves the constraint and can land on a version nobody tested. terraform init -lockfile=readonly has nothing to check. Ch3 states the hazard; the controls belong here, in three layers.

The in-scope control here is the exact pin: version = "6.6.1" for a registry module. Enforcing that pin is A5; keeping pinned versions current is A3.

Don't try to commit modules.json as a substitute. Dir is repo-relative so it looks portable, but it's an undocumented internal snapshot that init rewrites, with no readonly enforcement.

📌 Git module sources: immutable pin or automated updates, not both

A registry module gets both properties at once — version = "6.6.1" is exact, and both update bots understand it. A Git source forces a real choice, and this is the reason to prefer registry sources where you have one.

ref=<tag> is what the bots can move, but a Git tag is mutable: whoever controls the source repo can force-move v1.2.0 to different code and your "pin" follows it silently. Mitigate by trusting the publisher, or by requiring tag-protection rules on the source repo.

ref=<full commit SHA> cannot be moved by anyone, which is the supply-chain-safe answer and mirrors the advice to SHA-pin GitHub Actions. The cost is that no update bot will move it for you, confirmed on both:

  • Renovate — not supported natively. The maintainer's reason in discussion #31006 is architectural: Renovate's HCL parser returns an AST with comments stripped, so it has nowhere to keep the version↔SHA annotation its Docker/Actions digest pinning relies on. Open request, no timeline. Worse, a global pinDigests: true breaks on Git-sourced Terraform modules (#14790); set "terraform": { "pinDigests": false }. A custom regex manager is the community workaround.
  • Dependabot — same gap, tracked at #10787 (SHA-pinned source reports "no update needed" even when newer commits exist) and #10926. It considers semantic versions and skips SHA refs.

How to choose. Third-party module you don't control: SHA-pin and accept manual upgrades, because the mutable-tag risk is a real supply-chain exposure. Module in your own org with protected tags: pin the tag and keep the automation, since you control whether the tag can move. Either way this is a deliberate trade, not an oversight — verified 2026-07-20.

A third thing a SHA pin costs you: shallow clones (added 2026-08-08). ?depth=1 on a Git source is the documented way to stop cloning a large repository's whole history — and it rejects a SHA ref outright. The Use modules page and Module Sources both describe depth with no caveat; the module block reference does carry it — "You cannot use raw commit IDs" — but no page connects the restriction to the SHA-pinning advice, so the cost only surfaces when the pin fails. go-getter passes --depth together with --branch <ref>, and git clone --branch takes only a branch or tag; a commit-shaped ref is caught by a regex and fails with "note that setting 'depth' requires 'ref' to be a branch or tag name". Version-gated: go-getter v1.8.6, the release Terraform 1.15.8 vendors. Immutable pin or shallow clone — not both. Evidence: cache/search/git-module-shallow-clone-vs-sha-pin.md, tf-modules-configuration.

🧪 Lab — KL has no module lab at all (corrected 2026-08-15)

This slot previously cited KL's Lab 06 as a "reusable-module section". That repository contains zero module "…" blocks, and the word module does not appear anywhere in Lab 06's instructions — "reusable" there means parameterized, not modularized. KL stops before modules entirely, so authoring them needs the other sources in this topic. See krausen-labs-facts.

Milestone: You can consume a versioned registry module, pass it inputs, and reference its outputs in your own resources.

items.title: ✅ I5 — Authoring modules
items.text:
What it is: Writing your own modules — standard file layout, input validation, sensible outputs, composition over inheritance, and module design principles.

Why you need it: Reusable, testable modules are the core skill of both certs and of any real Terraform codebase.

How to learn it: (hands-on first, then the design reading, then the six Develop modules reference pages in the docs' own sidebar order, then a module of your own. Entries name each other by page title rather than by number, because this list has been renumbered twice and the numeric cross-references rotted both times.)

  1. Interactive — HCTut "Build and use a local module" (~15 min) — author a local modules/aws-s3-static-website-bucket submodule and call it from the previous tutorial's root config. Notes: tut-module-create. This is the authoring counterpart to I4's consumption tutorials, and its content is the two interface-design questions rather than the syntax: which arguments become variables (its answer: not the ACL, because the module's purpose fixes it to public-read — a value your purpose decides is not a variable) and which values become outputs ("outputs are the only supported way for users to get information about resources configured by the module"). Also states the provider rule — no provider block in a module, inherit from the caller — which tut-for-each shows is a hard constraint, not a recommendation, once count/for_each is on the module block. ⚠️ The rendered module main.tf cannot apply on a current AWS account: new buckets default to Bucket-owner-enforced (ACLs disabled, AccessControlListNotSupported) with Block Public Access on, so both its aws_s3_bucket_acl and its public aws_s3_bucket_policy are rejected. The example repo is already fixed — six resources with aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls, aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, and depends_on chains — so clone it rather than copying the page. Evidence: cache/search/s3-acl-bpa-defaults.md.
  2. Interactive — HCTut "Customize modules with object attributes" (~17 min, Terraform 1.3+) — refactor a module's four flat file-related variables into one object variable with optional() attributes, then add a list(object(...)) for CORS. Notes: tut-module-object-attributes. This is the clearest interface-design exercise in the collection, and the argument for it is API evolution, in the page's words: optional attributes "make it easier for you to ship new module versions without changing the variables that module users need to define" — the additive counterpart to the deprecated mechanism below. Two things to take beyond the syntax: a qualifier baked into a flat variable name is a namespace you are hand-rolling (terraform_managed_files → files.terraform_managed, where the suffix existed only because a flat namespace had nowhere to say which group the variable belonged to), and path.module vs path.root — the module's fallback resolves against its own directory while the caller's value resolves against theirs, which is the whole reason the path is worth exposing. ⚠️ The page has real defects: its transcripts predate its own repo (printed counts are 6 where a current clone gives 8), the "Clean up" section shows an apply that adds a resource under a terraform destroy heading, and the delete-these-variables snippet lists five. Its repo also omits the depends_on that the sibling learn-terraform-modules-create repo uses to order the bucket policy after the public-access block.
  3. Interactive — HCTut "Write Terraform tests" (~1.5 hrs) — A2 owns this tutorial, and the framework, the validation/precondition/check distinction and Terratest all belong there. Do the module half here, because a module is not finished until something asserts its interface. TUR Ch 8's structural rule below is that every module gets an example and every example gets a test, and .tftest.hcl is what makes that rule executable: a run block applies the configuration with a chosen set of inputs and asserts on the result, so the interface you designed in the two exercises above acquires a regression test before it has consumers rather than after. Sequence it here for the same reason Ch 8 writes examples/ first — a test is the second caller your module ever has, and the second caller is what exposes an interface that only works once.
  4. Reference — HCTut "Module creation — recommended pattern" (~17 min, no code) — HashiCorp's Recommended Enterprise Patterns guide to module scoping, which is the question every other module resource skips. Notes: tut-pattern-module-creation. Learn the three axes: Encapsulation (group what always deploys together), Privileges (never span a segregation-of-duties boundary), Volatility (keep long-lived infrastructure out of a module that ships daily). The last two are blast-radius arguments, which is why they also decide state boundaries and not just module boundaries — the same argument A7 makes one granularity up. Its heuristic for "too big" is a good one: "If a module's function or purpose is hard to explain, the module is probably too complex." MVP rules: works for 80% of use cases, never code for edge cases, avoid conditionals in an MVP, expose only the most commonly modified arguments — but maximize outputs, because one module's output is the next module's input. And the default test worth carrying: var.vpc_id should never have a default, because if the right value differs on every use, a default is a trap. Nesting: don't go more than two deep (utility modules like tagging excepted), and know the trade — an external child module can change behavior "with no changes to the parent's calling code or version", while an embedded submodule is locked to its parent's version but cannot be reused elsewhere. ⚠️ Its naming table gives terraform-azure-database, but the provider is azurerm; the same table also mixes underscores and hyphens. Third page in the collection to fumble that convention.

  5. Book chapter — TUR Ch 4 + Ch 8 (~2.5 hrs) — module design and "production-grade" module conventions. Ch 4 captured as 04-reusable-modules; read it against 03-variables-modules (TID Ch3), which covers the ground TUR Ch4 skips — module flavors, the type system, validation, sensitive, and registry publishing. The comparison is written up on the Modules topic page.

    Ch 8 is now captured as 08-production-grade, and it is the design half of this topic. Four rules — small, composable, testable, versioned — plus the practice worth adopting immediately: write the examples/ code before any module code, so the API is designed from the caller's side. Its structural rule is that every module gets an example and every example gets a test, which is what turns modules/+examples/+test/ into a convention rather than a folder tree. It also closes the registry gap Ch 4 leaves: the four Public Registry requirements, and the <OWNER>/<REPO>/<PROVIDER> + version source form. ⚠️ Its self-validation section is stale — see the correction under A2.

  6. Reference — HCDocs "Module Development" standards (~40 min) — the standard module structure and publishing rules. The section index itself is captured as tf-modules-develop, and its "when not to write a module" section is the part to read twice: "over-using modules can make your overall Terraform configuration harder to understand and maintain", a good module "raise[s] the level of abstraction by describing a new concept in your architecture", and the naming test — "If you have trouble finding a name for your module that isn't the same as the main resource type inside it, that may be a sign that your module is not creating any new abstraction." Pair it with the recommended-pattern guide's complexity test above and the target sharpens: a module should be nameable in a phrase that is neither a paragraph nor a resource type. It also restates the two-deep nesting rule from a different angle — keep the tree flat and compose, because a flat set of modules can be assembled in more combinations than a deep one.

    ⚠️ The requirements are not on the page the sidebar calls "Publish modules." That page (tf-modules-publish) is thin — publish to the registry, it versions and documents your module — and the repository-naming, semver-tag and structure rules live under the separate Registry Publishing section instead. It does supply the cleanest one-line case for a registry source over a Git one: "The alternative sources do not support the first-class versioning mechanism." And note its own example omits the version argument on the same page that sells version constraints.

  7. Reference — HCDocs "Standard Module Structure" (~25 min) — the layout half of the overview above, and the page the registry's tooling actually depends on: it parses submodules, examples and documentation out of this structure. Notes: tf-modules-structure.

    Four of its rules are not guessable from the file tree. A submodule's README.md is its public/private marker — "Any nested module with a README.md is considered usable by an external user. If a README doesn't exist, it is considered for internal use only" — and it is "purely advisory", so a private submodule stays private by staying undocumented. The two source-address rules point opposite ways: a root calling its own nested module uses a relative path so it isn't downloaded twice, while an examples/ block uses the external address, because examples are expected to be copied out. Resources may be split across files but module blocks must stay in main.tf. ⚠️ It also contradicts the recommended-pattern guide above on READMEs, and this path cites both sides. This page says the README "doesn't need to document inputs or outputs of the module because tooling will automatically generate this"; the recommended-pattern guide says to document required inputs, optional inputs and outputs in the README. The reconciliation is that the registry generates those tables from the description arguments, so writing good descriptions is documenting the interface, and a hand-written table beside it is a copy that goes stale. Read that guide as "the interface must be documented" and this page as "here is where that documentation comes from". And the root module "is expected to be opinionated", with nested modules as the escape hatch — the structural form of the recommended-pattern guide's 80%-of-use-cases rule. Also: use commit-specific absolute URLs for links and images in a module README, or the registry renders them against the wrong version. The registry's own bar is short and worth memorizing: public GitHub repo named terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME> (<NAME> = infrastructure type, <PROVIDER> = the provider creating it), adherence to the standard module structure so the registry can generate docs and parse submodules/examples, and at least one semver release tag x.y.z (optional v prefix). (Publishing Modules, verified 2026-08-08; the minimal file set — LICENSE, README.md, main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf — and the best-practice framing are in tut-module, which misnames this convention as a provider rule.)

  8. Reference — HCDocs "Providers Within Modules" (~35 min) — the third page in the Develop modules group, and the one that states the authoring rule the other two assume. Notes: tf-modules-providers. A reusable module must not contain its own provider block, and the reason is a lifecycle one rather than the count/for_each conflict every tutorial cites: a provider configuration is needed to destroy a resource as well as create it, and state records which configuration last applied each object, so "a provider configuration must always stay present in the overall Terraform configuration for longer than all of the resources it manages." A module holding both removes them at the same moment. The authoring consequence is configuration_aliases in required_providers, plus the inheritance asymmetry to design around: default provider configurations inherit into child modules, aliased ones never do, and source/version requirements never do either — every child declares its own. The caller-side mechanics of the same contract belong to I8, which cites this page too; read it there if you are configuring providers rather than authoring a module.

  9. Reference — HCDocs "Best practices for composing modules" (~40 min) — the design reference, and the most substantial page in the Modules section. Notes: tf-modules-composition. It is stricter than the recommended-pattern guide's two-deep rule: keep the tree flat, one level of child modules, and wire them with expressions, because "instead of a module embedding its dependencies… the module receives its dependencies from the root module, which can therefore connect the same modules in different ways." Three patterns to take away. Conditional creation — never write a module that detects whether something exists; declare an object(...) input listing only the attributes you need, and let the caller pass either a resource or a data source. Assumptions versus guarantees — an assumption is what must hold for a resource to be usable, a guarantee is what the rest of the configuration may rely on, and preconditions on outputs are how you assert the latter (A2). Data-only modules — a module of pure data sources, whose real trick is that a join-network module with the same outputs as a create-network module makes the two swappable, so promoting an environment to owning its infrastructure is a one-line source change (relevant to A7, and neither module tutorial mentions it). Also worth reading for the flat statement that Terraform "intentionally does not attempt to abstract over similar services offered by different vendors" — multi-cloud abstractions are yours to build, out of shared object types and matching output names. ⚠️ Two of its examples would fail validate: aws_ami takes owners (a list), not owner, and aws_subnet_ids no longer exists in the AWS provider (aws_subnets replaced it).
  10. Reference — HCDocs "Publishing Modules" (~10 min) — short, and worth the ten minutes for one sentence: "The alternative sources do not support the first-class versioning mechanism." That is the argument for publishing at all rather than pinning a Git ?ref=. Notes: tf-modules-publish. ⚠️ The publishing requirements are not on this page — repository naming, semver tags and the standard structure live under Registry Publishing, summarised under Standard Module Structure above. Note also that its own example omits the version argument on the page that sells version constraints. Actually getting a module into a registry is A4, which covers the HCP private registry hands-on and, since 2026-08-16, the open-source alternative.
  11. Reference — HCDocs "Refactor modules" (~20 min for the author's half) — the last page in the Develop modules group, and the one that covers how a module's internal structure changes once it has consumers. Notes: tf-modules-refactoring. The deep moved reference is A8 — addressing rules, instance keys, count ↔ for_each migrations, the cross-type and managed-to-data limits. What belongs here is the part addressed to an author. Scoping is what makes refactoring an author's privilege: addresses resolve relative to the module the block is written in, and "a module may only make moved statements about its own objects and objects of its child modules", so you can rename and re-shape internals across a version bump and every consumer gets the migration in their next plan without touching their own code. moved blocks are the upgrade path, not a courtesy changelog. Chain them (a→b, then b→c) when the same object moves twice, because each block covers consumers arriving from a different starting version, and keep them — removal is safe only for a private module, once you are certain every consumer has applied. The section to read as an author is splitting a published module. The original module is not deleted; it becomes a shim that calls the new modules and carries the moved blocks, so new users take the pieces directly and existing users upgrade in place. HashiCorp names the compromise rather than hiding it: the shim's blocks address resources inside child modules, which "violates the typical rule that a parent module sees its child module as a 'closed box'", and it attaches a precondition — "all three of these modules are maintained by the same people and distributed together in a single module package." That licence covers your own package and never someone else's module. Read with the deprecated callout below, this is the full toolkit for evolving a published interface: moved re-shapes structure, deprecated retires API surface.
  12. Interactive — HCTut "Create and use no-code modules" (~14 min, HCP Terraform Standard edition + an AWS account) — E6 owns this tutorial for the self-service platform half; read it here for the author half, because it is the one page that documents where two of the rules above stop applying. Notes: tut-no-code-provisioning. A no-code module declares its own provider blocks, and the page gives the cleanest statement of why the prohibition exists at all: “Since users will not reference no-code modules in written configuration, there is no risk of this conflict.” So the ban was never about providers, it was about count/for_each/depends_on on a module block — remove the possibility of that block and the ban evaporates, at the price of the organization having to arrange provider credentials for every workspace HCP launches per provision. It tightens the standard structure rather than relaxing it: “No-code modules must follow standard module structure and define all resources in the root repository of the directory.” And it is the only page in the Modules collection that has been kept current — ephemeral resources (1.10) and write-only arguments (1.11) — where eight of the other nine still pin 2022 provider versions, so it is the one whose configuration is worth copying as written.
  13. Interactive — refactor (~1.5 hrs) — extract your Beginner project into a reusable module with a clean input/output surface.

📌 Type your module's outputs, for the same reason you type its inputs

A module's outputs deserve type constraints as much as its inputs do (TF 1.15+, B6): the constraint is checked, and a consumer reads your interface without reading your implementation. That is the case, and it's enough. A visible side effect is that a fully-typed output set makes module.<NAME> a list/map under count/for_each rather than a tuple/object (verified 1.15.8; Ch 7 §3 has the machinery) — but treat that as a curiosity, not a reason: auto-conversion means callers almost never notice, since a tuple splats, converts, and satisfies a list(object(...)) constraint exactly as a list does. OpenTofu has no typed outputs as of 1.12.4, so a module written for both can't rely on the argument at all. Evidence: conditional-branch-evaluation.

📌 Module API deprecation (Terraform 1.15)

Terraform 1.15 added a deprecation mechanism for a module's public API: put deprecated = "message" on a variable or output and callers get a warning at terraform validate. This is how you evolve a published module's interface without breaking consumers overnight — deprecate, warn, then remove a version later. Pairs with the moved blocks in the Refactor modules reference above — deprecated retires interface surface, moved re-shapes the structure behind it — and with the refactoring-at-scale workflow in A8. (See tf115-ot112-features; argument specs in tf-block-variable and tf-block-output. Output-specifics: deprecated is child-modules-only, only consumers see the warning (not the defining module), and ignore_nested_deprecations on the module block suppresses nested warnings.)

📌 Publishing is the step after authoring — and the workflow choice is not cosmetic

Writing the module is this topic; getting it into a registry is A4, captured in tut-module-private-registry-share. Two things belong in an author's head, though. Your repository name is your module's identity — terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>, required for the public registry and recommended for HCP's private one — and your git tags are your version numbers, semver x.y.z with an optional v, with non-matching tags ignored and at least one tag needed to publish at all. So versioning is a release-process decision made in the repo, not an argument you write in HCL.

HCP's branch-based publishing is the one to know about, because it is the only workflow that supports module testing — relevant the moment terraform test (A2) is part of how you ship a module.

📌 Generate the README's input/output tables — and make its links absolute

A module README goes stale the moment a variable is added, which is why code-styling treats module docs as a generated artifact: run terraform-docs manually, or wire it into pre-commit so the inputs/outputs tables refresh on every commit. The reference implementation the book points at is terraform-aws-vpc, which uses exactly this setup.

The registry-specific trap: "All links in README.md files should be absolute". The Terraform Registry renders your README off-repo, so a relative link that works fine on GitHub resolves to nothing there. This is a publishing constraint rather than a style preference, and it belongs with the publishing rules above. The rest of the toolchain is in B4.

Milestone: You can package infrastructure into a module with validated inputs, documented outputs, and a README, and consume it from two callers. Written up as Chapter 14 — Authoring modules, whose lab measures typed outputs against both engines, the deprecated warnings each engine emits and when, and a module split that leaves the consumer's plan at 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

items.title: ✅ I6 — Remote state & backends
items.text:
What it is: Where Terraform keeps state, taught on three backends and one idea. local is where you already are. s3 and gcs are the two object-store backends worth knowing properly — bootstrap, migration, locking, IAM, encryption — and reading them side by side is what turns "the S3 backend" into a general model of what a backend does. Then terraform_remote_state for sharing outputs, and enough of the rest of the catalogue to recognise it.

Why you need it: Teams cannot share local state; remote state with locking is the baseline for any collaboration and is exam-critical. Two backends rather than one, because everything that matters here — the bucket you must create first, the lock that is really a conditional write, the plaintext secrets you are now storing centrally — is a property of the pattern, not of AWS.

How to learn it:

  1. Video — TF2026 "Remote state & backends" (Lecture 07) (~35 min) — the only video coverage this topic has, and the one that shows the bootstrap as a sequence rather than a paragraph: build the S3 bucket with server-side encryption, versioning and a public-access block first, then add the backend "s3" block and re-init. Companion code is Lecture07/ in the course repo. ⚠️ Its backend block locks with dynamodb_table, which the S3 backend reference now deprecates in favour of use_lockfile — see the S3 reference below and the native-locking callout further down. The same lecture also predates the endpoints {} block, using the deprecated endpoint and force_path_style arguments. The bucket setup it teaches is still right; the locking argument is not. (Verified 2026-08-15 against the local checkout — see docs/research-cache/tf2026-course-facts.md.)
  2. 🧪 Lab — the local backend, said out loud (~20 min, nothing required) — start where every earlier chapter already was, and make it explicit. backend "local" { path = "state/dev.tfstate" } moves the file; deleting the block and re-running init migrates it back, which is the whole of “removing a backend” — there is no separate command for it. Measured 2026-08-19 on 1.15.8, and not what the docs imply: only a first backend adoption prompts on a plain init. Once a backend is recorded in .terraform/, changing or deleting the block errors with Backend configuration changed and makes you choose -migrate-state or -reconfigure. And the migration copies without cleaning up — the old state file survives complete, so a plaintext snapshot stays on the disk you just moved it off (Book Ch 15 §6). Reference: tf-backend-local, including the legacy -state / -backup flags that switch off workspace-aware state filenames, which HashiCorp recommends against “even if you are running Terraform in automation.” Lab: labs/chapter15/lab1/.
  3. 🧪 Lab — the s3 backend: bootstrap, migrate, lock (~1.5 hrs, no cloud account) — the core exercise of this topic, run against the book's AWS emulator. Three things in one sitting. The two-step bootstrap: a local-backend configuration creates the bucket with versioning and a public-access block, because the bucket holding your state cannot be tracked in that state before it exists. The migration: apply with local state, add an empty backend "s3" {} plus a config.s3.tfbackend partial configuration, then init -migrate-state and answer the copy prompt. The lock: use_lockfile = true, an apply held open, and a second command refused with 412 PreconditionFailed on the <key>.tflock object. Verified transcripts in the callout below. Lab: labs/chapter15/lab2/.
  4. 🧪 Lab — the gcs backend (~45 min, no cloud account) — the same shape against a second cloud, which is what turns one backend into a general idea. It runs on a local GCP emulator behind a compose profile, because the AWS one cannot stand in: gcs speaks the Google JSON API at /storage/v1/b. Two differences to carry away. There is no key — state is <prefix>/<workspace>.tfstate, so the workspace name is always in the path, where S3 prefixes only non-default workspaces, with the literal env:. And locking is on by default, with no use_lockfile equivalent to forget. The refusal names the mechanism: googleapi: Error 412: ifGenerationMatch: … conditionNotMet. Lab: labs/chapter15/lab3/.
  5. Reference — HCDocs “Backends” + “local” (~40 min) — what a backend is, before which one you pick. Captured as tf-backend-configure and tf-backend-local: the three limitations (one block per configuration, no named values, nothing declared inside it referenceable elsewhere), backend and cloud being mutually exclusive, the full partial-configuration surface, and the documented *.backendname.tfbackend filename convention the labs use. The State-section framing of the same ground is tf-state-backends: a backend's two responsibilities — storage, plus an optional locking API — and the guarantee that a non-local backend never writes state to local disk except when persisting to the backend fails. The dedicated locking page is tf-state-locking, which is where the force-unlock rules below come from.
  6. Reference — HCDocs “S3 backend” (~35 min) — the one backend worth reading argument by argument, captured as tf-backend-s3. Locking is opt-in and the old way is going out: use_lockfile defaults to false, while dynamodb_table and dynamodb_endpoint are deprecated and “will be removed in a future minor version”; both may be set at once purely as a migration path. Workspaces change the object path to <workspace_key_prefix>/<workspace_name>/<key>, default prefix the literal env: (A7). The IAM set is more specific than “read and write the bucket”: s3:DeleteObject is needed on the .tflock object but explicitly not on the state object, “as Terraform does not delete it.” Encryption has three shapes, and the third bites: sse_customer_key set in a .tf file “will cause it to be persisted to disk in terraform.tfstate.” The page also carries assume_role_with_web_identity, which is how a backend authenticates from CI with no stored key (A6).
  7. Reference — HCDocs “gcs backend” (~30 min) — the Google counterpart, captured as tf-backend-gcs, and the page that makes the S3 one legible by contrast. Locking needs no argument at all. Addressing is prefix plus workspace, never a key. Authentication is organised by where Terraform runs: workstation ADC, an attached service account on Google Cloud, a key file outside it, or impersonate_service_account. The encryption asymmetry is the part to plan around — a customer-supplied key (CSEK) cannot be migrated automatically and needs an out-of-band rewrite first, while a KMS key can, but only takes effect on the first write after migration, so the old key has to outlive it. And a 403 immediately after granting IAM may be nothing: “Terraform will return 403 errors till it is eventually consistent.” The argument that decides whether the backend and your resources share an identity is the environment variable you export: every option here reads both a backend-scoped GOOGLE_BACKEND_* name and a shared GOOGLE_* one, and the page warns that “if using the Google Cloud Platform provider as well, it will also pick up the GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS environment variable.” Exporting the shared name authenticates the backend and every google provider as the same principal, which is the collapse of exactly the split the S3 page’s multi-account architecture is built on (A7). Its IAM story is correspondingly coarse: one line asking for Storage Object Admin on the bucket, against S3’s four-statement policy with a separate .tflock statement.
  8. Book chapter — TUR Ch 3 (~1.5 hrs) — the canonical remote-state + isolation discussion, now captured as 03-manage-state. What it gives this topic that the references do not: the two-step bootstrap (apply the bucket with a local backend, then add the backend block and init to migrate, and the same in reverse to tear it down), partial configuration as the answer to key being the one argument you must not copy-paste, and the honest list of what the backend block cannot do. ⚠️ Two of its limitations are now engine-specific — OpenTofu 1.7 state encryption and 1.8 early variable evaluation in backend blocks both close gaps the chapter presents as inherent (notes: ot-early-eval-backend, and the encryption reference below) — and its DynamoDB lock table is superseded by use_lockfile (see the callouts below). Cross-source synthesis: State.
  9. Book chapter — TID Ch 6 §6.4 "Storing state" (~1 hr) — the reference-shaped counterpart to TUR Ch 3’s narrative, and the treatment that enumerates where TUR argues: §6.4.1 the possible backends, §6.4.3 the backend block, §6.4.4 alternative authentication methods, §6.4.5 the cloud block as the other way to do the same job, §6.4.6 migrating between backends and §6.4.8 upgrading one. Ch 6 is already cited from I7 for its state-surgery half (§6.5) and from B9 for §6.1–§6.3; §6.4 belongs to this topic, and it is the section that turns the backend catalogue from a list of names into something you can configure.
  10. 🧪 Lab — pipeline on the forge, state in the bucket (~1.5 hrs) — the arrangement most teams actually run, and this topic's answer to “where does state live when our code is on GitLab, GitHub or Bitbucket?” A self-hosted GitLab runs validate → plan → manual apply against the same s3 backend as lab 2, with the job container on the emulator's network. It ends with two objects in one bucket — app/terraform.tfstate written from a workstation, ci/terraform.tfstate written by a runner — and no Terraform state on the forge at all. Lab: labs/chapter15/gitlab/. The credential half is OIDC: gha-oidc for GitHub, bitbucket-pipelines-oidc for Bitbucket, feeding the assume_role_with_web_identity block above so no long-lived key sits in CI (A6). ⚠️ Two traps the lab records because each cost a failed pipeline: gitlab/gitlab-runner:latest is a pre-release whose helper image does not exist, so every job dies in prepare_executor; and the runner needs an explicit --clone-url, because the URL GitLab advertises to a browser is unreachable from a job container.
  11. Reference — the backends that are not object stores (~40 min, read once) — enough to recognise the rest of the catalogue rather than adopt it. http is a protocol rather than a vendor (tf-backend-http): GET/POST/DELETE plus LOCK/UNLOCK, 423 when the lock is held, and lock addresses that default to disabled, so a minimal block is silently unlocked. GitLab-managed state is that protocol implemented inside GitLab (gitlab-tf-state) — an empty backend "http" {} against /api/v4/projects/<ID>/terraform/state/<NAME>, where project roles replace bucket IAM and, the fact that decides it, “any user with the Developer role or higher can download and view Terraform state files.” HCP Terraform is a cloud block rather than a backend type, and Terrakube (terrakube-migrating) speaks the same API self-hosted, needing only an extra hostname. The remainder — azurerm, consul, kubernetes, pg, oci (1.12), oss, cos — is chosen by the platform you are already on.
  12. Interactive — the managed-platform comparison (~1.5 hrs total, optional) — three HashiCorp tutorials, kept because they show what a managed backend does that a bucket does not, not because this topic depends on them. “Migrate state to HCP Terraform” is the cheapest — a random_pet, no cloud account — and is captured as tut-cloud-migrate: the cloud block, terraform login storing its token “in plain text”, and an init prompt whose no branch adopts the workspace's existing state rather than cancelling. “Version remote state with the HCP Terraform API” is the disaster-recovery half, captured as tut-cloud-state-api: download, edit, increment serial by hand, and upload a new state version, with the workspace lock a precondition of the upload. “Migrate state from S3 to HCP Terraform” is the long one, and lab 2 already covers the migration mechanics it teaches.
  13. Reference — HCDocs "terraform_remote_state data source" (~25 min) — reading another config's root outputs, the config object (nested backend blocks become = attributes), defaults, and — most of the page — HashiCorp's case against using it. Notes: tf-remote-state-data.
  14. Reference — OTDocs "State and Plan Encryption" (~40 min, OpenTofu only) — the direct answer to the hardening callout below, and a capability Terraform has no equivalent of. An encryption {} block inside terraform pairs a key_provider with a method and applies it to state {}, plan {} and — the part that bears on the terraform_remote_state warning further down — remote_state_data_sources {}. The whole configuration can also arrive through TF_ENCRYPTION, with the environment overriding code. Read its threat model before adopting it, because the page is unusually honest about the limits: encryption protects state at rest, and “does not protect against data loss … and it also does not protect against replay attack”, nor against “the person running the tofu command.” Two operational facts to plan around. Migration is deliberately not seamless — turning encryption on over an existing state is not enough, because OpenTofu “will refuse to read plain text data”, described as “a protection mechanism to prevent OpenTofu from reading manipulated, unencrypted data”, so there is a documented initial-setup path to follow. And the compatibility promise is narrow: key providers and methods are supported for +1 minor version, with a console warning at plan/apply before removal, so an encrypted state is something you keep current rather than set and forget. Rotate keys where the method can saturate — AES-GCM is named. Engine history and the rest of the divergences are E3. Now captured as ot-state-encryption, which adds four things this entry did not carry. The unencrypted method is the documented migration path in both directions, temporarily named in a fallback block, and fallback is the general rollover mechanism rather than a migration-only tool: OpenTofu reads with either method and “will always use the new method and not the fallback” when writing. enforced = true is the guard for environment-driven configuration, because an unset TF_ENCRYPTION otherwise means plaintext written silently — the same shape of failure as use_lockfile defaulting to false. Renaming a key provider breaks decryption, since the encrypted data carries metadata keyed to the block name, and encrypted_metadata_alias is what makes a rename or a cross-project name mismatch survivable. Key-provider authentication is inherited from the matching backend, so aws_kms and gcp_kms reuse the S3 and GCS credential chains and add nothing new to learn.

📌 s3 versus gcs — the same job, and where they genuinely differ

Read the two reference pages against each other; this is the summary the chapter is built on. Both verified in labs/chapter15/.

s3 gcs Object path key, verbatim, for the default workspace no key — always <prefix>/<workspace>.tfstate Other workspaces <workspace_key_prefix>/<name>/<key>, prefix defaults to the literal env: same rule as the default one; the name is already in the path Locking opt-in: use_lockfile = true, defaults to false on by default, and no argument exists to set or unset it Lock mechanism <key>.tflock object, conditional PUT → 412 PreconditionFailed <prefix>/<name>.tflock, ifGenerationMatch: 0 → 412 conditionNotMet Bucket must pre-exist must pre-exist — "prior to configuring the backend" Versioning recommended, not automatic recommended, not automatic Encryption encrypt, kms_key_id, sse_customer_key kms_encryption_key (migratable) or encryption_key (not migratable) CI credentials assume_role_with_web_identity ADC, attached service account, or impersonate_service_account IAM granularity four statements, s3:DeleteObject on the .tflock but not on state one line: Storage Object Admin on the bucket Backend/provider identity separable by design — the multi-account pattern depends on it (A7) GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS is read by both; use GOOGLE_BACKEND_CREDENTIALS to split them

The lock is the same idea twice. Neither cloud runs a lock service: both write one object that must not already exist, and both surface the failure as a 412. Once you have seen that, "does this backend support locking" becomes a question about whether the store offers a conditional write.

The differences that will actually catch you are use_lockfile defaulting to false — a valid S3 backend block can be silently unlocked — and GCS refusing to migrate a customer-supplied encryption key, which needs an out-of-band rewrite first.

🧪 Verified — a GitLab pipeline writing to the s3 backend

Run 2026-08-19 on Terraform 1.15.8, gitlab/gitlab-ce:19.2.4-ce.0 and gitlab-runner:v19.2.2, tuned per gitlab-memory-constrained. Walkthrough: labs/chapter15/gitlab/.

  • The pipeline is the point. validate → plan → manual apply, the job container on the emulator's network, backend "s3" initialising inside CI, and the bucket ending with app/terraform.tfstate from a workstation beside ci/terraform.tfstate from the runner. The forge held the code and ran the job; the object store held the state.
  • gitlab/gitlab-runner:latest breaks every job. It was a pre-release (19.3.0~pre.1819), and the runner derives its helper image tag from its own version, so prepare_executor failed on gitlab-runner-helper:x86_64-v19.3.0 — manifest unknown. Pin the runner to a released tag on GitLab's own line.

  • --clone-url is not optional here. GitLab advertises external_url, which must be 127.0.0.1 for a browser and is unreachable from a job container.

  • It fits. 3.54 GB image on disk, 2.3 GB resident at steady state with swap untouched, ~7 minutes from up -d to serving. GitLab's 16 GB headline is the untuned figure and is not what this needs.

  • healthy is not ready. The container reported healthy after ~1 minute while gitlab-ctl status still listed only gitaly, postgresql, redis, logrotate and sshd — no puma, no nginx. HTTP answered six minutes later. Wait on /users/sign_in, not on the health status.
  • 127.0.0.1, not localhost. On Windows, localhost resolves to ::1 first and the published IPv6 mapping gave an empty reply (curl exit 52) while 127.0.0.1 returned 200 — and the same request succeeded inside the container. external_url has to be the IPv4 literal or every link GitLab generates is unreachable.
  • The backend works exactly as documented. Empty backend "http" {} plus the eight -backend-config flags, terraform_data only, no provider plugin: init succeeded, apply wrote "serial": 1, and the state read back over /api/v4/projects/1/terraform/state/lab.
  • A lock taken by hand blocks the apply, with HTTP remote state already locked: ID=manual-holder. The interesting part is the Lock Info block: the request claimed Who: lab@host and Terraform printed Who: root. GitLab overwrites the holder with the token's own identity and stamps its own Created time — the lock belongs to a GitLab user, not to whatever the client asserted.
  • Versions are addressable by serial. After the second apply, /versions/1 and /versions/2 both return 200 and /versions/3 returns 404 — the counter ch09-state-fundamentals measured, doubling as version history.

🧪 Verified — the gcs backend against a local GCP emulator

Run 2026-08-19 on Terraform 1.15.8 against floci-gcp (MIT, port 4588), which the labs start behind a --profile gcp. The book's AWS emulator cannot serve this backend at all: gcs talks to the Google JSON API at /storage/v1/b, and a source grep of the AWS emulator finds no Google surface anywhere. Lab: labs/chapter15/lab3/.

  • State landed at terraform/state/default.tfstate from prefix = "terraform/state", confirming that the workspace name is part of every object path here rather than only of non-default ones.
  • Locking needed no argument and refused a concurrent run with googleapi: Error 412: ifGenerationMatch: 1787133258314 != 0, conditionNotMet against gs://tf-state-lab/terraform/state/default.tflock. Same conditional-write idea as S3's 412, in Google's spelling.
  • storage_custom_endpoint is being used off-label. HashiCorp documents it for Private Service Connect — "the protocol, the DNS name … and the path for the Cloud Storage API (/storage/v1/b)" — and it happens to be a plain URL override. That is this project's finding, not a documented promise.

🧪 Verified — the s3 backend against the lab emulator

Run on Terraform 1.15.8 against Floci 1.5.33 on :4566, so this whole topic is exercisable with no AWS account. Full transcripts in tf-backend-configure and tf-state-locking.

  • endpoints is an attribute, not a block. endpoints { s3 = … } fails to parse; write endpoints = { s3 = "http://localhost:4566" }, plus use_path_style and the skip_* flags.
  • The documented leak is real. .terraform/terraform.tfstate holds the resolved backend config as JSON including access_key/secret_key, and the same values are embedded in the msgpack tfplan entry inside a saved plan file.
  • use_lockfile locking is a <key>.tflock sibling object, present only while the operation runs. A concurrent command fails with PutObject … 412 PreconditionFailed — the conditional write is the lock — and prints the Lock Info block with the ID, holder, operation, and start time.
  • A partial block can be completely empty. backend "s3" {} plus -backend-config="./config.s3.tfbackend" initializes fine; the "keys set to empty values" the docs show is a style, not a requirement.

📌 init backend/provider flags

terraform init isn't just first-run setup — its flags manage the backend/providers over a project's life: -backend-config=… (partial/dynamic backend config), -migrate-state (move state to a new backend), -reconfigure (ignore existing state when switching), and -upgrade (re-resolve providers and refresh the lock file within constraints). (See feature-history.)

📌 Four properties of a hardened state backend

Ephemeral values don't cover every case — some secrets land in state even when you're doing it right (a data-source read you chose because the value must persist, or a resource that returns a credential on creation, like an IAM access key). When a secret has to be in the file, protect the file. Four properties matter: encrypted, versioned, locked, and readable only by the identities that run Terraform. On S3 the backend block carries two of them (encrypt = true, kms_key_id with your key rather than the S3 default, and use_lockfile = true); the other two live on the bucket (enable S3 Versioning so a corrupted state is recoverable, and scope the bucket IAM to the run identities). GCS uses kms_encryption_key plus Object Versioning; Azure Blob authenticates via use_oidc.

Backend config leaks harder than provider config: it is copied into .terraform/ and captured in plan files. Backend credentials come from the environment — never inline, and never as -backend-config values. (See infisical-terraform-secrets; the state-encryption backend list is in tf-manage-sensitive-data; cross-links A6.)

HashiCorp documents this directly (tf-backend-configure), and names the two plaintext files: .terraform/terraform.tfstate (the backend config for the working directory) and every plan file, each capturing that config as it stood at plan time. The consequence to plan around: a saved plan applies with its own frozen backend config, not current settings, so time-limited credentials baked into it can expire before the apply runs. Environment variables are read fresh at apply and are the documented fix.

📌 terraform_remote_state grants access to the whole state, not just outputs

The data source exposes only root outputs to your configuration — but "the state snapshot data is a single object, and so any user or server which has enough access to read the root module output values will also always have access to the full state snapshot data by direct network requests." State stores resource attributes in plaintext, secrets included. HashiCorp: "Don't use terraform_remote_state if any of the resources in your configuration work with data that you consider sensitive."

Two recommended alternatives:

  • On HCP Terraform / Enterprise — use the tfe_outputs data source, which "does not require full access to workspace state to fetch outputs."
  • Elsewhere — publish shared data explicitly to a store with its own access controls (SSM Parameter Store, Consul KV, a Kubernetes ConfigMap, DNS records, an S3 object + jsonencode/jsondecode). Bonus: non-Terraform systems can read it too. Encapsulate the choice in a data-only module so you can swap strategies later.

Also: only root-level outputs are readable. Nested-module outputs need an explicit passthrough output block in the producing config's root. (See tf-remote-state-data; cross-links A6 (secrets).)

📌 force-unlock — use with care

When a run crashes mid-apply the state lock can be left held; terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID releases it manually (the lock ID is printed in the error). Use only after confirming no run is actually in progress — force-unlocking a live run corrupts state. (See feature-history.)

HashiCorp scopes it tighter than "no run in progress": force-unlock is for your own lock, when automatic unlocking failed — not a tool for clearing a colleague's stuck run. The lock ID is a nonce identifying one acquisition, so you cannot unlock blind and a stale ID will not release the current lock. (See tf-state-locking.)

The command reference adds three things the concept page leaves out (tf-cmd-force-unlock). Its single option, -force, only suppresses the confirmation prompt: LOCK_ID stays a required positional argument either way, so there is no blind-unlock form of this command. It “does not modify your infrastructure”, which is worth knowing before running it during an incident, since the damage it can do is the second writer it permits rather than anything it touches itself. And “local state files cannot be unlocked by another process” — the local backend locks through system APIs, so a stuck local lock is a process to deal with, not a lock to break. This is a remote-backend command.

📌 S3 native state locking

The S3 backend now has native state locking via a lock file in the bucket (use_lockfile = true) — the separate DynamoDB table is no longer required. Older tutorials still show the S3+DynamoDB pairing; prefer native locking on new setups. (See feature-coverage-matrix.)

Corrected 2026-08-13 — Terraform got here first, not OpenTofu. This callout used to read "Terraform 1.11+; OpenTofu shipped native S3 locking in 1.10", which invites the wrong conclusion because both projects number releases 1.x on different schedules. By date: Terraform 1.10 (2024-11-27) introduced it as opt-in alongside DynamoDB, Terraform 1.11 (2025-02-27) made it GA and deprecated the DynamoDB arguments, and OpenTofu 1.10 (June 2025) shipped it about seven months after Terraform's first. Terraform 1.10 takes both locks during the transition. (See release-feature-map, opentofu-release-feature-map.)

📌 OCI Object Storage backend (Terraform 1.12)

Terraform 1.12 added a native OCI Object Storage backend (Oracle Cloud), joining S3/GCS/azurerm/HCP as a first-class remote-state store. (See feature-history.)

📌 Coming: pluggable state stores (state_store) — watch, don't adopt

The backend list is currently fixed and built in, which is why the catalogue above is finite. Terraform has been building a way out: a state_store block inside terraform, letting a provider supply state storage the way it supplies resources.

It has been in Terraform's config parser since 1.13 and is still gated behind AllowExperimentalFeatures in 1.16.0 (re-verified at the GA tag, parser_config.go:143), so it is alpha-build-only and unusable in a normal release. It appears in no changelog — not even the EXPERIMENTS sections that do list deferred actions and test cleanup — so there is no release note to watch. Found by diffing config schemas across tags. OpenTofu declares no state_store block — internal/configs has nothing corresponding — so this is the one place Terraform has in-flight architectural work the fork does not. One nuance worth stating precisely: OpenTofu does carry ValidateStateStoreConfig and ConfigureStateStore in its vendored tfplugin6 protobuf, because both tools share that plugin protocol. The wire surface exists on both sides; only Terraform exposes a configuration block for it. Nothing to do today; know the name so you recognise it when it lands. (See release-feature-map.)

Milestone: You can bootstrap a state bucket and migrate a project onto both the s3 and gcs backends on open-source Terraform or OpenTofu, explain where each one puts the object and why the workspace name appears in one path and not the other, and demonstrate a lock being refused on each — naming the conditional write behind both 412s. You can read another configuration's outputs with terraform_remote_state and say who else can read that state as a result. And you can run the whole thing from a pipeline on a forge, with the state in the bucket rather than on the forge, and no long-lived cloud credential in CI.

items.title: ✅ I7 — State management operations
items.text:
What it is: The state-surgery toolkit — import (+ import blocks), state mv/rm, refresh, detecting and reconciling drift, and moved/removed config blocks.

Why you need it: Real infrastructure predates your config, gets renamed, and drifts; you must bring it under management without destroying it.

How to learn it:

  1. Interactive — HCTut "Import" + "Manage resource drift" (~1.5 hrs) — import a manually-created resource and reconcile a deliberate drift. The import half is captured in tut-state-import and costs nothing to run, since the resource it adopts is a local Docker container rather than anything in a cloud account. It is the whole config-driven workflow end to end: the import block's two arguments (id, provider-specific; to, the state address), terraform plan -generate-config-out gen.tf for best-guess HCL (TF 1.5+), the pruning step that draft requires, and the apply that lands 1 to import, 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy. The drift half is tut-resource-drift, and it does cost money — the drift is manufactured with three aws ec2 calls against a real EC2 instance, so there is no local-emulator version of it. Findings from both are below.

    Then run the toolkit end to end — HCTut "Manage resource state" (~24 min, needs Terraform 1.7+ and an AWS account). This is the page that puts every operation in this topic into one narrative: read the raw state JSON, apply -replace, terraform state mv between two state files, a removed block, terraform import back, reconcile an out-of-band delete, destroy. Captured as tut-state-cli. Two cautions before running it, both below.

  2. Reference — HCDocs import resources (tf-import, with tf-import-single, tf-import-bulk, tf-import-generate, tf-block-import and tf-block-list behind it), moved (tf-block-moved), removed (tf-block-removed), state subcommands (tf-cmd-state, with tf-cmd-state-list and tf-cmd-state-show behind it), manually update state (tf-cli-state, the section index for everything that writes state) and its resource addressing reference (tf-resource-addressing, the grammar all of the above parse) (~45 min) — prefer config-driven import/moved over CLI surgery. Know the full state toolkit: list / show (inspect), mv / rm (surgery), pull / push (read/write raw state — dangerous, backup first; tf-cmd-state-pull, tf-cmd-state-push), and replace-provider (tf-cmd-state-replace-provider — rewrite a provider source address in state, e.g. after a registry namespace change or a Terraform→OpenTofu move). The forget-without-destroying procedure has its own page, captured in tf-state-remove: the five steps, why HashiCorp recommends the removed block over terraform state rm (the block goes through plan, so you preview the result), and the fact that re-adopting the resource later requires an import, not an edit.

  3. Book chapter — TID Ch 6 (state operations) (~1 hr) — safe patterns and recovery.
  4. Book chapter — TUR Ch 3 (the isolation half) (~30 min) — why state operations get easier the smaller each state file is. Captured as 03-manage-state: the bulkhead metaphor, the environment-then-component tree, and the three costs of it (many folders means many applies, duplication until modules, and cross-folder references that force terraform_remote_state).

🔧 Why moved avoids a destroy — the order of operations

Every other source states the effect; tf-block-moved states the mechanism:

Before creating a new plan for the resource specified in the to field, Terraform checks the state for an existing object at the address specified in the from field. Terraform renames existing objects to the string specified in the to field and then creates a plan. […] As a result, Terraform does not destroy the resource during the Terraform run.

The state rename happens before the plan is computed. So by the time Terraform diffs configuration against state, the new address already has an object bound to it and there is nothing to create. Without the block, the plan runs against a state where the new address is empty and the old one is unclaimed — one creation and one deletion, because an address is an identity.

It also explains why the block is safe to leave in place: a from that matches nothing in state finds nothing to rename, and planning proceeds unchanged.

📌 Instance keys across the three refactoring blocks — removed is the odd one out

With all three block references captured, the comparison is complete and it is not symmetric:

Block Instance keys in the address? import — to Yes — aws_instance.example[0], aws_instance.example["env"] (tf-block-import) moved — from / to Yes, on either side, and mixing an index with a key is exactly how a count → for_each migration is written (tf-modules-refactoring) removed — from No — "You cannot include instance keys… if the resource is configured to provision multiple instances" (tf-state-remove)

And the reason is not in any of the three pages. The address reference says an incomplete address is legal, and that "the meaning depends on the context, so you'll need to refer to the documentation for the specific feature you are using which parses resource addresses" (tf-resource-addressing). There is one grammar and several parsers. Nothing forbids removed from taking an instance key; removed declines to accept one.

A multi-instance resource can therefore be adopted per instance and rearranged per instance, but only forgotten wholesale. Worth knowing before planning a staged migration in either direction.

📌 state pull is not a byte copy — it upgrades the state on the way out

"This command downloads the state… upgrades the local copy to the latest state file version that is compatible with locally-installed Terraform, and outputs the raw format to stdout", and therefore "you cannot use this command to inspect the Terraform version of the remote state" (tf-cmd-state-pull).

Measured on v1.15.8: a state file reading "terraform_version": "1.9.0" came back as "1.15.8", with a "check_results": null field materialised that the older format did not carry. serial and lineage survive, which is what keeps the pull-edit-push loop legal.

So terraform state pull > backup.json is a format-upgraded copy, not the bytes the backend holds — fine as a rollback source, useless as evidence of what version wrote the original. For a true copy take the automatic terraform.tfstate.<unix>.backup a modifying command writes, or fetch the object from the backend directly.

It is also read-only: no -lock flags, no backup, only -var/-var-file. Consistent with the boundary in the callout above.

📌 On Windows, the docs' PowerShell advice depends on which PowerShell you have

State files "must be in UTF-8 format without a byte order mark (BOM)", and the page tells Windows readers to pipe into Set-Content. Measured here, both halves of that instruction behave differently across generations:

piped into Set-Content redirected with > PowerShell 7.6.5 UTF-8, no BOM ✅ UTF-8, no BOM ✅ Windows PowerShell 5.1 no BOM, but ANSI — é becomes E9, not C3 A9 ⚠️ UTF-16LE with a FF FE BOM ❌

On 7 the advice is redundant; on 5.1 it only avoids the BOM, and any non-ASCII value in state is written in the ANSI codepage. -Encoding UTF8 does not fix 5.1 either, since that writes UTF-8 with a BOM. The reliable form there, verified: [System.IO.File]::WriteAllText(path, text, (New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding $false)).

This is the third such instruction in the collection — after the address-quoting rows in tf-cmd-state-show and tf-cmd-state-mv, both verified broken on PowerShell 7. Treat any "For PowerShell" line in these docs as untested against the shell you are actually running.

📌 Approval defaults across the state-writing commands are not consistent

Three commands in this topic write state, and each handles confirmation differently. Verified on v1.15.8.

Command Preview? Prompt? state replace-provider Yes — lists every affected address Yes, and with no terminal it aborts: Error asking for approval: EOF (tf-cmd-state-replace-provider) state mv No No — it rewrites bindings immediately (tf-cmd-state-mv) refresh No No, and no flag asks for one — refresh has no -auto-approve, because it has no approval step to skip (tf-cmd-refresh)

state mv and state rm do have a preview; it is off by default. -dry-run on either prints Would move … / Would remove …, leaves state untouched and writes no backup, measured on v1.15.8. state push and replace-provider have no such flag, so the wholesale overwrite is the one operation that cannot be rehearsed.

The ordering is backwards from the risk. The command that merely rewrites a source string asks first; the one that rebinds objects to new addresses does not; and the one that can drop every tracked object on bad credentials has no way to be made to ask. Reach for -auto-approve only where a script genuinely needs it, and remember replace-provider is the one that will hang a CI job without it.

📌 The forced backup belongs to the local backend, not to the state family

From tf-cmd-state, the hub for the family, and it is the rule only one individual command page repeats — state replace-provider's, which is not the one that most needs it: "backups for state modification can not be disabled. Due to the sensitivity of the state file, Terraform forces every state modification command to write a backup file. You'll have to remove these files manually." The path is set with -backup; read-only subcommands (list, show) write nothing.

The guarantee is narrower than it sounds. It covers terraform state <subcommand> on the local backend only. A removed or moved block goes through apply, so the timestamped backup never applies to that path — which is the path this topic otherwise recommends, and which gets only the local backend's single-slot terraform.tfstate.backup, overwritten by the next apply. The unconditional keep backups instruction on tf-cli-state is therefore aimed squarely at the config-driven route, where the CLI does nothing for you.

⚠️ And the rule is not even true of the whole family. terraform state push modifies state and writes no backup — verified on v1.15.8, and confirmed in the source at that tag, where state_push.go has no backup handling while state_mv.go threads one through (tf-cmd-state-push). The most destructive command in the topic keeps no copy of what it replaced.

The boundary is not the command family either. terraform untaint modifies state and takes the state lock, yet its -backup is grouped with -state/-state-out as a legacy, local-backend-only option (tf-cmd-untaint) — the flags tf-backend-local records the docs as disowning. So an untaint against a remote backend writes state with no automatic backup at all, exactly like the removed/moved path.

⚠️ Measured 2026-08-23 — against a remote backend no subcommand in the family writes a backup at all. tf-cmd-state says backups are "still written to disk" when operating on remote state; on v1.15.8 with an S3 backend, state mv and state rm write nothing anywhere, and -backup is refused with "legacy options that operate on a local state file only." state_meta.go applies the timestamped path only behind if lb, ok := realState.(*statemgr.Filesystem); ok, which a remote backend never satisfies. So the two documented sentences together promise the opposite of what happens, and the earlier reading here — that a remote state mv leaks a plaintext copy onto the CI runner — is withdrawn; gitlab-tf-state and tf-state-backends keep their access-control argument, and what is lost is the rollback. Take the copy deliberately with terraform state pull before remote state surgery. Measured in labs/chapter16/section10/remote/.

⚠️ And the timestamp is whole seconds, time.Now().UTC().Unix(), so two operations in the same second share one filename and the second overwrites the first. Eight runs of labs/chapter16/section10/same-second/ gave 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 backup files; on a collision the survivor holds the state after the first move. A script issuing several state mv calls is the shape that hits it.

On the local backend, backups accumulate, each a full copy of a file the same page calls sensitive, and nothing prunes them.

Measured on v1.15.8 (tf-cmd-state-mv): the forced backup is written as terraform.tfstate.<unix-timestamp>.backup, so successive operations do not overwrite each other and none of them overwrites the local backend's own terraform.tfstate.backup. They accumulate. The binary is blunter than the docs about why — "Due to the destructive nature of this command, backups are required" — and on a cross-state move it writes one per state file.

On PowerShell, write -backup path or quote the pair; an unquoted -backup=path gets split and the backup lands somewhere else.

📌 An address with the index left off means every instance

From tf-resource-addressing, and it is the sentence to keep from that page: "Omitting an index when addressing a resource where count > 1 means that the address references all instances." The same holds one level up — module.foo is every resource in every instance of that module call, and module.foo[0] is the narrowing.

An address identifies zero or more instances, so how big the set is depends on how much you left off. What that means in practice depends entirely on which command is parsing it:

Parser A bare aws_instance.web with count = 4 terraform state list filters to all four (tf-cmd-state-list) terraform state show error — it requires an address resolving to one instance (tf-cmd-state-show) -target the whole set, and its dependency walk is per resource anyway, not per instance (this topic's -target callout below) terraform state rm the whole set — which is the dangerous one

Two legacy rules from the same page, both of which changed what an unchanged address means. Module indexes need v0.13+, since before that a module could not have multiple instances. And a bare resource spec has meant the root module only since v0.12 — earlier versions matched the same type and name in any descendant module, so a pre-0.12 terraform taint aws_instance.web could reach into a child module where today's cannot.

📌 Two arguments for moved, and module authors need the second one

The path already carries the mechanism argument from tf-block-moved: Terraform renames the object in state before computing the plan, so no destroy is ever proposed. tf-cli-state-move gives a different one, and it is the argument that decides the question for anyone publishing a module: "we recommend using the Terraform language's refactoring features to document in your module exactly how the resource names have changed over time. Terraform reacts to this information automatically during planning, so users of your module do not need to take any unusual extra steps."

A state mv fixes your state; a moved block fixes everyone's. The CLI path cannot be shipped — every consumer would have to learn the operation and perform it correctly against their own state.

The same page is also the source for why losing an address is normal rather than exceptional: Terraform loses track when you rename a resource, move it to a different module, or change its provider, and "usually that's fine" — destroy-and-recreate is the correct outcome of a new address. These commands exist only for the minority of cases where the object must survive. That third trigger also explains the sidebar: a provider change is an address change, which is why replace-provider is filed under Moving Resources rather than anywhere provider-shaped.

📌 moved is captured hands-on in A8 — two things to bring back here

The moved block's own tutorial sits in A8 (tut-move-config), but two of its findings belong to this topic's model of state. An address is an identity, so a plan line reading "because X is not in configuration" means an address in state has no matching block — indistinguishable, to Terraform, between a deletion and a rename. And moved preserves identity, not configuration: moving a resource into a differently-implemented module produced 0 to add, 3 to change, 0 to destroy, because the destination's defaults differ from the source's. A zero-destroy plan is not a zero-impact plan.

moved also works only within one state file. Splitting a state still needs tf-state-refactor's machinery, which is the migration tax tut-organize-configuration names and then dodges by destroying everything.

📌 state mv moves state and leaves the configuration behind

The cross-file form is shorter than tf-state-refactor's two-file version — run from the source directory, only the destination needs naming:

terraform state mv -state-out=../terraform.tfstate aws_instance.example_new aws_instance.example_new

But "the move command will update the resource in state, but not in your configuration file", so a successful move leaves the destination one plan away from undoing it:

  # aws_instance.example_new will be destroyed
  # (because aws_instance.example_new is not in configuration)

The fix is manual — paste the resource block into the destination configuration, then the next apply is a no-op. moved has no such step, but works only within one state file, which is why the cross-file case still needs state mv (or removed + import, which tf-state-refactor prefers for new migrations). Verified in tut-state-cli.

📌 The . plan symbol — the forget marker

A removed block with lifecycle { destroy = false } plans as a lone period where +/-/~/-/+ would go, and no legend the plan prints explains it:

 # aws_instance.example_new will no longer be managed by Terraform, but will not be destroyed
 # (destroy = false is set in the configuration)
 . resource "aws_instance" "example_new" {

Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

0 to destroy on a plan that rewrites state — same counter semantics as apply -refresh-only. The accompanying warning names the exit cost: "You will need to import them into Terraform to manage them again." Transcript from tut-state-cli; the contrasting 1 to destroy for a bare removed block was measured in tf-block-removed.

📌 Forget a resource without destroying it — removed alone is NOT enough

Terraform's config-driven way to drop a resource from state is the removed block (preferred over terraform state rm) — but you must write lifecycle { destroy = false }. A bare removed block destroys the object.

removed {
  from = aws_instance.legacy
  lifecycle { destroy = false }   # omit this and the instance is destroyed
}

Verified on v1.15.6: without the lifecycle block, plan reports 1 to destroy; with destroy = false it reports 0 to destroy and warns "will no longer be managed by Terraform, but will not be destroyed." Corrected 2026-08-21: this used to read "the removed block was forget-only in v1.7, so older material describes the old behavior." Verified in the source instead — internal/configs/removed.go at tag v1.7.0 already defaults Destroy to true and already parses lifecycle { destroy }, and the v1.7.0 CHANGELOG announces both directions. There is no version in which a bare block was safe, so TID Ch2 §2.9 was imprecise when written rather than overtaken by a change. (See tf-block-removed.)

Two more constraints from tf-state-remove. from cannot take an instance key — aws_instance.example[1] is rejected, so a count/for_each resource is forgotten in full or not at all. And you must delete every reference to the resource's attributes before applying; terraform validate enumerates them.

OpenTofu 1.12 adds a lifecycle alternative — destroy = false on the resource itself — doing the same "forget, don't destroy" without a removed block. No longer OpenTofu-only: Terraform 1.16 adds the same lifecycle argument (destroy = false to prevent a resource being destroyed), so this converges rather than staying a fork difference. Until 1.16 is stable, the removed block is still the Terraform answer. (See release-feature-map, tf115-ot112-features, ot-dynamic-prevent-destroy.)

🔧 Hand-write or generate? The docs have a rule

We recommend manually writing the resource block when you know how to configure all or most of the resource's arguments. Use generated configuration when importing multiple resources or a single complex resource that you do not already have the configuration for.

So -generate-config-out is the fallback for resources you do not already understand, not the default route (tf-import-single). Worth knowing before reading tut-state-import, which generates because it is teaching the flag.

Either way the target is identical, and both pages state it from opposite ends. Hand-writing: the strict minimum block is just type and label, but "you should include provider-specific resource arguments that have non-default values", because "Terraform uses default values for arguments you do not include" and a substituted default that does not match reality plans an update — or a replacement, if the argument forces one. Generating: prune the all-arguments draft down to "only required arguments and arguments whose values differ from defaults."

The configuration should name exactly the arguments whose values differ from the provider's defaults. Too many is noise; too few is tut-state-import's env = null, which turned an adoption into a destroy.

📌 You can adopt one instance of a count/for_each resource. You cannot forget one.

import's to takes an instance key (tf-import-single):

import {
  to = aws_instance.example[0]        # count
  id = "i-abcd1234"
}

import {
  to = aws_instance.example["env"]    # for_each
  id = "i-abcd1234"
}

The removed block's from explicitly cannot — "You cannot include instance keys, such as aws_instance.example[1], if the resource is configured to provision multiple instances" (tf-state-remove). So a multi-instance resource is populated per instance and forgotten wholesale. A staged migration into Terraform is possible; a staged migration out is not.

Two more things to and the block accept. A module. prefix, so the destination resource block can live in a child module while the import block stays in the root — to = module.instances.aws_instance.example. And a provider argument taking an alias, provider = aws.europe, which is how you import an object that the default provider configuration cannot see. That is the correct fix for tut-refresh's scenario, where a wrong-region provider made a live instance refresh as has been deleted.

📌 import blocks are idempotent, which is why you can leave them in

Because the import block is idempotent, applying an import action and running another plan does not generate another import action as long as that resource remains in your state. Furthermore, attempting to import a resource into the same address more than once has no impact.

Terraform also "records that it imported the resources and that it did not create them." Both tf-import-single and tf-import-bulk therefore recommend keeping the block "as a record of the resource's origin for future module maintainers" — free on every later plan, and the only thing in the configuration distinguishing an adopted resource from a created one. Same disposition as a moved block (tut-move-config).

📌 Resource identity — id or identity, and the choice is not stylistic

Terraform 1.12 added an identity attribute to import blocks as an alternative to id (the two are mutually exclusive). The reason is in tf-import: Terraform identifies a resource "according to either the ID assigned by the cloud provider or a collection of specific attributes defined by the provider."

The page's own example shows what it means. An AWS s3_bucket identity is three attributes, account_id, bucket and region, where an aws_instance is identified by id alone. The page gives no reason for the split and sends you to the provider for one.
