📌 Automated dependency updates (Dependabot / Renovate) → now A10

A pipeline gates changes you make. It does nothing about dependencies going stale, and exact pins turn into a frozen ratchet without something to move them. Dependabot covers registry modules, publicly reachable Git repos, and private registries, plus OpenTofu .tofu files and terragrunt.hcl, and is GitHub-only. Renovate covers the same ground on GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket alike, and now has its own topic — A10 — because the multi-forge setup, the platform-by-platform feature gaps and the lock-file behaviour need more room than a callout. Either turns an upgrade into a PR carrying a version diff, which is what gives module upgrades the reviewable surface the lock file already gives providers (see I4).

Neither bot updates a SHA-pinned Git module source. Renovate can't (its HCL parser drops the comments a digest annotation would need) and Dependabot skips non-semver refs. So a module SHA-pinned for supply-chain safety is one this note cannot keep current, and it needs a manual review cadence instead. The trade-off and the per-case choice are in I4; the Renovate-side detail is in A10.

📌 Two machine contracts, not one — and what a parser has to know

TID Ch11 §11.1.1 draws the line the docs leave implicit. Commands with a single answer — show, validate, output — return one JSON object carrying format_version. Long-running ones — plan, apply — speak the machine-readable UI: JSONL, one object per line, each with @level, @message, @module, @timestamp and type, where type decides which further fields exist. A CI step that pipes plan -json into a parser is consuming the second contract, so it must read line by line and switch on type.

Three things measured on 1.15.8 that a pipeline parser gets wrong otherwise: validate -json exits 1 on an invalid configuration while still emitting a complete document (so "non-zero" must not be read as "no output to parse"); change_summary arrives twice on an apply that also plans, distinguished by operation: "plan" then "apply", so keeping the last value silently discards the planned counts a gate might want to compare against; and the counters now include action_invocation alongside add/change/remove/import.

📌 Machine-readable plan/apply output

For machine-readable plan/apply output, -json replaces stdout entirely (you lose the human view). OpenTofu 1.12's -json-into=FILENAME writes the JSON to a file while keeping the normal UI on stdout — so CI can parse the JSON and a human can read the log. OpenTofu-only. (See tf115-ot112-features.)

📌 The saved plan is a secret, and it expires by itself

B3 teaches plan -out=FILE → apply FILE. Two disciplines belong to the pipeline that carries it.

Never commit a plan file. HCDocs is explicit: "If your plan includes any sort of sensitive data, even if obscured in Terraform's terminal output, it will be saved in cleartext in the plan file." It also embeds a full prior-state snapshot and every input variable value. Move it between jobs as a CI artifact with short retention (upload-artifact/download-artifact, GitLab artifacts:), restrict who can download it, and never let it reach VCS. Same hazard class as state, so pair with A6.

Staleness is enforced for you. The plan records the prior state's lineage and serial. apply FILE compares both against current state before doing anything and refuses on mismatch: "Saved plan is stale — the state was changed by another operation after the plan was created", or "Saved plan does not match the given state" for a different lineage. Any apply landing in the gap invalidates the pending plan. Verified in repos/terraform at internal/backend/local/backend_local.go:319-331; the check dates to v1.1.0, so it holds everywhere you'll run. Consequence for pipeline design: a long approval window doesn't risk a wrong apply, it just guarantees a re-plan. Combine with state locking so two applies can't interleave. HCP Terraform handles this server-side with its own refusal reasons.

📌 OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp in a pipeline fails the run when the collector is down

Tracing a pipeline's Terraform/OpenTofu runs is worth doing (E5), but the enable switch is not free. Both binaries exit 1 with "Could not initialize telemetry: …" when the exporter cannot be constructed while that variable is set, so exporting it globally in a runner image means a collector outage breaks plan, not just observability. Set it per-step, and treat the collector as a dependency of the pipeline.

The payoff is OpenTofu-only for now: it reads TRACEPARENT (1.10), so if the pipeline exports a W3C trace context before invoking tofu, the run's spans parent under the pipeline span and one trace covers checkout → plan → apply. Terraform ignores TRACEPARENT (#35444), so its spans always start a detached trace. Also mind the endpoint: the default protocol is http/protobuf (port 4318), and pointing at 4317 without OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc sends HTTP at a gRPC port. (See otel-tracing-facts.)

📌 Making a local plan and a CI plan agree

Byte-identical output is the wrong goal — rendering depends on terminal width and TTY detection, and CI has no TTY. Two plans taken at different moments also should differ if reality drifted. What you actually want is the same actions.

Compare structurally with terraform show -json tfplan (tf-cmd-show — note that plan JSON carries plan + configuration + prior state, three documents, while state JSON carries only values; and a plan made with -refresh=false may not be renderable as JSON at all after a provider schema upgrade). Per the JSON format spec, resource_changes[].change.actions is a closed set — ["no-op"], ["create"], ["read"], ["update"], ["delete","create"], ["create","delete"], ["delete"] — with replace_paths naming what forced a replacement. Project to {address, actions}, sort, hash, compare. Never dump that JSON into a build log: before/after hold real values, and before_sensitive/after_sensitive only mark sensitivity rather than redacting it.

Then pin what causes illegitimate divergence. CLI version (required_version plus an exact version in the runner). Provider versions (committed lock file plus init -lockfile=readonly, B3). The lock file carrying the runner's platform hashes (providers lock -platform=…, B3). Module versions, which nothing locks (I4). Same backend and workspace (I6). Variable inputs, watching for a gitignored *.auto.tfvars or a stray TF_VAR_* in your shell. Cloud identity, since AWS_PROFILE/AWS_REGION differences mean CI is reading a different account altogether. And configuration that is nondeterministic by construction: timestamp(), uuid(), and most_recent = true data-source lookups will differ between any two runs no matter what you pin.

When the goal is "what I reviewed is what runs", stop comparing: plan once in CI, review that artifact, apply that file. Chase local↔CI equality only to debug why CI sees something you don't, and the answer is nearly always state or credentials.

Milestone: You can build a pipeline that posts a plan on pull requests and applies a saved plan on merge, with remote state and locking — passing the plan as a restricted CI artifact rather than committing it, and explaining what makes apply FILE refuse a stale one.

items.title: ⬜ A4 — HCP Terraform / Terraform Cloud
items.text:
What it is: HashiCorp's managed platform — workspaces, VCS-driven and CLI-driven runs, remote execution, remote state, private module registry, and run tasks.

Why you need it: It's on both the Associate and Pro exams, and it's the most common way teams run Terraform at scale without building their own automation.

How to learn it:

  1. Interactive — HCTut "HCP Terraform get started" track (~1.5 hrs) — connect a VCS repo, run a remote plan/apply, use remote state.
  2. Reference — HCDocs "HCP Terraform" workspaces + run workflow (~40 min) — workspace settings, variable sets, and the run lifecycle. Also know the platform extras: cost estimation (shows $ delta on a plan for supported providers), run triggers (one workspace's apply queues another's run), and run notifications. A .terraformignore file controls which files are excluded from the config upload on remote runs. To reach infra on a private network, HCP runs through self-hosted agents (the agent pool executes runs inside your network).
  3. Interactive — HCTut "Share modules in the private registry" (~8 min, HCP-only) — publish a module from a VCS repo into the org's private registry, then consume it from a VCS-driven workspace. Notes: tut-module-private-registry-share. The address form is <HOSTNAME>/<ORGANIZATION>/<MODULE_NAME>/<PROVIDER_NAME> — four segments, app.terraform.io on SaaS — and versions come from git release tags, semver x.y.z with an optional v, non-matching tags ignored, at least one tag required to publish at all. Know the two publishing workflows and what actually separates them: tag-based imports a new version when you push a tag, branch-based makes you click Publish New Version and pick a commit SHA (versions still pin to a commit, so this is not the mutable-ref hazard from I4), cannot re-use a version number, and is the only one that supports module testing — a constraint that lives in the docs, not the tutorial. Registry scope differs by product: HCP shares within an org, Terraform Enterprise within or across orgs. ⚠️ The page misstates its own source-address format with a spurious terraform/ segment and tells you to set the registry Module Name to the repository name; both contradict its own working example. Take the address from the registry page's Usage Instructions. Evidence: cache/search/hcp-private-registry-publishing.md.

  4. Interactive — HCTut "Add public providers and modules to your private registry" (~5 min, HCP-only, no config) — curate public registry entries into the org registry. Notes: tut-private-registry-add. Short, but the thing to get right is what curation isn't: the private registry "stores a pointer" and lets you "designate which public providers and modules are recommended", and after removal "Users in the organization can still use the removed provider or module without changing their configurations." So the source address never changes, uncurated modules stay usable, and nothing breaks on removal — it is a bookmark list with docs attached, and enforcement lives in A5, not here. Worth knowing beyond the page: curation is delegable via the Manage Private Registry permission rather than requiring org ownership, it is drivable through the Registry Providers/Modules APIs, Terraform Enterprise must reach both registry.terraform.io and the Algolia search host or the search box silently returns nothing, and no-code provisioning can be enabled on a curated public module (Standard/Premium) — which turns a community module into UI-provisionable self-service without you maintaining it.

  5. Reference — the open-source private registry: Terrakube (~45 min) — HCP is not the only way to run a private registry, and the comparison is what makes the HCP tutorials above legible as product rather than protocol. Terrakube's registry component implements the module and provider protocols directly (ModuleWebServiceImpl, ProviderWebServiceImpl, WellKnownWebServiceImpl for service discovery), so a source of <host>/<org>/<name>/<provider> works the same way it does against HCP. Verified against repos/terrakube at de53c946, 2026-08-16 — details in terrakube-facts.

    The publish loop is register-then-tag. A Terrakube module is a registration record pointing at a VCS repository, not an upload: name, provider, source, an organization and a VCS connection or SSH credential. Versions are discovered from Git tags by a scheduled refresh job, so you publish a new version by pushing a semver tag — the same contract the public registry enforces. Writes are gated on the manageModule permission, which is admin-only under the predefined roles (see A9).

    Two fields worth knowing because they contradict a rule taught as universal. folder puts the module in a subdirectory and tagPrefix namespaces its tags, so one repository can hold many independently versioned modules. The terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME> naming rule and one-module-per-repository constraint from I5's Standard Module Structure reference are public-registry rules, not Terraform rules, and a private registry can relax them.

  6. Book chapter — TID Ch 8 §8.7 "CD platform overview" (p283) / TUR Ch 10 (~1 hr) — where a managed platform fits versus self-hosted CI. This path previously cited a vague "TID Ch on HCP"; the book has no HCP chapter. Verified against the TOC 2026-08-15: HCP Terraform is §8.7 inside the continuous-delivery chapter, and it is a comparison section — HCP Terraform (p283) is one of six platforms alongside Env0, Spacelift, Scalr, Digger and Terrateam, which is the part worth reading, since it is the only source here that positions HCP against its competitors. ⚠️ Its Terrateam row has since been overtaken: Terrateam's engine was open-sourced under MPL-2.0 and the product is folding into Stategraph (stategraph/stategraph, OCaml), which stores state as a graph in PostgreSQL rather than one JSON blob behind one lock, with enterprise features staying proprietary. Verified 2026-08-15; see the open-source landscape callout in A9. (The cloud block half is already captured in TID Ch 6 §6.4.5 — see the callout below. TID Ch 11 "Alternative interfaces" is not about HCP: it covers wrapping Terraform in a client library, JSON-instead-of-HCL, and CDKTF.)

📌 Already captured — workspaces

The cloud block half of HCP workspaces is written up in workspaces and TID Ch6 §6.4.5: tags versus name selection, project, what an HCP workspace owns beyond state, and the asymmetry when you edit tags later (adds are pushed to HCP, removals are not). A4 adds the platform side — workspace settings, variable sets, and the run lifecycle.

📌 HCP's run queue is not the same guarantee as a state lock

A state lock is held for the duration of one command and released when it ends, so two people can each produce a plan against the same state and the second apply silently invalidates the first person's reviewed plan. HCP Terraform "can also detect attempts to create a new plan when an existing plan is already awaiting approval, by queuing Terraform operations in a central location" — it holds the whole plan-then-approve cycle, not the command. Keep the two apart when comparing HCP against a self-hosted backend: S3 with use_lockfile gives you the lock, not the queue. (See tf-state-remote, tf-state-locking.)

📌 HCP free tier cap

HCP free tier caps at 500 managed resources (legacy free plan ended 2026-03-31).

📌 The cloud block (TF 1.1)

Wire a config to HCP with the cloud block (TF 1.1) inside terraform {} — it sets the org/workspace(s) for remote runs and state, and is the modern replacement for the older remote backend. (See feature-history.)

📌 terraform login / logout

Authenticate the CLI to HCP Terraform (or any private registry host) with terraform login — it runs an OAuth flow and stores a token in ~/.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json; terraform logout revokes it. This is how CLI-driven runs and private-module pulls get credentials. (HCDocs)

📌 Agents are the only layer that emits metrics

Self-hosted HCP Terraform agents ship first-class OpenTelemetry support, unlike either CLI: point them at a collector with -otlp-address / TFC_AGENT_OTLP_ADDRESS (a host:port gRPC address), optionally encrypting that link with -otlp-cert-file / TFC_AGENT_OTLP_CERT_FILE. Without the cert file the connection is unsecured. Use the collector's contrib distribution, not core; a DataDog agent can be targeted directly instead.

The agent emits traces and metrics, where the CLIs emit traces only. Metrics are prefixed tfc-agent. with the unit last (.milliseconds, .bytes): tfc-agent.core.* for agent status and job fetch, …core.runtime.* for Go heap/GC/goroutines, …core.profiler.* for CPU and I/O while busy, …core.terraform.* for 30+ init/plan/apply measurements, …core.policy.* for OPA/Sentinel (Premium only). Spans and metrics carry agent_id, agent_pool_id, organization_name, workspace_name, run_id, run_operation, which is what lets you slice run duration by workspace. Span names are plain English and deliberately undocumented, so explore them in the backend rather than expecting a reference list. ([HCDocs telemetry · tracing · metrics]; see otel-tracing-facts.)

📌 Health assessments (managed drift detection)

Health assessments are HCP Terraform's managed drift detection + continuous validation: HCP periodically runs an out-of-band plan on a workspace and reports whether real infrastructure has drifted from state, and whether the config's check assertions still hold — without you triggering a run. Enable per-workspace (or org default); trigger an on-demand assessment from the workspace Health section. This is the managed counterpart to the CLI-side -refresh-only drift check in I7. Interactive: HCTut "Use health assessments to detect infrastructure drift"; the combined drift-plus-policy flow is "Detect infrastructure drift and enforce policies". (HCDocs)

Milestone: You can run a VCS-driven workspace in HCP Terraform that plans on PR, applies on merge, and stores state remotely.

items.title: ⬜ A5 — Policy as Code
items.text:
What it is: Governance guardrails at three layers — plan-time policy (Sentinel, open-source OPA/Conftest) enforced against a plan in HCP Terraform or CI; static analysis (SAST) of the HCL source (Checkov, Trivy/tfsec, KICS); and cost gating (Infracost).

Why you need it: Organizations must prevent non-compliant infra (untagged, wrong region, oversized) before apply; the Pro exam covers policy/governance.

How to learn it:

  1. Video — HashiCorp "Introduction to Sentinel, Policy as Code Framework" (~40 min) — what policy-as-code enforces and where it runs in the flow.
  2. Interactive — HCTut Sentinel / OPA policy lab (~1.5 hrs) — write a policy that blocks a plan violating a tagging rule.
  3. Reference — HCDocs policy enforcement / Sentinel + OPA Conftest docs (~40 min) — Sentinel for HCP, OPA/Conftest for provider-agnostic CI.
  4. Interactive — run a static scanner in CI (~45 min) — add one of the SAST scanners below to your A3 pipeline and fail the build on a deliberately misconfigured resource.
  5. Book chapter — TID Ch 7 §7.4–§7.5 (~45 min) — the source-side half of this topic, worked end to end: Checkov and Trivy run side by side (they are free and overlap imperfectly, so run both), then custom policy in either Rego-via-TFLint or Checkov YAML. Take the recommendation as given — the book tells you to skip its own Rego section unless your team already runs OPA elsewhere, because a Checkov YAML policy expresses the same rule with no new language. Its motivating example is worth having, since it is not a security rule at all: AWS's GP3 volumes were strictly faster and cheaper than GP2, so "still using GP2" is a policy violation no generic ruleset will ever flag. Two operational details generalise beyond the tools. Suppression asymmetry — #checkov:skip=ID:reason carries a mandatory justification while #trivy:ignore:ID takes none, so a Trivy exception needs an ordinary comment above it or the audit trail is gone; and .trivyignore is project-wide, which is almost never what you mean. Policy distribution — checkov --external-checks-git <repo> loads the rule set from one shared repository, so a policy change reaches every project on its next run, with no PR anywhere (worth pinning to a tag once the set matters). Plan-time policy — Sentinel/OPA against what Terraform will do — is the complementary layer this chapter defers to its Ch8.

📌 Policy is where module governance becomes binding — A4 only makes it discoverable

A curated private registry does not restrict what practitioners can use: it "stores a pointer", designates what is "recommended", and after an entry is removed "Users in the organization can still use the removed provider or module without changing their configurations" (tut-private-registry-add). HashiCorp names the control explicitly in its module-design guide (tut-pattern-module-creation): "With Sentinel, you can assign policy criteria to all Terraform plans before execution. This allows for enforcement such that only modules from the private Terraform registry can be used."

So "approved module list" is two mechanisms, not one — A4 publishes and curates the set, A5 makes it mandatory. Write that policy as a worked example alongside the untagged/oversized ones in the milestone. The complementary control on versions rather than sources is I4's exact-pin discipline, since tf-dependency-lock never locks modules.

📌 Static analysis (SAST) layer

Sentinel/OPA evaluate the plan (what Terraform will do). A second, complementary layer is static analysis (SAST) that scans the HCL source for insecure defaults before a plan — public S3 buckets, 0.0.0.0/0 ingress, unencrypted volumes — against a built-in rule library. The common tools: Checkov (Prisma/Bridgecrew, largest policy set, also does terraform_plan JSON), Trivy (Aqua — absorbed the now-archived tfsec; use Trivy for new work), and KICS (Checkmarx, multi-IaC). Run one on every PR next to fmt/validate; they need no cloud creds and no state, so they're the cheapest guardrail you can add.

📌 tflint — the correctness linter next to the security scanners

The SAST tools above hunt insecure defaults. tflint is the complementary correctness/style linter: deprecated syntax, invalid provider arguments, unpinned dependencies. Two of its terraform ruleset rules enforce the module pinning that I4 recommends but Terraform itself cannot check, because there is no module lock file. terraform_module_version requires registry modules to carry a version, and takes exact = true (default false) to reject every constraint operator except =. terraform_module_pinned_source catches Git and Mercurial sources with no pin at all. Both are cheap PR-time checks needing no creds and no state, so they belong in the same pipeline stage as Checkov/Trivy.

📌 Cost governance (Infracost)

Cost governance — Infracost estimates the $ delta of a plan (it reads terraform plan -json against cloud price APIs) and posts it as a PR comment, so reviewers see cost impact before merge. It's the open, CI-native counterpart to HCP Terraform's built-in cost estimation (A4). Pair it with a policy (infracost has its own policy/threshold gating) to block a PR that blows a budget.

📌 Multi-tenant note — policy scoping is per project, policy authoring is not

A5 assumes one team writing policy for one organization. On a shared platform the two halves separate, and only one of them delegates. A policy set scopes to specific projects, workspaces or tags with exclusions, so each tenant can carry its own mandatory policies on top of a global baseline. Authoring does not scope: creating, editing or deleting Sentinel policies needs the organization-level Manage policies permission, which additionally "implicitly gives permission to read runs on all workspaces". So there is no way to let a tenant write its own policies without also handing it visibility into every other tenant's runs.

The consequence is a workable division rather than a blocker: the platform team owns the policy code, tenants own which sets apply to their project, and a tenant's policy request is a pull request against the platform team's repository. Two override paths need the same care, since Manage policy overrides grants org-wide workspace read (use Delegate policy overrides), and a policy set marked overridable beats even Hard mandatory. Full treatment in A9.

📌 Sentinel and SCPs are not competing policy engines — they fire at different moments

The clearest statement of the split is in the AWS landing-zone guide cited from A7 (VP), and it settles a question this topic otherwise leaves open: what policy as code does not cover. Sentinel evaluates Terraform plans and applies, resource by resource, before anything is provisioned — mandatory tags, IAM boundaries, per-environment rules. An AWS service control policy evaluates every AWS API call, at the account or OU level, at execution time, regardless of what the calling principal was granted — deny a region, deny turning off CloudTrail or GuardDuty, deny wildcard IAM.

So Sentinel is fine-grained, customisable and bypassable by anything that does not go through Terraform, while an SCP is blunt, rigid and unbypassable. A control that must hold against a console user or a rogue script belongs in the SCP; a control about how infrastructure is written belongs in Sentinel. HashiCorp and AWS publish pre-written Sentinel policies as a starting set.

Milestone: You can write a policy that fails any plan creating an untagged or oversized resource, wire it into a run, and add a SAST scanner (Checkov/Trivy/KICS) plus an Infracost cost check to the PR pipeline.

items.title: ⬜ A6 — Secrets & sensitive data
items.text:
What it is: Handling secrets — the sensitive flag, sensitive values in state, ephemeral values / ephemeral resources / ephemeral input variables & outputs / write-only arguments (the modern keep-secrets-out-of-state mechanism), the Vault provider, and dynamic/short-lived provider credentials (OIDC into AWS/Azure/GCP).

Why you need it: State holds secrets in plaintext by default; long-lived cloud keys in pipelines are a top risk. The Pro exam tests sensitive-data best practices.

How to learn it:

  1. Reference — HCDocs "Manage sensitive data" (umbrella) + "Sensitive data in state" + "Dynamic Provider Credentials" (~40 min) — why sensitive isn't encryption and how OIDC removes static keys. (Umbrella captured in tf-manage-sensitive-data — the hide-vs-omit-vs-both decision framework, the version-requirements matrix (0.15 sensitive / 1.10 ephemeral / 1.11 write-only), write-only _wo/_wo_version, and the state-encryption backends.)
  2. Reference — HCDocs "Ephemeral values" (~40 min) — the current best-practice for secrets. sensitive only hides a value in output; it's still written to state in plaintext. Ephemeral values (TF 1.10) exist only during a single command run and are never written to state or plan. Ephemeral resources (a block type that opens/closes a short-lived external object, e.g. fetch a token) and write-only arguments (TF 1.11 — resource arguments like a DB password that Terraform can write but never read back, versioned via a companion *_wo_version attribute) together let you pass a secret straight into a resource with nothing persisted. OpenTofu reached parity in 1.11.
  3. Interactive — HCTut dynamic credentials lab (~1.5 hrs) — configure OIDC so a pipeline assumes a role with no stored secret.

  4. Book chapter — TID Ch 8 §8.5 "Managing secrets" + TUR Ch 6 "Managing Secrets with Terraform" (~1 hr) — Vault integration and secret-injection patterns. Read them together through Secrets and state, which reconciles the two. TID's contribution is the hierarchy: eliminate the secret with OIDC, else a secret manager, else orchestrator storage — in that order, with the last two carrying explicit costs. Three things it gets right that the reference pages underplay. Registering an IdP is authentication, not authorization, and without trust-policy conditions scoping to your repository and workflow, any other customer of that IdP can assume your role — the role ARN is not a secret and does not need to be. A secret manager does not keep secrets out of state: a value pulled by a data source is still written there, so where the platform supports it (ECS taking a Secrets Manager ARN directly) prefer machine-to-machine retrieval that never passes through Terraform. And the argument for eliminating secrets at all is Travis CI's 2021 disclosure — your orchestrator can always read what you store in it. ⚠️ Its thumbprint_list pattern is obsolete: the argument is now Optional, and for Auth0/GitHub/GitLab/Google AWS validates against its own trusted-CA library and ignores any configured value, so the data "tls_certificate" step can go.

    TUR Ch 6's contribution is the trade space TID skips, plus one dated conclusion worth reading as history. Its three techniques for getting a secret into a resource — environment variables, encrypted files, centralised stores — come with advantage and drawback lists that are mirror images: files are versioned, packaged and tested with the code but are near-impossible to rotate or revoke, because the ciphertext stays in Git and a compromised key retroactively opens every past version; stores rotate, revoke and audit per secret but drift out of sync with the code, so a secret added in staging goes missing in production. Nothing wins both, which is why "which technique" is a choice of failure mode rather than a ranking. It is also the only source here that prices the options, and both figures were still exact when re-checked in 2026 ($1/month per KMS key, $0.40 per Secrets Manager secret per month). ⚠️ Its conclusion that secrets in state have "no clear plans for a first-class solution" is the one thing that expired: hashicorp/terraform#516, opened 2014-10-28, was closed as completed on 2025-05-21 once write-only arguments shipped. Version detail and tool status in secrets-tooling-facts.

  5. Reference — Infisical, "A Guide to Terraform Secrets Management" (~25 min) — the end-to-end workflow the HashiCorp reference pages leave out, captured as infisical-terraform-secrets. A vendor post (every example routes through the infisical provider), so read the product comparison as marketing — but the Terraform mechanics check out and three things here have no equivalent in the official docs: a grep that finds random_password stored three times in state (attribute, output, bcrypt hash) against an apply that printed <sensitive> throughout; the same secret fetched ephemerally leaving a 181-byte state with no trace; and an anti-pattern review table. Also the vendor-neutral criteria for picking a secrets manager (official registry provider · ephemeral reads · dynamic secrets + rotation · hosting/license), the note that cloud KMS is not a secrets manager (no per-secret ACLs, audit, or rotation), and where SOPS fits (file encryption whose committed ciphertext still diffs — a complement, not a replacement).

  6. Reference — VP "Integrate Terraform with Vault" (~14 min, marked beta) + "HCP Terraform Vault-backed dynamic credentials for the AWS provider" (~30 min) — the Vault half of this topic, at the scale where it becomes a design question rather than a provider call. The first guide separates the four surfaces people conflate: authenticating Terraform to Vault, dynamic provider credentials for AWS/Azure/GCP, reading and writing secrets with the Vault provider, and the Terraform secrets engine, which runs the relationship the other way by having Vault mint credentials for Terraform runs. It recommends HCP Terraform’s native OIDC trust over any static Vault credential, and — the deployment detail that is easy to miss — Terraform Cloud agents, so “Vault DNS is not exposed to the public internet”. Its mapping advice is the part worth arguing about in your own org: organisation → Vault root namespace, line of business → namespace, environment → its own secrets-engine mount (aws-dev, aws-uat, aws-prod), with the honest caveat that no mapping is correct, only consistent. The second guide is the worked AWS build of that pattern, and it supplies the operational trap: align the TTL of Vault’s STS credentials with the JWT lifetime HCP Terraform issues, then keep runs short, or a long apply dies partway on expired credentials. Both are HCP-side, so they sit beside the direct-OIDC dynamic credentials in A9 rather than replacing them. Cached under cache/web/vp-terraform-integrate-vault.txt and cache/web/vp-terraform-vault-backed-dynamic-credentials-aws.txt.

📌 Role chaining caps the session at one hour, and the provider documentation never says so

Step 6's Vault trap has a native-AWS twin with no Vault in it. AWS defines role chaining as using one role's credentials to assume a second role, and the IAM reference states the limit without qualification: "Role chaining limits your AWS Management Console, AWS CLI or AWS API role session to a maximum of one hour. It applies regardless of the maximum session duration configured for individual roles." Asking for longer is not clamped, it is refused, because the operation fails if you "provide a DurationSeconds parameter value greater than one hour".

The trap is that the AWS provider's own documentation teaches chaining and never mentions the ceiling. It raises role chaining three times, including "IAM Role Chaining is supported by specifying the roles to assume in order", and it describes duration with one identical sentence on both assume_role and assume_role_with_web_identity, "a value from 15 minutes up to the maximum session duration setting for the role". That sentence holds only for a block that is not chaining. Set duration = "4h" on an assume_role layered over an already-assumed identity and the run dies at credential acquisition, with nothing in the provider reference to explain why. Book Ch 17 carried that unqualified wording in its assume_role argument table until this landed; the row is now qualified and the chapter states the cap in full.

Why it decides a CI design. A pipeline that exchanges its OIDC token once for a bootstrap role and then chains from it into a state role and an apply role has bought the one-hour ceiling for the entire run, so a long apply dies partway through. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is not chaining, because its base is a token rather than a role session. Its own DurationSeconds reaches "the maximum session duration setting for the role" with no chaining clause anywhere on the page, up to 12 hours, and the word chaining appears there only in the session-tag paragraph. So let the backend and the provider each exchange the same identity token for their own role instead of chaining from a shared one. That keeps state operations and infrastructure operations as separate principals, which is the split A7 takes from HashiCorp's own multi-account recipe, and it keeps the full session length available.

Verified 2026-08-25 against the IAM Roles terms and concepts page and the AssumeRole and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity API references. Cached as cache/web/aws-iam-role-chaining.txt, cache/web/aws-sts-assumerole.txt and cache/web/aws-sts-assumerolewithwebidentity.txt.

📌 A worked ephemeral + write-only example, end to end

The Manage sensitive data and Ephemeral values references explain the mechanism; tut-no-code-provisioning's RDS module is the shortest complete example of it. An ephemeral "random_password" feeds two write-only arguments — aws_db_instance.password_wo sets the database password, aws_ssm_parameter.value_wo stores it — so the generated secret lands in neither state nor plan file, and "the only way to retrieve that password is by querying the AWS SSM parameter". Contrast infisical-terraform-secrets, where a plain random_password showed up in state three times.

The detail worth stealing is the _version companions. Because the value is never stored, Terraform cannot diff it, so password_wo_version / value_wo_version are what signal a change. The module points both at one local.db_password_version, which is how the database and its SSM copy rotate in the same apply instead of drifting apart. Requires Terraform 1.10 (ephemeral resources) and 1.11 (write-only arguments).

The framing that organizes this topic: Terraform touches secrets it manages (the DB passwords and API keys it sets on your infrastructure) and secrets it uses (the credentials that let it call your cloud and your secrets manager). The first kind is fixed inside the config — ephemeral blocks and write-only arguments. The second is fixed outside it: the credential should reach Terraform from the environment it runs in, never from the code it runs, which in CI means a short-lived OIDC token exchanged against a machine-identity binding (repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main) rather than a stored client secret. The identity ID is public and safe to commit. The TF_VAR_-prefixed secret name is the tie-in — store TF_VAR_db_admin_password and the plan step reads var.db_admin_password with nothing on the command line. (See infisical-terraform-secrets; precedence in tf-input-variables.)

📌 Pass coordinates into modules, not values

A module input like db_password = var.db_password multiplies the problem: every caller must hold the raw value, and it lands in each calling configuration's own state once the module uses it — one secret copied into every stack. Pass the location instead (workspace_id / env_slug / secret_path) and let the module fetch its own value with a data source or, better, an ephemeral block. Access is then controlled in the secrets manager rather than by who holds the variable. (See infisical-terraform-secrets.)

📌 Dynamic secrets vs. rotation — shrinking the theft window

Both replace "one static value that's worth stealing for as long as it lives," and they are not the same mechanism. Dynamic secrets: the platform holds a privileged login to the backend and mints a new user per lease (creation statement in, revocation statement at expiry) — Terraform's apply stores only the instructions, and generating a lease is a separate out-of-band step, so a leaked credential is worthless within hours. Rotation: for systems that need a single standing login — keep two users, one live and one idle, set a new password on the idle one, and switch the mapped secret keys over, so consumers migrate with no downtime and nothing redeploys. Reach for rotation only when dynamic isn't possible. (See infisical-terraform-secrets.)

📌 sensitive leaks through terraform output -json / -raw

sensitive redacts values in normal CLI logs and the HCP UI, but the redaction is narrower than it looks. It redacts on plan/apply/destroy and on terraform output (all). It does not redact when you query by name (terraform output db_password → plaintext), with -json, or with -raw, nor when a child module's output is used in the root — the flags feed automation, so they bypass redaction by design. Combined with the fact that sensitive values are stored in state/plan as plain text anyway, this is why sensitive alone is hiding, not protecting. Use ephemeral (+ write-only args) to keep a secret out of state entirely. (See tf-manage-sensitive-data; the full redaction matrix is in tut-outputs.)

Verified on v1.15.8, because the docs disagree with each other here. terraform output with no argument prints password = <sensitive>; terraform output password prints "notasecurepassword". The language Output Values page claims a named query shows <sensitive> — that is wrong, and the CLI command reference has it right. Transcript in tf-cmd-output. Also settled: terraform output can never surface an ephemeral value, since an ephemeral output is rejected in a root module and a root output cannot derive from a child's ephemeral output.

📌 A saved plan file is as sensitive as state

State gets all the attention, but terraform plan -out=FILE produces a second plaintext artifact with the same problem. HCDocs puts it plainly: "If your plan includes any sort of sensitive data, even if obscured in Terraform's terminal output, it will be saved in cleartext in the plan file." It carries a full prior-state snapshot and every input variable value, so sensitive does nothing for it — the same hiding not protecting gap as the redaction warning above. terraform show -json on that file exposes the lot, with before_sensitive/after_sensitive merely marking which values are secret. Never commit one, never paste one into a build log. The pipeline handling is in A3; the durable fix is the same as for state, which is ephemeral and write-only arguments so the value never enters plan or state at all.

📌 terraform_remote_state is a state-exfiltration path

Granting a config the ability to read another workspace's outputs via terraform_remote_state necessarily grants it read access to that workspace's entire state snapshot — outputs and state live in one object, and anything that can fetch the outputs can fetch the object by direct network request. Secrets in that state are plaintext.

Treat "who may read this state" as the real permission boundary, not "which outputs do I expose." On HCP Terraform use tfe_outputs, which authorizes outputs without full state access; elsewhere publish shared values to a store with its own ACLs. (See tf-remote-state-data; full treatment in I6.)

Milestone: You can run a pipeline that authenticates to a cloud via short-lived OIDC credentials (no static keys), set a resource secret via a write-only argument so it never lands in state, and explain why sensitive alone doesn't protect the state file. (See feature-coverage-matrix.)

items.title: ⬜ A7 — Multi-environment & multi-account patterns
items.text:
What it is: Structuring dev/stage/prod and multiple accounts/regions — CLI workspaces vs directory-per-env vs HCP workspaces, and DRY strategies.

Why you need it: Environment isolation done wrong causes cross-env blast radius; the Pro exam and every real org need a scalable layout.

How to learn it:

  1. Book chapter — TUR Ch 3 (§ "Isolation via Workspaces" p94 / "Isolation via File Layout" p100) + Ch 7 "Working with Multiple Providers" (~2 hrs) — file-layout vs workspace tradeoffs (the definitive treatment), then Ch 7 for the multi-account/multi-region half of this topic (§ "Working with Multiple AWS Accounts" p238). Ch 3 is captured as 03-manage-state, and it is the third source contradicting the terraform.workspace lookup-map pattern the warning below names: its two requirements for real isolation are a folder per environment and a separate backend with different credentials and access controls, with the second doing the actual work. Its footnote also explains why the anti-pattern survives — workspaces were once called "environments", so the feature's own former name taught it.
  2. Reference — HCDocs "Workspaces" (CLI) vs HCP workspaces (~30 min) — understand why CLI workspaces are not environment isolation. In automation, TF_WORKSPACE selects the workspace non-interactively (instead of terraform workspace select). The CLI page is captured in tf-state-workspaces, which pins down the piece the other sources leave vague: which backends actually support named workspaces (ten, enumerated — http and oci are not among them), so "remote backend" and "multiple states" are separate properties. The licensing angle is in workspaces-facts: CLI workspaces ship in OpenTofu too (tofu workspace), while the HCP workspace is a proprietary unit with its own config, variables, run history and RBAC — no single open-source product replaces it, but Terragrunt covers the isolation half and Atlantis or ordinary CI covers the platform half.
  3. Interactive — HCTut "Refactor monolithic Terraform configuration" (~18 min) — walk one dev+prod configuration through monolith → separate files → separate state, with directories and workspaces as alternative endings. Notes: tut-organize-configuration. Do this one for its middle step, which is the best demonstration of blast radius anywhere in the tutorials: a shared random_pet feeds both bucket names, so bumping its length in dev.tf — a file containing nothing but development resources — destroys and recreates production too. Splitting main.tf into dev.tf and prod.tf changes readability and nothing else, because the coupling lives in the reference graph, not the filesystem. Take three more things from it: -target is named and dismissed as "risky and not a sustainable way to manage distinct environments"; converting one state into per-directory states requires state mv work, which the exercise dodges by destroying everything first and real projects cannot; and the local backend moves non-default workspace state to terraform.tfstate.d/<name>/terraform.tfstate. ⚠️ The page teaches CLI workspaces as environment separation, which the HCDocs "Workspaces" (CLI) vs HCP workspaces reference above exists to contradict — read its decision rule as being about configuration duplication, not isolation. Its resource counts are wrong twice over (says 5, describes 9, repo defines 15) and it tells you to comment out a terraform block the current repo does not contain — that repo pins no provider versions at all.
  4. Reference — VP "Use Terraform to build an AWS landing zone" (~40 min) — the account-structure layer this topic otherwise stops short of, and the only landing-zone material in this path. Its organising split is platform landing zone (PLZ) versus workload landing zone (WLZ): the PLZ carries AWS Organizations and the OU tree, federated IAM, hub-and-spoke networking, the security services and centralised logging, and “is not intended for workloads, but rather for enabling and governing them”; each WLZ is an application’s own set of accounts, autonomous to deploy but inheriting the PLZ’s guardrails. The rule that makes it this topic’s material rather than A9’s is one line of its design principles: deploy each zone in a dedicated AWS account and a dedicated Terraform workspace, so the account boundary and the state boundary are the same boundary — A7’s isolation argument at organisation scale. Read it after the file-layout material above, and pair it with the Sentinel-versus-SCP split in A5. Cached: cache/web/vp-build-aws-lz-with-terraform.txt.
  5. Reference — HCDocs "S3 backend" § "Multi-account AWS Architecture" (~25 min) — the one place HashiCorp publishes a multi-account layout as a worked recipe rather than as advice, captured in tf-backend-s3. Read it against the file-layout material above, because it is also the strongest published case for the workspace pattern this topic otherwise argues against. What makes it defensible is that the workspace name is not merely a state path: the provider does assume_role = { role_arn = var.workspace_iam_roles[terraform.workspace] }, so selecting a workspace selects the AWS account the apply runs in. The isolation is real, not nominal, which is exactly what TF2026's Lecture 09 demo below lacks. Its structural rule is that the tool's own infrastructure lives outside what the tool manages — "ideally the infrastructure that is used by Terraform should exist outside of the infrastructure that Terraform manages" — so one administrative account holds the human IAM users and the single state bucket for every workspace, while each environment account holds only a role that trusts the administrative account. The split that makes it work: the backend authenticates as the administrator's own user in the administrative account, and the provider assumes the environment role, so state operations and infrastructure operations run as different principals. In automation, put the runner on an EC2 instance in the administrative account with an instance profile, and use "a separate EC2 instance for each target account so that its access can be limited only to the single account." The page then closes the hole its own default leaves — "all users can read and write states for all workspaces" — with a per-object IAM policy, and the statement people omit is the third one: s3:DeleteObject on <key>.tflock, because a policy written before use_lockfile existed fails at lock acquisition rather than at write. The per-person half of this is A9.
  6. Interactive — restructure (~1.5 hrs) — lay out one module consumed by isolated dev/prod stacks with separate state.

📌 TF2026's environment lecture teaches the pattern this topic argues against

Worth knowing before watching it, since the course is cited elsewhere in this path. Its Lecture 09 demo keys instance size off the workspace name — lookup(var.instance_type, terraform.workspace) over a { dev, staging, prod } map — so production differs from development by one string inside one backend, one credential set and one directory. That is the shape the HCDocs "Workspaces" (CLI) vs HCP workspaces reference exists to contradict. The course's README does list folder-per-environment as an alternative, but the runnable demo is the workspace one. Its own bug is a useful tell: a two-argument lookup errors on a missing key and the map has no default entry, so the demo fails in the workspace a learner is in before creating any. Full read-through in tf2026-course-facts.

📌 Already captured — workspaces

The two meanings of "workspace" are already written up in workspaces, from TID Ch6 §6.4.5 + §6.4.7 and the official docs: the CLI-vs-HCP comparison table, where each backend stores per-workspace state, terraform.workspace at plan time, and the documented limit that workspaces "are not appropriate for system decomposition or deployments requiring separate credentials and access controls." That second clause is the seam to A9, which picks up separate credentials and access controls as its own topic. What remains for A7 is the decision — TUR Ch3's file-layout-versus-workspace tradeoff — and the multi-account half from TUR Ch7.

📌 DRY across environments → Terragrunt (E4)

A7 covers isolation with native Terraform primitives — the scope the Pro exam tests. The DRY tooling that removes the copy-paste between per-env directories is Terragrunt (third-party, Gruntwork), deep-dived in E4 — Large-scale state & repo architecture below. Reach for it once you have many states and teams, not for a single dev/prod split.

Note that DRY is no longer how Terragrunt describes itself. Its own docs say the focus "has shifted to offering more tooling for orchestrating infrastructure," and warn that you "might miss the forest for the trees" by evaluating it on DRY alone. Evaluate it as a run orchestrator — discovery, a run queue, a cross-unit DAG — not as a config deduplicator. See terragrunt-facts.

Milestone: You can design an env layout where prod and dev have fully isolated state and blast radius, sharing modules but not state.

items.title: ⬜ A8 — Refactoring at scale
items.text:
What it is: Safely evolving large codebases — moved/import/removed blocks, module version bumps across consumers, splitting monolith state, and state migration.

Why you need it: Big Terraform codebases must be refactored without downtime or resource re-creation; this is a senior/Pro-level skill.

How to learn it:

  1. Interactive — HCTut "Use configuration to move resources" (~14 min) — do this before the reading; it is the moved block end to end. Notes: tut-move-config. Extract a root resource into a local module and swap a hand-written module for a registry one, watch the un-moved plan report 4 to add, 4 to destroy with the tell-tale reason line "because X is not in configuration", then add moved blocks and re-plan. The find worth carrying is that the fixed plan is 0 to add, 3 to change, 0 to destroy — not empty. moved preserves identity, not configuration, so swapping implementations is a move and a config change arriving in one apply, while extracting your own code into a module is a clean move (has moved to, no action symbol). A zero-destroy plan is not a zero-impact plan. Also: a module-level moved { from = module.vpc, to = module.learn_vpc } cascades to every address beneath it, but requires terraform init because the install key changes; and moved blocks are written in the root, naming addresses inside modules on both sides, with the target's [0] index keys taken from the destination module's internal addressing.
  2. Reference — HCDocs "Refactor modules" (moved blocks) (~40 min) — config-driven refactors that keep the plan empty. Captured as tf-modules-refactoring. Its author-side half — scoping, chaining, and the module-split shim — is I5's Refactor modules entry; this is the whole page, read as an operator refactoring a live codebase. The governing rule is the addressing one: a bare address moves a resource as a whole, covering every instance, but an instance key on either side switches the block into instance mode — which is what makes count ↔ for_each ↔ neither migrations expressible at all, one moved block per index. Neither tut-count nor tut-for-each mentions this, so the migration they walk you through is a destroy-and-recreate without it. Adding count to a resource that lacked it is the one free case — Terraform auto-proposes moving the object to index 0 — but for_each needs a key you choose, and renaming is never free. Two hard limits: cross-type moves exist but are provider-dependent, and a managed resource can never become a data block (use removed with lifecycle { destroy = false } and a separate data block). The section worth reading twice is splitting a published module — the original becomes a shim that calls the new modules and declares the moved blocks, so existing consumers upgrade in place. The docs flag this as violating the closed-box rule and attach a precondition: "all three of these modules are maintained by the same people and distributed together in a single module package." Scoping keeps it safe — addresses resolve relative to the module they are written in, and "a module may only make moved statements about its own objects and objects of its child modules", so you can reach down, never up or sideways. Chain blocks when the same object moves twice (a→b, b→c): each covers consumers arriving from a different starting version, which is why they accumulate like database migrations rather than as a courtesy changelog. Pair it with HCDocs "Refactor Terraform state", captured in tf-state-refactor — the cross-configuration half that moved blocks can't do: the four refactor triggers, the three grouping properties (volatility, stateful-vs-stateless, team ownership), the three ways to keep references dynamic after the split, and the removed + import migration (1.7+) that HashiCorp now recommends over legacy state mv -state/-state-out (1.0+).
  3. Book chapter — TID Ch 9 §9.5 "Refactoring" + §9.6 "External refactoring" / TUR Ch 5 "Refactoring Can Be Tricky" (p186) — TUR Ch 5 is captured as 05-tips-and-tricks, and its contribution is the why: renaming a variable, a resource identifier or a module — or adding count/for_each to something that lacked it — reads to Terraform as delete-and-create, which on an ALB or a security group is an outage. Its case for moved blocks over terraform state mv is social rather than technical: a CLI step must be remembered by every team consuming the module, a moved block travels with the code. (~1 hr) — splitting state and versioned module rollouts. The state-surgery side (terraform state mv, moved blocks) is Ch 6 §6.5 Manipulating state.
  4. Reference — VP "Upgrade and refactor Terraform modules" (~23 min) — the consumer side of a module version bump, and the exact bill that comes due when a module author did not ship the moved blocks I5 teaches. Worked on terraform-aws-modules/s3-bucket 2.15.0 → 3.0.0, where the module split server-side encryption out into its own resource: the consumer’s plan then proposes to destroy and recreate, and the fix is an import block naming an address inside the module — module.s3_bucket.aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration.this[0] — with the id of the bucket the same module already made. The rule to carry is the acceptance criterion: “Imports are the only acceptable change to see in a speculative plan when upgrading to a newer module version.” Anything else is the module changing your infrastructure, not your infrastructure catching up to the module. It also states the preference the "Use configuration to move resources" tutorial leaves implicit — configuration-driven import blocks over the legacy terraform import command, because they are “predictable, can be automated, and let you preview an import operation before modifying state”. Same discipline as the provider guide in A10: one branch, one issue at a time, apply only on a plan with no errors, warnings or actions. Cached: cache/web/vp-upgrade-refactor-modules.txt.
  5. Interactive — split a monolith (~1.5 hrs) — carve one big config into two states with moved/removed and state mv, verifying empty plans.

Milestone: You can split a monolithic configuration into two independently-stated configs with no resource re-creation.

items.title: ⬜ A9 — Multitenancy, teams & RBAC
items.text:
What it is: Serving several teams or tenants from one Terraform platform. The HCP Terraform access model supplies the control plane half: permission scopes at organization, project and workspace level, teams and team tokens, four fixed workspace roles alongside custom ones. The cloud half is making each tenant's runs carry only that tenant's credentials.

Why you need it: A7 isolates environments; this isolates people. State is where the boundary actually sits, because a workspace's state holds every secret its configuration touched, and the built-in read-only role can already read it in full.

How to learn it:

  1. Interactive — HCTut "Manage permissions in HCP Terraform" (4 min stated; Essentials edition, organization-owner required) — create a Dev-Team, deliberately leave its organization-level permissions blank, grant it the fixed Write set on one workspace, then invite a user by email. It is a UI walkthrough with no HCL, and its one teaching point is the sequencing: "The owners team … has every available permission in the organization, so it is important to create restricted team access before adding new members." You need a second email address you control to finish the invite step.
  2. Reference — HCDocs permissions overview then the three role tables: organization · project · workspace (~1 hr) — the role tables are ground truth for this topic. Read the overview first, because the effective-permissions rule it states governs how every table below it composes.
  3. Reference — HCDocs "Teams overview" (~20 min) — the owners team (capped at five members on free organizations, never deletable, never empty), per-team API tokens not tied to a user, and the Teams / Team Members / Team Tokens / Team Access APIs. Those APIs have provider equivalents in tfe_team, tfe_team_members and tfe_team_access, which is how the access model itself becomes reviewable code instead of console clicks.
  4. Book chapter — TUR Ch 10 § "A Workflow for Deploying Infrastructure Code" (pp. 390–411) (~1 hr) — the pre-HCP form of the same problem. Covers the live-repo-versus-modules-repo split and one infrastructure team publishing versioned modules that every other team consumes "a bit like a service catalog". Its core argument is that infrastructure CI is a harder permission problem than application CI, because arbitrary infrastructure changes need arbitrary permissions, so the CI server ends up holding admin credentials on a box that is "accessible to all the developers at your company" and "used to execute arbitrary code". Five mitigations follow: lock the server down, keep it off the public internet (accepting that webhooks stop working and you must poll instead), require an approval from someone other than the requester who can see both the diff and the plan output, use temporary credentials such as IAM roles and OIDC rather than permanent keys (A6), and isolate the admin credentials on a separate locked-down worker whose API allows only specific commands, in specific repos, on specific branches.
  5. Reference — HCDocs dynamic provider credentials + the AWS configuration (~1 hr) — the cloud half of the boundary, and the page that makes this topic concrete rather than a permissions tour. HCP mints an OIDC workload identity token per run, the cloud verifies it against HCP's public signing key and returns temporary credentials, and the run environment is torn down with the credentials discarded. What matters for multitenancy is the sub claim, which is literally organization:ORG_NAME:project:PROJECT_NAME:workspace:WORKSPACE_NAME:run_phase:RUN_PHASE, so the tenant boundary is expressible in the AWS trust policy itself.
  6. Reference — HCDocs single sign-on + API tokens + audit trails API (~45 min) — the three pages that decide how membership arrives, how automation authenticates, and how you reconstruct who did what. Read them together, because they interlock: SAML mapping makes the directory authoritative over team membership, team tokens deliberately strip user attribution from API actions, and the audit trail is the only place those two facts get reconciled after the event.
  7. Reference — the open-source stack: Atlantis security + repo and project permissions + Terrakube team management (~45 min) — how the same boundary is drawn without a control plane. Read the Atlantis security page first and for one specific sentence, that malicious code runs during plan, because it decides the architecture of every self-hosted option.
  8. Interactive — build a two-tenant organization (~3 hrs) — two projects with one team each, a project-owned variable set per tenant carrying that tenant's TFC_AWS_* dynamic-credential variables, and a custom auditor role granting Read outputs only rather than state read. Verify from the second account that tenant B can reach none of tenant A's state, variables or outputs, then verify the harder half: set TFC_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN as a workspace variable in tenant B pointing at tenant A's role, confirm the override takes effect (the platform allows it), and confirm the run still fails because A's trust policy rejects B's token. Re-create the whole arrangement with the tfe provider.

📌 No book covers this topic — the docs are the only source

Both books predate the current HCP permission model. TUR Ch 10 covers the team workflow and the CI-server permission problem, which is the pre-platform form of the question, and Ch 6 "Managing Secrets with Terraform" supplies the temporary-credentials argument Ch 10 leans on, but neither touches organizations, projects, teams or roles. TID has no access-control section at all: Ch 10 "Advanced Terraform topics" is naming schemes, network topology, provisioners, the external and local providers, and checks, and its only platform material is the six-way comparison in §8.7. So step 2's reference pages are not supplementary reading here, they are the primary text, and the role tables in them are the part to read rather than the prose.

📌 Every built-in workspace role reads the entire state file

In the workspace role table, Read state is ✅ for Admin, Write, Plan and Read alike — only Read and write state narrows to Admin and Write. So the least-privileged preset still hands a user every secret the configuration touched (A6), the docs granting it permission to "read complete state files from the workspace". The same holds one level up: project Read state is ✅ down to the project Read role.

The fix is a custom role, which can grant Read outputs only and stop there. Custom permissions can assign anything in the workspace table except the admin-only rows. This is the single most important thing on this page: if a tenant boundary is supposed to be a secrecy boundary, none of the four presets implement it.

📌 Who can terraform state pull whose secrets

The docs split state access four ways: No access, Read outputs only, Read, Read and write. Read them as three different consumers rather than as a ladder.

Read outputs only is the cross-tenant level. It is what the docs require for the /state-version-outputs endpoint, for terraform output, and for terraform_remote_state against the workspace, and it exposes only values a configuration author explicitly published as root outputs (B9, I6). One tenant consuming another's VPC ID should hold exactly this and nothing more.

Read is where secrecy ends. The docs describe the state file as often containing sensitive information and grant this level "read complete state files from the workspace" through the UI and API. Read and write is required for local-execution runs and, per the docs, "to use any of the Terraform CLI's state manipulation and maintenance commands against this workspace, including terraform import, terraform taint, and the various terraform state subcommands". So the CLI and the API do not present the same surface at the same level, and a tenant boundary drawn only from CLI behaviour will be wrong. Assume anyone at Read or above has already pulled everything.

The practical consequence for a shared platform: a tenant's secret is exposed to every principal with Read on the workspace that touched it, which is a larger set than the tenant. That set only shrinks by keeping the secret out of state in the first place (A6 ephemeral values and write-only arguments) or by not putting the workspaces in reach of the same teams.

📌 Workspace-to-workspace state access is a second, separate control — and it has a documented bypass

Team permissions answer "which people can read this state". They do not answer "which workspaces can read it during a run", which is a different setting called Remote State Sharing with three modes: share with all workspaces in the organization, share with all workspaces in this project, or share with a named list. The default is the safe one, since "new workspaces in HCP Terraform do not allow other workspaces to access their state", and the docs recommend least privilege here explicitly.

Read the middle mode as the tenant-shaped one. Sharing within the project lets a tenant's own workspaces compose while keeping other tenants out, which is the same boundary the project draws everywhere else in this topic. Organization-wide sharing is the setting that quietly turns every tenant's outputs into a shared bus.

Two things that break the mental model. The control does not cover everything that reads outputs: "Remote state access controls do not apply when using the tfe_outputs data source", so a tenant that switches from terraform_remote_state to tfe_outputs is governed by token permissions alone, which is the Read outputs only level above rather than this setting. And local execution mode moves the check to a user token, which must carry permission to read and write state versions for the workspace, plus read state outputs for any workspace it references. Auditing sharing settings while ignoring who holds tokens audits half the surface.

There is also a visibility floor worth knowing before you trust a review: configuring sharing requires read access to the destination workspace, so a reviewer with scoped project or workspace permissions will not see the complete list of workspaces that can reach a given state.

📌 Agent pools are the compute half of the boundary, and they scope like everything else

A tenant boundary that stops at identity still runs both tenants' code on the same execution surface. Agent pools are HCP's answer for private or on-premises infrastructure, and they scope the same way projects do: "Scoping an agent pool lets you specify which workspaces, projects, or Stacks can use it", after which the pool "does not appear in other workspace's, project's, or Stack's lists of available agent pools". A per-tenant pool sitting in the tenant's own network is what keeps tenant B's run from having route-level reach into tenant A's estate.

Two operational catches. Creating and scoping pools needs the organization-level Manage agent pools permission, which the docs note "implicitly grants access to read all workspaces and projects" — another org-level grant that widens read access as a side effect, exactly like Manage policy overrides. And scoping is not revocation: "Scoping an agent pool does not remove it from workspaces, projects, or Stacks that are actively using it", so a tightened scope leaves existing users attached until you detach them in each workspace.

📌 Policy sets scope to tenants; the private registry does not

Two governance surfaces, two different answers, and the asymmetry decides how far one organization can be stretched.

Policy sets scope. A set applies "globally, to specific projects and workspaces, or to workspaces with specific tags" (tag scoping is beta), and any project, workspace or tag can be excluded from a set. So a tenant can carry its own mandatory policies while the platform team keeps a global baseline. Two traps sit next to it. The organization-level Manage policy overrides permission "also gives teams read access to all workspaces in the organization", which the docs themselves say to avoid by using Delegate policy overrides instead, so the naive way to let a tenant override its own soft failures hands it read access to every other tenant. And a policy set carrying This policy set can be overridden in the event of mandatory failures lets holders override even Hard mandatory policies, because that switch "takes precedence over the individual policy's enforcement level".

The private registry does not scope. Private modules and providers are "only available to members of that organization", and that is the entire access model. Nothing in the organization permission table is a registry read scope: Manage modules, Manage providers and Manage Stack component configurations control publishing and deletion, and the two remaining entries govern attaching project tags and reserved keys to registry artifacts. So every member of the organization can see every private module, including its documentation, examples and source address. If tenants must not see each other's modules, they need separate organizations, not separate projects. What you can control is consumption rather than visibility, through Sentinel: the docs point at policies that "mandate that all non-root modules in Terraform configurations must be private or public modules from your own private registry", which is the enforcement half A5 already owns.

(In Terraform Enterprise the direction is the opposite of tenant isolation: private modules "are also available to other organizations that are configured to share with that organization".)

📌 Permissions are additive across scopes, and the most permissive one wins

"Each permission is additive, granting a user the highest level of permissions possible, regardless of which scope set that permission." An organization-level Manage all workspaces silently overrides a carefully scoped workspace Read. The relationship is not symmetric: organization View all workspaces does not cut a team's workspace Write down to read-only. Treat organization scope as the floor a team can never fall below, and project or workspace scope as the ceiling. Granting broadly at the top and then "restricting" further down does nothing.

📌 The boundary leaks through everything integrated with it

HCDocs is explicit that the model covers only what HCP Terraform manages, and names three leaks. A VCS-connected workspace inherits the repository's permissions, so anyone who can merge to its tracked branch can queue plans there "regardless of whether they have explicit permission to queue plans or are even a member of your HCP Terraform organization", and with auto-apply enabled the merge applies them. An API-driven Slack bot lets anyone who can issue it commands act with the bot's permissions. A run task receives an access token good for the plan JSON and the callback, with a 10-minute lifetime. The governing sentence: "An integrated system is able to delegate any level of access that it has been granted."

📌 Two more ways tenant data escapes the role you granted

Sentinel mocks are downloadable at workspace Write and above, and the docs describe that run data as "detailed and may contain unredacted sensitive information". A mock download is a state read wearing a different name, which matters when you hand Write to a tenant on the assumption that Write means "can deploy".

Secret teams are invisible to workspace and project admins unless those admins are also organization owners. An admin auditing who can reach a workspace is therefore reading a list that may be incomplete by design.

📌 Projects are the tenant container; teams are the subject

A project is "a folder containing one or more workspaces, Stacks, or both", and its four roles (Admin / Maintain / Write / Read) apply to every workspace and Stack inside it. Grant per project rather than per workspace, or the model stops scaling at the tenant's tenth workspace. Only project Admin can update or delete the project, manage other teams' access, move workspaces between projects, or manage run tasks. Maintain is the useful middle: full control of everything inside, including creating and deleting workspaces, with no authority over the project itself.

⚠️ Two docs pages disagree about variable sets, and the gap matters here. The project permission table marks both Manage variable sets and Read variable sets as Admin-only. The variables page instead says that creating, editing or applying a project-owned variable set needs any of project Write, Maintain, Admin, a Manage variable sets project permission, or organization Manage all projects. Since variable sets are how per-tenant credentials get delivered, assume the looser page describes the behaviour and verify in your own organization before treating "only Admin can change the credentials" as a control.

Team management requires Essentials, Standard or Premium. In HCP Europe organizations the subject is an HCP group rather than a team, HCP roles (Admin / Contributor / Viewer) grant HCP Terraform permissions automatically, and project permissions cannot be assigned in HCP Terraform at all. The least-privilege advice there is to add narrow HCP Terraform permissions instead of a broader HCP role.

📌 RBAC governs who starts a run, not what the run may do

A tenant's plan executes with the workspace's provider credentials, and those credentials answer to the cloud's IAM, not to HCP's permission model. Two tenants whose workspaces share one AWS role are one tenant with extra paperwork. The access model only becomes a tenant boundary when the cloud identity is per-tenant too, which is the next callout. Blast-radius isolation of the state itself is A7, and the module-consumption half is A4 plus E6.

📌 The tenant boundary is a trust-policy condition, and one wildcard erases it

Dynamic credentials put the boundary somewhere HCP permissions cannot reach it. The workload identity token's sub claim is organization:ORG_NAME:project:PROJECT_NAME:workspace:WORKSPACE_NAME:run_phase:RUN_PHASE, so an AWS role's trust policy can require, by StringEquals, that the assumer be exactly one workspace in one project of one organization. Give each tenant its own role, condition that role on the tenant's project segment, and no configuration change inside tenant B's workspace can reach tenant A's role — the ARN is not a secret, and it does not need to be, because the trust policy refuses the token.

Everything hangs on how that condition is written. The docs' own convenience variant relaxes StringEquals to StringLike with run_phase:* in order to share one role across plan and apply. A wildcard that drifts one segment left, to the workspace or the project, silently widens the role to every workspace in the organization, and nothing in HCP will report it. HashiCorp states the floor directly: "you should always check, at minimum, the audience and the name of the organization in order to prevent unauthorized access from other HCP Terraform organizations!" Treat that as the floor, not the target — the organization is the platform boundary, and the project is the tenant boundary.

Two refinements worth taking. Separate roles for the two phases (TFC_AWS_PLAN_ROLE_ARN and TFC_AWS_APPLY_ROLE_ARN, falling back to TFC_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN) give a read-only plan and a writing apply, which is the credential-side version of the workspace Plan role. And the variables selecting the role belong in a project-owned variable set applied to the whole project, so a new workspace joins the tenant's identity by construction rather than by someone remembering to set three variables.

📌 A variable set does not pin anything by default — a workspace variable beats it

The obvious next assumption is that putting the credential variables in a project-owned set stops a tenant from changing them. It does not. The docs state the rule flatly: "Workspace-specific variables always overwrite variables from variable sets that have the same key", and they offer credential swapping as the motivating example, that you "may want to use a different set of provider credentials in a specific workspace". So workspace Write, which carries Read and write variables, is enough to repoint TFC_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN at another tenant's role. The UI flags it with an OVERWRITTEN badge, which is a notification, not a control.

The control is marking the set priority: "When a variable set is priority, the values take precedence over any variables with the same key set at a more specific scope", and only the set's owner decides that. Do this for anything that carries identity.

Even unpriorified, the attempt fails — but for a different reason than the one you configured. Repointing the ARN gets tenant B nothing, because the token HCP mints still carries B's own project and workspace in its sub claim, and A's trust policy rejects it. That is worth internalising rather than treating as luck: the trust policy is the control that holds, and the variable-set arrangement is only hygiene. A design that relies on variable placement for isolation is one workspace variable away from failing, and would fail today if the two tenants shared a role that trusted the project segment loosely.

📌 Cross-account tenants: assume_role is the other half

Where tenants live in separate cloud accounts, the provider does the crossing (I8). The AWS provider's assume_role block takes role_arn, external_id, session_name, source_identity, duration, tags/transitive_tag_keys, and — the argument that matters most here — policy and policy_arns, which further restrict the assumed role's permissions for this session. Repeating the block chains roles in order, so a platform role can hop into a tenant account without either side holding the other's keys.

external_id exists to stop the confused deputy, and its rule is about control rather than secrecy. A role ARN, as AWS puts it, "isn't a secret", so any tenant that learns another tenant's role ARN could ask the platform to assume it. The external ID defeats that only because the platform generates a distinct value per tenant and supplies it on every call: AWS is explicit that the value "must be unique among Example Corp's customers and controlled by Example Corp, not its customers". A platform that lets a tenant choose its own external ID has implemented the field and none of the protection.

session_name and source_identity are what make CloudTrail readable per tenant, which is the difference between an audit trail and a list of identical terraform sessions.

⚠️ Readable is not enforceable, and the distinction decides designs. AWS is explicit that "AWS doesn't control the value of the source identity" and that you "must ensure that you can control how those values are provided". Under OIDC that means the value has to arrive inside the signed token, in the https://aws.amazon.com/source_identity namespace, and neither GitHub's nor GitLab's documented claim list contains it. A pipeline that sets source_identity from its own actor variable is asserting the identity, not proving it. What is enforceable is a trust-policy condition on a claim the forge signs — actor_id on GitHub, user_id on GitLab — and that is still the wrong default, because it costs an IAM edit per joiner and leaver. Group membership belongs in the forge, on the environment. See ci-identity-and-groups, which also carries what source_identity genuinely guarantees: it cannot be changed during a session, it survives role chaining, and it needs sts:SetSourceIdentity in two places to cross an account boundary.
