(See tut-troubleshooting-workflow, dependency-graph.)

Terraform 1.16 makes the error itself readable. Today Error: Cycle: prints the members on one long line, which is why the -draw-cycles detour above exists at all. From 1.16 it renders one node per line, ordered by reference rather than graph-traversal order, and from a consistent starting node, so a loop spanning many nodes can be read without rendering an SVG. Same error, same fix, and -draw-cycles still wins when you need the edges rather than the members. This is in no changelog — it is commit 4c4adca78b on the v1.16 branch, found by reading the tree. It shipped in 1.16.0: git tag --contains 4c4adca78b lists v1.16.0, and internal/dag/dag.go:270 at that tag joins the members with a newline and two spaces. (See release-feature-map.)

The graph shows what Terraform knows, not what's true

terraform graph renders every edge Terraform built — and a missing hidden dependency has no edge, so it looks identical to a resource with no dependencies. Use the graph to confirm a suspected ordering bug, never to discover one. When a plan passes locally and races in CI, suspect a missing depends_on (I1) before you suspect -parallelism. (See dependency-graph.)

Cleaning up the noisy terraform graph output

The raw DOT carries provider, root, and (expand) nodes on top of your resources, so a real config's graph is hard to read. Three easier-to-read options:

  • SVG over PNG. terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg is zoomable and searchable.
  • Online renderer. Paste the DOT into edotor.net; no Graphviz install needed.
  • Prune with InfraMap. cycloidio/inframap (v0.8.1, actively maintained as of mid-2026) reads state or HCL and emits only the resources that matter, dropping provider and meta nodes. It auto-detects the input: inframap generate main.tf | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg, or a state file with inframap generate terraform.tfstate. Force it with --hcl/--tfstate if detection guesses wrong.

Interactive browser viewers (Rover, Blast Radius) exist, but the well-known ones are unmaintained (Rover's last release was 2022), so check that a tool is current before relying on it. (See tf-cmd-graph.)

📌 Global provider plugin cache

A shared global provider plugin cache (TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR / plugin_cache_dir) avoids re-downloading providers per project. It historically wasn't safe for concurrent inits; OpenTofu 1.10 added filesystem cache locking (flock/LockFileEx) so parallel CI jobs can share one cache without corruption. (See opentofu-feature-history.)

📌 Provider mirrors for air-gapped setups

For air-gapped or locked-down environments, the CLI config's provider_installation block configures filesystem_mirror (serve providers from a local directory) and network_mirror (serve from an internal HTTPS mirror) instead of the public registry. Populate a mirror with terraform providers mirror DIR. (HCDocs CLI config)

📌 Checkpoint telemetry opt-out

The CLI phones home to HashiCorp's Checkpoint service for version + security-bulletin checks (this drives the "newer version available" line in terraform version). Only anonymous data is sent. Disable it in airgapped/privacy-sensitive setups: CHECKPOINT_DISABLE=1 (env, all HashiCorp tools) or CLI-config disable_checkpoint = true (all calls) / disable_checkpoint_signature = true (keep bulletin checks, drop the anonymous signature). (See tf-cli-commands.)

📌 experiments — not for production

The terraform {} block's experiments = [...] argument opts a module into pre-release language features for feedback (e.g. optional object attrs before 1.3 GA'd them). Advanced and not for production — it warns on every plan/apply and can break in minor/patch releases. (HCDocs terraform block)

📌 OpenTelemetry tracing — OpenTofu documents it, Terraform hides it

Both binaries enable an experimental OTLP trace exporter on OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp, and both delegate every other knob to the standard OTEL_* variables. This path previously said "Terraform has no built-in OTel equivalent" — wrong: the hook exists in telemetry.go, it is simply undocumented (a grep of the Terraform repo's website/ for opentelemetry returns nothing). What differs is what you get back.

OpenTofu 1.10+ traces the graph walk: Validation phase / Plan phase / Apply phase, then one span per graph node (Plan resource instance changes, Apply resource instance changes, Configure provider), tagged with opentofu.resource_instance.address, opentofu.resource.type, and opentofu.provider.source. That is what makes "which resource dominates the apply" answerable.

Terraform 1.15 has ~10 span sites, all in main, checkpoint.go, and internal/command — module and provider installation, backend init. The graph walk is not traced at all, so a trace of terraform apply tells you nothing about which resource was slow. The instrumented plan/apply code lives in the Stacks runtime (internal/stacks/stackruntime, internal/rpcapi), which HCP Terraform drives over RPC rather than the CLI.

Three more differences that decide whether this is usable in CI: OpenTofu reads TRACEPARENT (1.10) so a run nests inside the pipeline's trace, and Terraform does not (hashicorp/terraform#35444, open since 2024-07-10); OpenTofu batches span export while Terraform uses a SimpleSpanProcessor that exports synchronously per span; and Terraform names its root span terraform <full command line>, so a -var="password=…" lands in the tracing backend, where OpenTofu's root span is just tofu. Sampling is fixed at 100% in both. Details and the version gating: ot-otel-tracing, otel-tracing-facts.

📌 High-cardinality perf + rpcapi (Terraform 1.13)

Terraform 1.13 made evaluation of high-cardinality count/for_each (hundreds+ of instances) much faster — relevant when a big config's graph is the bottleneck. For building tooling around Terraform, terraform rpcapi (1.13, GA) exposes core operations over a plugin RPC interface. (See feature-history.)

Read it against TID Ch11 §11.1, which says the CLI is the only way in. Source settles it — commands.go registers rpcapi under a comment saying its "whole point … is to bypass the CLI layer so wrapping automation can get as-direct-as-possible access to Terraform Core functionality", bypassing the command package entirely. Verified out of experimental as of v1.13.0 by git tag --contains. Two limits worth knowing before betting on it: it lives in HiddenCommands, so it is plumbing rather than an advertised interface, and it came out of the Stacks work rather than as a general integration API. For Go specifically there is also hashicorp/terraform-exec, HashiCorp's own CLI wrapper returning terraform-json types, which is what a Go integration should start from instead of hand-rolling one.

⚠️ OpenTofu has neither — no rpcapi package, no registration, zero occurrences in the 1.12.5 tree. So anything that must run on both engines still wraps the CLI, and that, rather than the absence of an API, is the reason the wrapper pattern is worth learning.

Milestone: You can diagnose a failing/slow apply from TF_LOG output and cut plan time on a large config via caching and parallelism tuning.

items.title: ⬜ E6 — Platform engineering & self-service
items.text:
What it is: Terraform as an internal platform — golden/opinionated modules, self-service via HCP no-code modules or an IDP (e.g. Backstage), run tasks, and org-wide drift detection.

Why you need it: The end state of Terraform maturity is letting product teams provision safely without writing raw HCL; this is the platform-engineering frontier.

How to learn it:

  1. Reference — HCDocs "No-Code modules" + Run Tasks + private registry (~1 hr) — the self-service building blocks.
  2. Video — HashiCorp "Terraform for platform engineers" (Armon Dadgar) (~45 min) — how mature orgs expose Terraform to non-experts via golden modules.
  3. Interactive — HCTut "Create and use no-code modules" (~14 min stated, budget ~1.5 hrs with AWS; HCP Standard edition) — put a golden module in the private registry and let users provision it with no HCL, straight from the HCP UI. Notes: tut-no-code-provisioning. The design rule that defines the model: a no-code workspace's entire change surface is (variable values) × (module version) — "You cannot directly apply configuration changes to existing no-code workspaces" — so anything you did not expose as a variable is fixed until the author ships a release. That makes minimizing inputs (tut-pattern-module-creation) a hard requirement rather than a style preference. It also inverts the no-provider-blocks-in-modules rule and explains why the rule existed: provider blocks are forbidden because they conflict with count/for_each/depends_on, and "Since users will not reference no-code modules in written configuration, there is no risk of this conflict." The cost is that HCP spawns a workspace per provision, so provider credentials must arrive automatically — a project-scoped variable set here, dynamic credentials in practice. Governance sits in Configure Settings → Edit versions and variable options: you pin which module version no-code deploys (pushing a tag publishes a version but does not roll it out), and you can turn a free-text variable into a dropdown of allowed values. ⚠️ Its own 1.0.1 upgrade adds a variable with no default, forcing every consuming workspace to answer a prompt — the breaking way to make an additive change, and a live counterexample to tut-module-object-attributes. Two things not to copy from its module: publicly_accessible = true on the RDS instance, and an ingress CIDR of 192.80.0.0/16 described as an internal VPN when it is public address space. Also cited from I5, which takes the author half — this is the one page documenting where the no-provider-block rule and the standard-structure rule change shape for a module nobody calls from HCL.

📌 OpenTofu — MCP server (1.10)

OpenTofu 1.10 ships an MCP server — exposes OpenTofu operations to AI agents / LLM tooling via the Model Context Protocol, an emerging building block for AI-assisted self-service IaC. OpenTofu-only. (See opentofu-feature-history.)

📌 Multi-tenant note — no-code provisioning is the one thing here a tenant can run for itself

Most platform capabilities need an organization-level grant, which is why A9 keeps pushing them back to the platform team. No-code provisioning is the exception, and it fits the project boundary cleanly. Provisioning requires Manage all projects, Manage all workspaces, or project Admin, and with custom project permissions a team needs only the ability to create workspaces, write variables and apply runs. So a tenant with admin over its own project self-serves without any org-wide permission.

Two mechanics make it work inside a tenant boundary. The provisioning flow asks which project the new workspace goes in, and "teams with access to the specified project can view the workspace automatically", so the tenant's existing team access carries over. And "if the specified project contains any project-scoped variable sets, HCP Terraform automatically applies those sets to the workspace", which is exactly how a per-tenant dynamic-credential set reaches a workspace nobody configured by hand.

Two cautions. Auto apply is the default for a no-code workspace, so self-service provisioning applies without review unless you change it. And no-code readiness is a property of a module in the organization's private registry, which has no per-team read scope, so every tenant can provision every no-code module you publish. Restricting who may provision what is a policy question (A5), not a registry one.

Milestone: You can publish a governed golden module to a private registry and let another team provision it self-service with policy enforcement.

items.title: ⬜ Expert Checkpoint
items.text: You have mastered Terraform when you can: - Build and ship a custom provider with the Plugin Framework. - Architect large-scale, multi-team state with Stacks/Terragrunt and fast, small plans. - Choose and migrate between Terraform and OpenTofu on real technical merits, and stand up a self-service platform with governance.

items.title: Suggested study sequence
items.text:
Beginner (B1–B9)        → ~30 hrs
    ↓
Intermediate (I1–I8)    → ~45 hrs  →  [Terraform Associate 004]
    ↓
Advanced (A1–A10)       → ~76 hrs  →  [Authoring & Operations Professional]
    ↓
Expert (E1–E6)          → ~70 hrs

You are currently here: Beginner and Intermediate complete — B1–B9, I1–I8 done — and the Advanced level is open: A1 (Provisioners, terraform_data & escape hatches) is done (Ch 1–18 written). The Intermediate Checkpoint and the Terraform Associate (004) attempt are still outstanding and can be taken in parallel. Next topic: A2 (Testing, validation & checks).

2026-08-27 (twenty-first) — The five patterns believed 404 are captured, and fetching them was the final disproof: every one returned real content on the first attempt. The Validated Patterns collection is now complete at twelve of twelve. vp-azure-landing-zone is the one the 2026-08-17 audit named as the absence that cost this path something, and it delivers. It is the twin of vp-aws-landing-zone, so A7 now has both clouds: subscriptions and management groups where AWS has accounts and OUs, Entra ID where AWS has IAM, Azure Policy where AWS has SCPs, Sentinel in both. Terminology drift worth knowing — AWS says workload landing zone, Azure says application landing zone, for the same thing. Its sharpest control has no AWS counterpart: separate federations for the plan and apply stages, so proposing and executing are different privileges. Terraform's plan/apply split is usually taught as a safety mechanism; here it is an authorisation boundary. That belongs in A6 as much as A5. Both landing-zone guides also align themselves to the cloud vendor's framework — Well-Architected and Microsoft CAF — which is the honest description of what a validated pattern is. vp-orgs-to-projects supplies history the notes lacked: organizations were the original segregation unit, projects arrived through 2023 to give RBAC delegation inside one line of business, and the recommendation is now to minimise organizations. Its operational half is a list of what does not migrate — run history cannot be migrated at all, and sensitive variable values cannot be retrieved via the UI or API by design, so they are unmigratable by construction. That is the strongest argument in the collection for sourcing secrets from Vault: a Vault-sourced value migrates because there is nothing to migrate. Ordering matters too — policy sets before workspaces, or runs execute in an unguarded window. vp-vulnerability-patch-management answers what tut-packer leaves open: what keeps a golden image current. A 30-day repave cycle, with scheduled image revocation in the HCP Packer registry, channels rather than image IDs in the configuration, and drift detection turning a channel update into a work queue. Revoke → channel → drift → remediate, with no one maintaining a list. It also splits two cadences deliberately: merge freely, build only on git tags and releases. vp-cortex-cloud is the collection's only third-party run task, and it is the counterweight to vp-aap-integration ruling the same mechanism out. Together they give the rule: run tasks suit verdicts, not work — the 10-minute response ceiling is fatal for an Ansible run and irrelevant for a policy scan. It completes the enforcement-point set alongside Sentinel and SCPs, adds the practice worth generalising (ship the local runner with the gate — Checkov CLI and an IDE plugin, so the gate is a backstop and not the discovery mechanism), and is unusually honest that enabling it retroactively blocks runs that previously worked. vp-servicenow-catalog is the self-service story, and its load-bearing setting is stated in half a sentence: auto-apply is true, so nobody sees the plan. Approval moves entirely to the ServiceNow request workflow, and the only remaining bounds are the no-code module and the variable set. The guide does not flag that trade; the note does. Its underrated half is that the run log lands in the RITM ticket, making the ITSM record the audit trail. 2026-08-27 (twentieth) — The six cached Validated Patterns captured, closing the borrowing the course was opened to stop. All seven guides read on 2026-08-17 now have notes; their prose summaries in that entry point at them rather than standing in for them. Wired into A5, A6, A7, A8, A10 and I7. vp-aws-landing-zone is still the only landing-zone material anywhere in these notes, and its artifact is a vocabulary rather than a procedure: platform landing zone versus workload landing zone, “autonomous in terms of deployment but compliant with the policies and controls defined in the PLZ”; the rule that one AWS account = one HCP workspace = one state, so the IAM boundary and the state boundary cannot drift apart; and the Sentinel-versus-SCP table that A5 needed — Sentinel evaluates plans, resource-level, pre-deployment, and is bypassed by anything not going through Terraform, while an SCP evaluates every AWS API call at account level and cannot be bypassed. A control that must hold against a console user was never a Sentinel control. vp-integrate-vault separates four Terraform–Vault surfaces the path had been treating as one, and one runs backwards: the Terraform secrets engine has Vault issue HCP Terraform API tokens. Its sharpest operational fact is that the HCP Terraform API allows one active org or team token at a time, so Vault caches and re-serves those rather than minting per read — a “dynamic secret” that is deliberately not new each time, and a rotation schedule built on the opposite assumption would revoke every other consumer. 2026-08-27 (nineteenth) — vp-aap-integration captured, opening a Validated Patterns course and closing the last uncaptured reference A1 names. It is now A1 item 6, and it earns the slot for one reason: it is the only captured source in which Terraform pushes to the configuration tool rather than the configuration tool pulling from Terraform. pyinfra pulls via terraform output -json; Ansible's terraform_provider inventory plugin pulls via the state file; the AAP provider writes the inventory (aap_inventory) and launches the job (aap_job) from inside the apply, reading nothing. That reintroduces in-apply work — wait_for_completion = true blocks exactly as a remote-exec does — but a provider models the operation, so a failure is a failed resource rather than a taint on a healthy VM. 2026-08-27 (eighth) — tf-terraform-data re-fetched and extended rather than re-captured: Terraform 1.16 gave it a third job. The flag raised two entries ago is now followed up. The new store block “can hold ephemeral and sensitive values across plan and apply” (terraform#38298), which stated plainly means it exists to write an ephemeral value into state on purpose — an exit from the property that defines ephemeral values (tf-manage-sensitive-data), for the case where regenerating a secret would rotate the live credential. Four arguments: input (write-only, hence able to take ephemeral values), sensitive (routes to sensitive_output rather than output, and the two are mutually exclusive), version (the stored value is pinned until this changes), and replace (an output change replaces rather than updates). version is the one that makes the feature work: without it a freshly generated ephemeral value differs every run and the stored output would churn, so it is rotate-on-demand rather than rotate-on-every-plan. Three facts source-verified at tag v1.16.0 and stated nowhere in the docs: store is NestingSingle, so at most one block — which is why the example addresses it unindexed as terraform_data.test.store.sensitive_output; input carries WriteOnly: true in the schema rather than only in prose; and a code comment spells out the comparison the docs describe only by its outcome — “If there is no version value, then input will be compared directly against output.” Diffed against v1.15.8 in the local checkout: the whole block type is new and nothing else in the schema changed. 2026-08-27 (sixth) — tf-invoke-actions captured, completing the Extend CRUD operations group, and it does not merely add to A1 — it moves the line the whole topic rests on. Terraform 1.16.0 shipped 2026-08-26, one day before this capture, and three of its changes land here. action_trigger now accepts before_destroy and after_destroy (terraform#38668). Through 1.15 it accepted only the create/update pair — not inferred but measured, in tf-block-resource, where both destroy events were rejected with “No events specified”. So the strongest remaining argument for a destroy-time provisioner, that nothing else could hook teardown, is now provider-dependent rather than absolute: where a provider ships the action, none of the four holes in when = destroy applies. Second, on_failure on an action_trigger inverts the provisioner's default (terraform#38722). The values do not even overlap — halt / continue / taint against continue / fail — and the default halt explicitly “is not tainted” where the provisioner's default fail taints. This topic's fourth objection, the one these notes contributed because no book states it, is precisely what the replacement mechanism designs out. Tainting survives as an opt-in. Third, caller — self for actions, letting one action block serve many resource instances without a reference per instance — and the same release let -invoke combine with -target to say which caller (terraform#38845), which the page documents nowhere even though it documents caller. Two stale claims corrected rather than left standing. tf-block-resource's measured conclusion and the glossary's action_trigger entry both said there is no destroy event; both are now version-gated with the 1.15 measurement kept and the 1.16 changelog cited. No chapter flips to 🔄 — Ch11 names action_trigger and defers it to Ch18 without making a destroy claim, so nothing written has gone stale. One unrelated pending marker closed while reading the same changelog: tf-block-removed carried “⏳ Terraform 1.16 adds the resource-level form too (rc1 as of 2026-08-13)” for destroy = false; it shipped (terraform#38784), so that OpenTofu divergence is closed. Docs bugs recorded: a sentence saying Terraform “also updates the resource” where it means invokes the action, present since v1.15 and left untouched by the v1.16 edit that reflowed the paragraph around it; “meta-argments”; event in prose against events in every sample; and the conditions-versus-condition bug from first capture survives into v1.16. 2026-08-25 — A6 gains the one-hour role-chaining ceiling, an AWS limit the Terraform provider documentation walks you straight past. The question that surfaced it was whether the backend and the apply should hold separate credentials, which A7 already answers with HashiCorp's own multi-account recipe: the backend authenticates as the administrative account's principal and the provider assumes the environment role. Under OIDC that split has two shapes, and they are not equivalent. Chaining from one bootstrap role costs the whole run its session length. AWS defines role chaining as one role assuming a second, and "Role chaining limits your AWS Management Console, AWS CLI or AWS API role session to a maximum of one hour. It applies regardless of the maximum session duration configured for individual roles." Over-asking is refused rather than clamped. The provider never warns. hashicorp/aws raises role chaining three times, including "IAM Role Chaining is supported by specifying the roles to assume in order", and gives duration one identical description on assume_role and assume_role_with_web_identity alike, "a value from 15 minutes up to the maximum session duration setting for the role", which holds only when the block is not chaining. The escape is that a web-identity exchange is not chaining at all, since its base is a token and not a role session, so its DurationSeconds reaches the role's full maximum of up to 12 hours and the word chaining appears on that page only in the session-tag paragraph. So the two-role split wants two independent exchanges of one identity token, not a bootstrap role with two hops. ⚠️ This makes a written chapter stale. Book Ch 17 teaches chaining by repeating the block and carries the unqualified duration wording in its argument table, so I8 flips to 🔄 with the missing qualification named. 2026-08-16 — Renovate promoted out of a callout into its own Advanced topic, A10, because the question it answers is "what runs on GitLab and Bitbucket" and A3's aside could not carry that. Everything is from the Renovate docs, fetched rather than remembered, since no book here covers the tool: TID Ch 7 §7.7.5 is Dependabot with one passing sentence on Renovate, and TUR predates both. The extraction surface came out wider than the old callout claimed. The Terraform manager matches **/*.tf and **/*.tofu and emits module, provider, required_provider, required_version, helm_release and tfe_workspace alongside about twenty Kubernetes kinds and the docker_* ones, each disableable by depType — and the sources are asymmetric, with modules resolvable from GitTags/GithubTags/registry but providers from a registry only. Three findings are the reason the topic exists. The OpenTofu default is stated in the docs as an admitted limitation, "Renovate can not know if you want to use the Terraform or OpenTofu registry", so an unqualified provider on an OpenTofu project resolves against registry.terraform.io — which lands directly on opentofu-migration-mechanics's finding that the two registries do not ship byte-for-byte identical builds, making it a supply-chain mistake rather than a cosmetic one. The lock file is computed, not delegated: Renovate "performs lock file maintenance itself, without calling the underlying package manager", so no engine binary is needed in the runner image, but lockFileMaintenance defaults to false, meaning a default install bumps constraints and leaves the recorded checksums behind. And the failure mode of computing hashes yourself is silent: discussion #30984 is aws 5.64.0 producing no regenerated lock and no error, self-healing at 5.65.0. The platform gaps are per-forge and worth checking before promising a workflow: GitLab has not implemented automergeStrategy at all and needs gitAuthor to match the bot where push rules verify committers; Bitbucket Cloud has no assignees, no rebase merge strategy and no collapsible markdown, which is what Renovate's PR bodies use; Bitbucket Data Center adds no labels and no config-error issues. The Dependency Dashboard needs "issues with dynamic Markdown checkboxes", so it is not a Bitbucket feature. The GitLab setup needs no marketplace app — the Renovate Runner templates run it from a scheduled pipeline (3 * * * * recommended) with RENOVATE_TOKEN, RENOVATE_GITHUB_COM_TOKEN and RENOVATE_EXTRA_FLAGS, which is the concrete answer to the question that started this. One thing carried over unchanged: neither bot moves a SHA-pinned Git module source, so I4's manual cadence survives automation; the Terragrunt manager says so outright, limiting itself to registry sources and GitHub sources with SemVer refs. 2026-08-16 — TID Ch 10 "Advanced Terraform topics" captured (10-advanced-topics), which is the chapter A1 has been citing without a note behind it. It is the book's grab-bag — naming schemes, a dynamically subnetted network module, provisioners, the external and local providers, checks and conditions, .tofu files, and when Terraform is the wrong tool — so it feeds A1 (which it largely owns), A2's condition half, E3, I3/I4 and B7. Three gaps between the chapter and the docs are folded into A1 rather than left in the note. The chapter's provisioner argument list omits environment, interpreter, working_dir and quiet on both local-exec and remote-exec, and environment is the difference between passing a secret and printing it. The external data source's failure contract — exit zero, or write to stderr and exit non-zero with stdout ignored — is in the provider docs and not in the chapter, as is the fact that Terraform Enterprise guarantees no language runtimes beyond shell utilities, which rules the whole technique out there. And direxists errors on a file path rather than returning false, and does not expand ~. The framing worth keeping from §10.6 is blocking versus reporting: precondition/postcondition stop the run, check only warns, and that is what makes a scoped data source doing a live HTTP health check safe on every plan — provided it carries depends_on, or it runs on the first plan before the infrastructure exists and reports a failure that means nothing. A2 gains that as its own item, and the four-mechanism ordering table (variable validation → precondition → postcondition → check) is in the chapter note. One existing claim reinforced from a second direction: the destroy-time provisioner in §10.3.4 has two ways to silently not run — deleting the resource block, which is the prevent_destroy trap, and create_before_destroy = true, which suppresses it outright (tf-meta-lifecycle) and can arrive by propagation from a dependent resource. A verification pass over the finished note then found three more errors, all behavioural rather than version-shaped, which is the harder class to spot. The largest: self is bound for postconditions only, settled in internal/terraform/eval_conditions.go, which sets a self reference for addrs.ResourcePostcondition and nothing else under the comment "Only resource postconditions can refer to self" — OpenTofu's internal/tofu/eval_conditions.go carries the identical line, so it is not a divergence, and it follows from a precondition running before the object exists. The chapter presents self under the joint precondition/postcondition heading; every example it prints is nonetheless correct. Second: an omitted query on the external data source sends an empty JSON object, not the "empty JSON array" the chapter states — the provider marshals a map[string]string, so {} is the only possible output. Third: content_base64sha256 on local_file is "Base64 encoded SHA256 checksum of file content", the base64sha256() output that AWS's source_code_hash wants, not the chapter's "hash of the base64 content", which would be a different value. A fourth pass found two more defects in the same network module, so §10.2 is now marked as a design sketch rather than runnable code. Its count is local.subnet_count — pow(2, subnet_bits), the number of networks the CIDR was divided into — where it should be var.availability_zones. Those agree at 1, 2 and 4 and diverge at 3, which is the value the chapter itself calls the standard for high availability: evaluated on 1.15.8, availability_zones = 3 builds four locations, a fourth NAT gateway included, and then reports the CIDR the fourth is using in spare_subnet_cidr_blocks, so one range is both allocated and advertised as free. Second: aws_internet_gateway appears nowhere in the chapter. The submodules build only a private route table and the §10.2.3 NOTE defers the gateway to "the high-level module that we'll be creating in the next section", which creates a VPC, a data source, two module calls and outputs — and no gateway, and no route-table association for the public subnet. So the public subnet inherits the VPC's local-only main route table, the NAT gateway in it cannot egress, and the private subnets behind that NAT have no internet either. That also settles the annotation on map_public_ip_on_launch reading "This is the field that makes this a public subnet": AWS's VPC guide says "The subnet type is determined by how you configure routing" and a public subnet is one with "a direct route to an internet gateway" — auto-assigned public IPs are a separate setting, so a subnet full of them and no gateway route is not public, just expensive. Two smaller items from the same pass: the file provisioner's trailing slash on source decides whether the directory itself or its contents land in the destination (internal/communicator/ssh/communicator.go, UploadDir), which the chapter's example gets right without saying why; and its "about a week" for aws_secretsmanager_secret name reuse is the floor — recovery_window_in_days is 7–30, default 30, the same defect Ch9 already records. A third pass ran the chapter's centrepiece listing instead of reading it, and it does not work. Listing 10.8's two topology toggles are inverted — two_tier_subnets is created when enable_isolated_subnet is true while the local a page later selects three_tier_subnets on the same condition — so the module either errors or lies. Reproduced with stub submodules on Terraform 1.15.8 and OpenTofu 1.12.5: true gives This object does not have an attribute named "isolated_subnet_id", and false gives no error at all and every output as [], with subnets created and nothing returned. Swapping the two count expressions fixes both branches, so the pattern is sound and only the direction is wrong. The generalisable half is worth more than the bug: module.x with count = 0 is an empty tuple, so a ternary between a populated module list and an empty one takes its element type from the populated branch — selecting the empty branch therefore yields a well-typed [] rather than a type error, which is exactly why the silent failure is silent, and why an integration test asserting non-empty outputs catches what terraform validate cannot. Also measured while checking a smaller claim: a provisioner on terraform_data can use self (self.id, self.output both resolve); what it lacks is an address, so the chapter's "no self values we can use here" is loose rather than wrong. And one of its examples is miswired: Listing 10.40 passes data.cloudinit_config.node.rendered to aws_instance.user_data, but cloudinit_config defaults gzip and base64_encode to true while the AWS provider says "Do not pass gzip-compressed data via this argument; see user_data_base64 instead" — so the listing needs either the other argument or both defaults turned off. One book-adjacent claim corrected in the note itself: §10.7.1's .tofu treatment is accurate, but .tofurc is not part of that feature — it is the renamed .terraformrc and dates to the 1.6 fork baseline, as E3 already records. Topic backlog gains provisioners-and-escape-hatches, checks-and-conditions and naming-and-domains; opentofu-divergence is now promotable, since TID's OpenTofu sections are captured. 2026-08-15 — The Terraform checkout has already given up its graph internals, its plan mechanics and its config schemas, so this pass took the surface nobody audits: environment variables. Swept os.Getenv/os.LookupEnv across internal/ and the root package, dropped the acceptance-test harness variables, and checked each survivor against the CLI environment-variables page. That page documents 14; the binary reads at least eight more that are on no page at all, plus two (TF_LOG_CORE, TF_LOG_PROVIDER) documented on the debugging page instead and TF_TOKEN_<host> on the credentials page. Captured as terraform-env-vars, with the sweep command recorded so it can be re-run on a later release. The one with immediate practical value is TF_DISABLE_PLUGIN_TLS. Terraform secures each provider's local gRPC channel with auto-generated mutual TLS, and any non-empty value turns that off — which makes it the way to confirm that a local traffic interceptor, not the provider, is behind Failed to load plugin schemas on every provider. The source is blunt that it exists for the plugin SDK test framework and "is not intended to be set by end-users", so it belongs in a diagnosis, not in a shell profile; with it set the plugin channel is unauthenticated on loopback. Folded into E5 alongside TF_LOG. TF_ENABLE_PLUGGABLE_STATE_STORAGE closes a loop from the 2026-08-13 schema sweep, which found a state_store block gated behind AllowExperimentalFeatures since 1.13 and announced nowhere: this is how you switch it on, introduced in f494ff5540 and first tagged v1.14.0, and initialising a backend under it prints warnings that describe the feature's maturity more candidly than any published page. Recorded on release-feature-map beside the original finding. Two more worth knowing. TF_WARN_OUTPUT_ERRORS lives in a file whose only contents are a comment reading "feature flags for the next release" and downgrades output interpolation errors to warnings, logging at [ERROR] and recording the output as unknown — a pre-0.12-era compatibility shim, and deliberately not applied to the newer sensitive-output checks, which the source excludes by name. And TF_SKIP_CREATE_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE, new in v1.15.0 with a matching -create-default-workspace flag on init, has inverted precedence on purpose: the variable beats an explicit -create-default-workspace=true, because a true on the command line "is indistinguishable from the default value being used". That is the first sign of Terraform treating the default workspace as optional, which is A7's territory. Also recorded as method: variables read by prefix scan (TF_VAR_, TF_CLI_ARGS_<name>, TF_TOKEN_<host>) do not show up in the sweep and must be searched for as prefixes, and TF_IGNORE is not read anywhere in the repository — it belongs to the config-upload library, not the CLI. A3 and E5 both gain the pointer. No status changes.

2026-08-15 — OpenTofu is the best-covered repo here, so the useful angle was the one thing the changelog-derived pages could not reach: the migration mechanism. The feature maps and the schema sweep already answer what OpenTofu added; nothing answered what it does to your project when you switch. Captured as opentofu-migration-mechanics, with three findings that appear in none of the migration documentation. State provider addresses are translated in memory rather than rewritten on disk — internal/tofumigrate deep-copies the state on every load, at tofu init, at every local plan/apply, and at state show — and, crucially, the translation is skipped for any provider the configuration pins in full form. random = {} becomes registry.opentofu.org/hashicorp/random; source = "registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/random" stays put, by design. That is the supported lever for running the OpenTofu CLI against HashiCorp-built providers, and it is stated only in a package comment. There is also an off switch documented nowhere: OPENTOFU_STATEFILE_PROVIDER_ADDRESS_TRANSLATION=0, present since v1.6.0 (commit 9c789368dc, opentofu#773) and absent from every .md in the repository. The lock-file half is the one with a real consequence. Since v1.10.0, UpgradeFromPredecessorProject mirrors registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/* entries into OpenTofu-registry ones — only that namespace, because the source says no equivalence can be assumed elsewhere — preserving version selections and discarding every hash, since the lock "can be used to select the same version number but not to guarantee that the provider package matches what was previously installed". The warning the user sees states the underlying fact plainly: "the OpenTofu project's provider releases are not byte-for-byte identical." Same provider source, different builds — which is the answer to the question people actually ask about the fork's providers, and it means the switch is a re-recording of provider checksums rather than continuity, worth a deliberate review for anyone treating the lock as a supply-chain control (I4, A6). A migration performed on 1.6–1.9 had no lock mirroring at all. One existing claim sharpened: two pages described the 1.8 .tofu extension as "parsed alongside .tf". True of the directory, misleading for a pair — the parser "will ignore the .tf file and only use the .tofu file", so main.tofu must be a complete replacement for main.tf, not a patch. Corrected in E3 and opentofu-feature-history. The same shadowing covers .tf.json/.tofu.json and the test extensions, which surfaced something the notes had never recorded: OpenTofu's test framework accepts .tofutest.hcl and .tofutest.json. E3 stays ⬜.

2026-08-15 — Reading hashicorp/hcl overturned an assumption the notes had already reasoned from: the two tools do not build against the same HCL. Checked in the two go.mod files rather than assumed — Terraform pins upstream github.com/hashicorp/hcl/v2 v2.24.0, while OpenTofu requires v2.20.1 and replaces it with its own fork, github.com/opentofu/hcl/v2 v2.20.2-0.20251021132045-587d123c2828, a pseudo-version from a commit dated 2025-10-21. Different code, from bases four minor versions apart. conditional-branch-evaluation had written "it holds for OpenTofu identically — both consume the same hcl/v2", which is a false premise; the conclusion survives because it rests on hclsyntax/spec.md, which both implement, but the reasoning did not, and it is corrected in place with the general rule: spec-level claims transfer between the tools, implementation-level ones need checking per tool. Captured as hcl-library-facts, with the upstream delta enumerated from the CHANGELOG and gated with git tag --contains — mark propagation through conditional and for expressions (v2.23.0, the machinery deciding whether sensitive survives them) and rejection of invalid nested splats (v2.24.0) are the two that would be visible in configuration terms. Recorded with an explicit limit: OpenTofu's fork carries ~19 months of its own commits and may have back-ported any of them, so the table is an upper bound on divergence, not a measurement — the fork is not cloned locally. Spec facts captured for the book, quoted rather than paraphrased: identifiers are UAX #31 plus a dash that the spec itself calls unidiomatic; numeric literals are decimal only, with no hex or octal syntax in the language; escape sequences are defined only for quoted templates, which independently confirms Ch 7's existing claim that a backslash in a heredoc is literal; <<- strips "the minimum number of leading spaces", not all indentation, and only from lines starting with a literal string; and strip markers work at syntax level, so ${"hello" ~}${" world"} still produces "hello world". One gap found in a written chapter, additive rather than contradictory, so nothing flips to 🔄: Ch 7 teaches [*] correctly but never covers the attribute-only .*. form, whose trailing index applies to the result list where [*]'s applies inside each element, nor the splat rules that have no for equivalent — a non-collection auto-wraps (any_number.* is [any_number]) and a null scalar splats to an empty tuple, which is the idiomatic zero-or-one conversion. Logged for the next revision of that chapter. Also worth knowing for future lookups: dynamic blocks and try/can live in ext/, so they are HCL extensions rather than language features, which is why the specs never mention them — and HCL defines no functions of its own, the host application supplies the table, which is how Terraform's and OpenTofu's function lists can differ without either breaking the spec. B4 gains the specs as a reference for when the docs paraphrase; E3 gains the fork finding. No status changes.

2026-08-15 — KL is cited in nine places, so this pass was a citation audit, and two citations pointed at content the repository does not contain. Two README claims that do not hold: it promises a pre-configured dev container and tells you to create a Codespace "from this repo", but there is no .devcontainer — the only hidden directory is .github holding FUNDING.yml, and the Codespaces badge points at a separate btkrausen/terraform-codespaces repository; and its "Terraform 1.12.2 — Tested" badge sits beside a CI badge pointing at terraform-testing, which installs Latest, validates a different set of lab directories, and per krausen-lab-ci-facts has a plan gate that cannot fail. The B3 lab entry now carries the Codespaces caveat. No status changes.

2026-08-15 — btkrausen/terraform-testing turned out not to be a testing-library repo at all, and is more useful than if it had been: it is a GitHub Actions harness, and it is a ready-made A3 case study — good pattern and cautionary tale in one file. Captured as krausen-lab-ci-facts. Three workflows run a matrix over 16 lab directories per provider, on push, on PR, and on a weekly cron — and that cron is the transferable idea, since its purpose is not to test the author's code but to detect the day someone else's release breaks it. The pattern half is worth copying wholesale and is now step 4 of A3: OIDC rather than static keys, the third-party action pinned by commit SHA, an explicit least-privilege permissions: block, TF_IN_AUTOMATION plus TF_CLI_ARGS: -no-color, terraform_wrapper: false so step outputs are real exit codes, init -backend=false so validation never touches real state, and fail-fast: false with per-leg mktemp -d isolation. The cautionary half is a matched pair of exit-code bugs in the same repository, failing in opposite directions, which is why they earned a callout rather than a footnote. The workflow runs terraform plan -detailed-exitcode || true and then echo $? > plan_exit_code.txt — $? is the status of true, so the file always holds 0, the checking step always reports success, and the plan gate cannot fail; a lab whose plan errors keeps the badge green. Present in all four jobs across all three workflows. The repo's standalone script captures the code correctly with PLAN_EXIT_CODE=$? but opens with set -e, under which the value 2 — "plan succeeded, changes present", the normal outcome — aborts the script before that line, so the branch written to translate 2 into success is unreachable and the gate cannot pass. -detailed-exitcode is genuinely awkward to consume: the value meaning "fine" is the value shell error handling treats as failure. This is the same lesson the path already draws about terraform fmt -check, with better evidence. Two more, both silent: the failure-notification job is gated on needs.test-labs.result while the jobs are named test-tfb-labs and test-hol-labs, so it never runs and the README's promise of an auto-filed issue does not happen — a skipped job looks like a passing one in a run summary, so alerting needs one deliberate failure to prove it — and the README says each module is run through fmt, which appears nowhere in the workflows. Scope note recorded so the labs are not mis-trusted: KL (terraform-associate-labs) is a different repository from the modules/tfb/** labs this harness checks, so nothing here changes KL's standing; what it changes is what the green badge supports — init and validate failures are caught for real, plan failures are not caught at all. Also noted: the AWS workflow's two jobs use two different credential models, OIDC in one and static access keys in the other, which is a partial migration frozen in place. A3 stays ⬜.

2026-08-15 — Floci was the one local repo already written up, so this pass was a re-verification, and it moved three claims. The checkout is a fork: origin is a personal one and upstream is floci-io/floci, with the working tree parked on the 1.6.0 release commit (2026-08-06) while upstream/main runs to 2026-08-15 with no tag since — so released and unreleased behaviour needed labelling separately, and floci-facts now says which is which. The claim that changed shape: "repeat CreateBucket in us-east-1 is idempotent here, AWS is not" is narrower than recorded. S3Service.createBucket does raise BucketAlreadyOwnedByYou (409), guarded by a region check on both sides, so the plain repeat-create case matches AWS deliberately. What still diverges is the creation-tags case, where the controller re-runs putBucketTagging on the existing bucket — a repeat create silently rewrites the tags instead of failing. The second open item, missing InvalidTag validation, is unchanged: the string appears nowhere in the source. The authentication caveat is now confirmed in code and is starting to change. Unreleased, pre-signed only, and the flag itself is undocumented — so the undocumented-flag pattern moved rather than went away, while FLOCI_SERVICES_IAM_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED, which the note had called undocumented, is documented now. The find that changes how much to trust the labs: Floci ships compatibility-tests/ with compat-terraform, compat-opentofu and compat-cdk beside five SDK suites, running real clients against a live instance with no mocks — and the Terraform case drives an S3 remote backend with a DynamoDB lock table, so I6's backend work is a path upstream tests. With one trap recorded: their backend.hcl uses endpoint, dynamodb_endpoint, force_path_style and dynamodb_table, all of which HashiCorp's current S3 backend reference marks deprecated in favour of an endpoints {} block, use_path_style and use_lockfile (DynamoDB locking "will be removed in a future minor version"), so a lab must not copy it verbatim. The B2 emulator callout gains the compatibility-suite and IAM-enforcement facts, and its bucket-tag example is now past tense with the 1.6.0 fix named. Also recorded: FLOCI_SERVICES_IAM_SEED_DEPLOYER_PRINCIPAL for a real lab principal instead of the god-mode test key, and FLOCI_PROTOCOLS_REJECT_UNKNOWN_SERVICE_SCOPE, which is why an unimplemented service returns a clean error rather than a misleading NoSuchBucket. No status changes.

2026-08-15 — Reading Terrakube's source rather than its docs overturned the A9 claim that mattered most: its permissions are no longer organization-wide. The old callout said toggles apply across a whole organization with no project tier, so a tenant had to be an entire Terrakube organization — true of the pre-2.30 model, and wrong now. RBAC v2 landed in 2.30.0 (2026-02-26, commit 5cfc9638) with HCP-shaped roles (admin, write, plan, read, custom), and project-level team permissions in 2.32.0 (2026-05-17, commit e99e40c9), both gated by git tag --contains. Permissions now hang off three entities — Team, ProjectAccess, Access — so a tenant can be a project, which removes the main structural objection A9 raised against it. The verdict paragraph, which called the open-source permission surface uniformly coarse, now names Terrakube as the exception and keeps the charge against Atlantis. Captured as terrakube-facts. Why the source was necessary: unlike the other two checkouts, Terrakube's docs are a separate site, and the model is stated loosely there and precisely in the entity classes, which is a consequence of the API being built on Elide — authorization lives in annotations on the fields, so Team.java is the permission spec. Two behaviours only readable there: under a predefined role the fine-grained booleans are ignored, and a null or blank role normalizes to custom, which is what silently preserves pre-2.30 rows. The roles are also not a ladder — write plans and applies, but registry, VCS and template management are admin-only. Three capabilities were missing from the path entirely. RemoteTfeController implements the TFE v2 API at /remote/tfe/v2/, including workspace lock/unlock, state and configuration versions, run apply/discard, and remote-state-consumers — so the cloud {} block works against a self-hosted Terrakube and cross-workspace state reads are a modelled relationship rather than a bucket IAM condition, which was the specific gap A9 left open for the pure-CI design. There is an HCP Terraform importer carrying workspaces, variables, variable sets, tags and state versions, with a preview step for sensitive ones. And federated credentials (2.31.0) invert the dynamic-credentials pattern: a CI job authenticates to the platform with a workload-identity token matched on issuer, audience and claims, list-valued claims matching any element, which is exactly a GitHub Actions token's shape. The run-isolation finding deserved its own callout, since it is the constraint the whole topic turns on: the ephemeral executor runs each job as its own Kubernetes Job, and EPHEMERAL_CONFIG_POD_ANNOTATIONS annotates the generated pod so Vault Agent Injector or GKE Workload Identity can give that single run its own credentials. Recorded with its limit — the tenant's code still runs inside that pod, so plan-time code execution still reaches whatever identity the pod holds. Status unchanged: A9 stays ⬜ — the topic gained accuracy, not completion.

2026-08-15 — Terratest was three docs links and one wrong version fact; it is now source-derived, and the fact was wrong in a way that mattered. terraform-testing recorded "Terratest latest published 2026-05-11," which is really v1.0.0, the first stable release — v1.0.1 followed 2026-06-27 and the v2 betas on 2026-07-20 and 2026-08-10. Corrected there and captured properly as terratest-facts. Everything v2 here was read with git show origin/main:<path>, which needs no checkout change and leaves the user's tree alone. v2 is a multi-module split, not a rewrite: sixteen independently versioned Go modules under /v2 paths, so a Terraform-only test stops pulling in every cloud SDK; random/retry/logger/shell/files consolidate into modules/core; http-helper, test-structure and dns-helper lose their hyphens; and six packages — collections, environment, git, version-checker, slack, oci — were deleted outright in one commit, so those imports do not port by editing a path. Three hygiene rules got their own callout because each one silently breaks a suite: defer the destroy or a failed assertion leaks paid resources; -count=1 or Go's test cache returns a stale pass when only .tf files changed; -timeout 30m or Go kills the process at ten minutes and the deferred destroy never runs. Added random.UniqueID() namespacing and ApplyAndIdempotentContext to the A2 milestone. One tie-in to the previous entry: Terratest ships a full terragrunt helper module — run --all, stack generate, stack run, stack output, dag graph — so E4's stack layout is testable end to end, noted there. Status unchanged: A2 stays ⬜.

The clone at repos\terragrunt (commit 54c43a44c, tags to v1.1.3) ships its own documentation site under docs/, which is what renders at docs.terragrunt.com — so the checkout gives the docs, a per-release changelog as one file per change, and the code to settle anything the docs leave vague, all version-gated by tag. 2026-08-15 — The open-source half went from an architecture sketch to a buildable blueprint, and it answers the "is this doable" question with a yes. The previous pass named where each control relocates but stopped before the mechanism, and "use CI OIDC" is not an architecture until the claim is named. Grounded it on GitHub's OIDC docs: the subject is repo:octo-org/octo-repo:environment:prod, conditioned in the cloud trust policy exactly as HCP's organization:…:project:…:workspace:… is, with the same wildcard failure mode, and the token is "only valid for a single job, and then automatically expires", which is what makes the shared-runner risk survivable. Two timely findings. Repositories "created after July 15, 2026 use an immutable default subject format that includes owner and repository IDs" rather than names, not available on GitHub Enterprise Server — that is a direct fix for the reuse hazard this topic flagged in offboarding, since an ID never repeats and a stale trust policy cannot be reactivated by recreating a same-named thing; trust policies written against the old format need re-checking. And repository custom properties can be surfaced as OIDC claims, enabling ABAC "driven by repository metadata rather than hard-coded allow lists", which is the open-source counterpart to HCP's project segment and the thing that makes fifty tenants tractable. Also wrote the state recipe (prefix per tenant, IAM condition, per-tenant KMS key, OpenTofu encryption on top), and the pipeline-ownership mechanism (CODEOWNERS on the workflow path, or a platform-owned reusable workflow), which is the structural equivalent of Manage policies being organization-level. The finding worth carrying: open source is strictly stronger on modules. HCP's private registry has no per-team read scope, so tenants who must not see each other's modules need separate organizations; with git sources, module visibility is repository visibility, so the capability HCP charges an organization split for is the VCS's default. Verdict recorded in the topic: achievable, stronger on module visibility and state encryption, harder on run isolation, coarse permission surfaces, and the absence of a single console answering "who can reach this tenant".

2026-08-15 — A9 was an HCP topic wearing a general title; it now covers the open-source stack too. The old treatment was a single callout saying OpenTofu has no user model and naming three products. Replaced with real coverage, and the framing that makes it teachable is that the four controls relocate rather than disappear: who may start a run becomes VCS branch protection, what the run may touch becomes CI OIDC federation, policy becomes a pipeline step the tenant cannot edit, and state access becomes backend IAM on bucket, prefix and key. Two properties transfer badly and are called out — there is no equivalent of Remote State Sharing, so cross-workspace reads must be an object-prefix IAM condition, and the audit trail becomes the CI's plus the cloud's, usually better than HCP's 14 days but requiring manual correlation. The load-bearing finding came from Atlantis's own security page, and it governs every self-hosted design: apply approval is not a boundary, because "it is possible to run malicious code in a terraform plan using the external data source or by specifying a malicious provider", which "could then exfiltrate your credentials". A single runner holding every tenant's credentials therefore has no boundary regardless of approval rules, so the rule is one runner per trust domain with per-run OIDC credentials. Atlantis details recorded: authorization runs twice (repo, then per project after pre-workflow hooks, since affected projects are unknown at the first check), --gh-team-allowlist maps VCS teams to commands with the documented trap that omitting policy_check makes manual plans skip policy while autoplans still run it, and the external command in server-side config is the real per-tenant hook. Terrakube (Apache-2.0) is the closest workalike but scopes differently: teams are named after Dex groups so membership federates by construction, while permissions are organization-wide booleans, so a tenant is an organization rather than a project — though its separate Manage State toggle is better-grained than HCP, where all four fixed workspace roles read full state. Digger (MIT) sidesteps the runner problem by executing in the user's existing CI. A rename worth catching: terrateamio/terrateam now redirects to stategraph/stategraph (MPL-2.0, OCaml) — Terrateam's engine was open-sourced and the product is folding into Stategraph, which stores state as a graph in PostgreSQL; A4's TID §8.7 citation now carries that warning, since the book's six-way comparison predates the move. Closed with OpenTofu state encryption as the one tenant control HCP lacks, per-tenant KMS keys making a bucket-wide read useless, alongside its documented limit that encryption "cannot protect the sensitive values in the state file from the person running the tofu command" — it defends a tenant against the operator and other tenants, never against itself. 2026-08-15 — Third coverage check on A9: onboarding was complete, the lifecycle was not. 2026-08-15 — A9's five stated omissions closed, so the topic no longer defers anything. The previous pass listed SSO mapping, audit trails, token attribution, non-AWS credentials and chargeback as deliberate exclusions; all five are now written from verbatim docs, and the exclusions callout is gone. SAML mapping turns out to be the one with teeth: membership is authoritative and re-evaluated at every login, "this automatic mapping overrides any manually set team memberships", so a directory edit moves a person between tenants and a manual UI fix survives only until their next sign-in. Two failure modes recorded, one silent and one fail-open — a team name not matching exactly is ignored with no team created, and a missing attribute drops users into a default sso team while "not removing them from any existing teams", so a broken assertion preserves stale access instead of revoking it. Also the permanent owner bypass: non-owners must use SSO, owners keep username-and-password access by design, hence the two break-glass accounts. Audit trails carry three constraints that shape any design: 14-day retention, Standard/Premium only and not available in Terraform Enterprise, and an endpoint that "cannot be accessed with a user token or team token", requiring an organization or audit-trail token, which is why the exporter is structurally a platform-team job. Team tokens trade attribution for durability, and the docs state the worst case plainly, that an owners-team token "will have all of the same permissions that an organization owner would" — one string crossing every boundary in the topic. The per-cloud comparison was the most useful find: the sub claim is identical everywhere but the matching primitive is not. AWS conditions on StringEquals/StringLike, GCP uses a workload identity pool attribute condition with assertion.sub.startsWith(...) so a project prefix is natural, and Azure cannot wildcard at all — the federated credential's subject "is a direct string match", requiring "two federated identity credentials … for each workspace", one per run phase. So Azure is safe by construction and heavy to automate, while AWS is flexible and one wildcard from being wrong. Chargeback closes on a constraint rather than a feature: cost estimation is a single organization-wide toggle with no per-project granularity, and gating on it forces the policy set onto Legacy policy execution mode capped at Sentinel 0.40.x, which is the strongest argument in the topic for doing cost governance with Infracost in the pipeline instead.

2026-08-15 — Observability with OpenTelemetry researched across all three layers, and the path's own claim about it was false. E5 said "Terraform has no built-in OTel equivalent". It has one: OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp enables an OTLP exporter in telemetry.go, and the reason nobody knows is that it is undocumented — a grep of the Terraform repo's website/ for opentelemetry returns nothing, so the only public description is a source comment reading "BEWARE! This is not a committed external interface." The real divergence is depth. OpenTofu 1.10+ traces the graph walk: Validation/Plan/Apply phase spans, then one span per graph node (Plan resource instance changes, Apply resource instance changes, Configure provider) carrying opentofu.resource_instance.address and opentofu.provider.source, which is what makes "which resource is slow" answerable. Terraform 1.15 has ~10 span sites, all in main, checkpoint.go, and internal/command — module and provider install, backend init — and no graph-walk spans at all; the instrumented plan/apply code lives in internal/stacks/stackruntime and internal/rpcapi, which HCP Terraform drives over RPC, not the CLI. Three consequences worth carrying: OpenTofu reads TRACEPARENT (1.10) so a run nests inside a pipeline trace while Terraform ignores it (#35444, open since 2024-07-10); Terraform exports spans through a SimpleSpanProcessor (synchronous, per span) where OpenTofu batches; and Terraform's root span is named terraform <full command line>, so -var="password=…" reaches the tracing backend, where OpenTofu's root span is just tofu. Version-gated with git tag --contains: init spans, node spans and TRACEPARENT all first ship in v1.10.0, OTEL_SERVICE_NAME in v1.11.0, and 1.13 (unreleased) adds TRACEPARENT propagation into local-exec children plus OTel library logs in TF_LOG. Two CI traps recorded in A3: a broken collector fails the command (both binaries exit 1 while the variable is set), and autoexport's default protocol is http/protobuf/4318, so the OpenTofu docs' own 4317 example needs OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc — the docs page contains both port numbers in different sections. A4 gains the one layer that emits metrics: HCP Terraform agents (-otlp-address, tfc-agent.* metric families, per-run attributes like workspace_name/run_id), which neither CLI does. Two stale claims fixed in feature-history and opentofu-feature-history ("no OTel in Terraform" / "None"). Notes: ot-otel-tracing, otel-tracing-facts. E5 and E3 stay ⬜ — no chapter was written, so nothing flips.

2026-07-17 — Reference shapes are structural, and typed module outputs change what callers receive. A contradiction inside Ch 7 (§2 "every resource reference is an object" vs §3 "references look like objects but aren't") turned out to be an instance-vs-container confusion: an instance is an object, a bare type name is not a value, and the container depends on the meta-argument. Chasing it found the shape line itself wrong — count gives a tuple, for_each an object, not the list/map the docs say (the docs declare that conflation openly; §2 is the section that breaks it). Why structural: a collection needs one element type and instances aren't guaranteed to share one — for_each = { a = "str", b = 5 } yields a with input: string and b with input: number, two different object types no map could hold. Resources take that path unconditionally (evaluate.go:931/952). The find worth keeping: modules do switch. GetModule branches on "does the module fully define all output types", so adding type = string to a module's output flips module.c from tuple → list and module.f from object → map (verified, TF 1.15.8). So output type (1.15+) does change the type callers receive — but measuring that turned out to deflate it: auto-conversion means callers can't tell, since a tuple splats, converts, and satisfies a list(object(...)) constraint exactly as a list does. Ch 6's modest "improves matching across validation, plan, and apply" was right all along, and the B6 🔄 I raised against it was my over-claim, not the chapter's under-claim — retracted, along with a flatly false line in I5 saying callers "feel the difference". Noted in B6/I5/E3 as a curiosity, not a reason. Finding a real mechanism is not the same as finding it matters. Also fixed: the splat section justified itself with "a count resource is a list" (it's a tuple — right conclusion, wrong reason). Two method failures recorded: terraform_data is the only provider-free resource and is atypical (dynamic attributes), and the noDynamicTypes branch that nearly reverted a correct fix lives in GetModule, not the resource path. Evidence: conditional-branch-evaluation.

2026-08-08 — A8's primary reference captured (tf-modules-refactoring, HCDocs "Refactor modules"), folded into A8's Refactor modules reference — the deep moved reference whose removal rules tut-move-config already quoted, with everything else new. The governing rule is about addressing: a bare address moves a resource as a whole and covers every instance, but an instance key on either side flips the block into instance mode. That single toggle is what makes count ↔ for_each ↔ neither migrations expressible, one moved block per index — and neither tut-count nor tut-for-each mentions moved at all, so the migration those tutorials walk through is a destroy-and-recreate as written. One case is already free: adding count to a resource that lacked it auto-proposes a move to index 0, while for_each needs a key you pick and a rename is never free — which is exactly the "8 added, 4 destroyed" tut-count measured. Two hard limits worth memorizing: cross-type moves exist but are provider-dependent (ask the provider docs, not the language docs), and a managed resource can never become a data block — that path is removed with lifecycle { destroy = false } plus a separate data block. The find worth keeping is the module-split shim, which solves something nothing else in the docs addresses: splitting a published module without breaking consumers. The original module is kept as a shim that calls the new modules and carries the moved blocks, so existing users upgrade in place. HashiCorp flags it as violating the closed-box rule and attaches the precondition — "all three of these modules are maintained by the same people and distributed together in a single module package" — so this licence does not extend to writing cross-module moved blocks against someone else's module. Scoping bounds it: addresses resolve relative to the module they are written in, and "a module may only make moved statements about its own objects and objects of its child modules" — down, never up or sideways. Finally, chaining (a→b, b→c) is the mechanism that makes retention make sense: each block covers consumers arriving from a different starting version, so a module's moved blocks accumulate like database migrations rather than as a courtesy changelog. A8 stays ⬜.

2026-08-08 — "Publish modules" captured, mostly to record where it isn't (tf-modules-publish), folded into I5's Module Development reference.
