items.title: 9. Replacement, targeting, and other blunt instruments
-replace: rebuild one object on purpose
items.text:
Sometimes the object is fine as far as the provider can tell and broken as far as you are concerned. A process crashed inside a running VM; the provider reports a healthy instance, because the instance is healthy at the layer the provider models.

Recreate resources states that boundary better than anything else in the docs:

"When remote objects become damaged or degraded, such as when software running inside a virtual machine crashes but the virtual machine is still running, Terraform does not have no way to detect and respond to the problem. This is because Terraform only directly manages the machine as a whole."

The double negative is theirs. An apply acts only on mismatches between object and configuration, and a crashed process is not a mismatch. So replacement is a manual instruction:

$ terraform plan -replace aws_s3_bucket.site

  # aws_s3_bucket.site will be replaced, as requested
-/+ resource "aws_s3_bucket" "site" {
      + acceleration_status         = (known after apply)
      + acl                         = (known after apply)
      ~ arn                         = "arn:aws:s3:::ch16-drift-site" -> (known after apply)
      ~ bucket_domain_name          = "ch16-drift-site.s3.amazonaws.com" -> (known after apply)
      ...

as requested is the plan distinguishing an operator-forced replacement from one the diff demanded. Measured on v1.15.8 in labs/chapter16/lab5.

items.title: taint is dead, untaint is not, and the asymmetry is the interesting part
items.text:
terraform taint has been deprecated since 0.15.2, the release that added -replace — its own command reference says "This command is deprecated" and points at -replace "For Terraform v0.15.2 and later". The reason Recreate resources gives is a mechanism rather than a preference:

"that approach is deprecated in favor of the -replace=... option, which avoids the need to create an interim state snapshot with a tainted object."

taint had to write state to record the intent, and the next apply acted on the mark. Two operations with a gap between them, which is the same flaw as the state mv race in section 2.

The state write is visible in the file, and one bucket is enough to see it. The configuration is committed at labs/chapter16/section9/tainted-field/:

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "t" {
  bucket = "ch16-taintstate"
}

tflocal apply -auto-approve
terraform taint aws_s3_bucket.t        # read the state file after each of these
terraform untaint aws_s3_bucket.t

Both moving parts come straight out of the file, with no Terraform command in between:

python -c "import json;d=json.load(open('terraform.tfstate'));i=d['resources'][0]['instances'][0];print(d['serial'], sorted(i.keys()))"

Measured on v1.15.8, the instance object gains one key and the serial moves, twice:

instance keys serial after apply attributes, identity, identity_schema_version, private, schema_version, sensitive_attributes 1 after taint the same, plus status 2 after untaint back to the first list 3

status holds the string tainted, which is section 1's field table met in the field. Two state writes to schedule and unschedule a replacement that -replace expresses as a planning flag, writing nothing until you apply.

But tainted is not only a command. It is a state field Terraform sets on its own when it can infer that an object was left half-built, which the untaint reference says out loud:

"Terraform automatically marks an object as “tainted” if an error occurs during a multi-step “create” action, because Terraform can't be sure that the object was left in a fully-functional state."

A failed provisioner is the common case, since a provisioner is a step of the create action. A tainted object also poisons everything downstream of it, and the mechanism is worth seeing because it is not a special rule about taint. It takes a bucket and one resource attached to it, committed at labs/chapter16/section9/taint-downstream/:

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "upstream" {
  bucket = "ch16-taintdown"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "downstream" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.upstream.id

  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

tflocal apply -auto-approve
terraform taint aws_s3_bucket.upstream      # only the upstream bucket
tflocal plan                                # two replacements

Measured on v1.15.8. The two headers are more than sixty lines apart in the real output, and the argument that explains the second one is inside its block:

  # aws_s3_bucket.upstream is tainted, so must be replaced
-/+ resource "aws_s3_bucket" "upstream" {
      ...
  # aws_s3_bucket_versioning.downstream must be replaced
-/+ resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "downstream" {
      ~ bucket                = "ch16-taintdown" -> (known after apply) # forces replacement
      ~ id                    = "ch16-taintdown" -> (known after apply)
      ...

Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 2 to destroy.

The downstream resource is replaced because the upstream id it points at becomes (known after apply) the moment the upstream is scheduled for replacement, and bucket is a forced-new argument. That is the same unknown-value rule section 6 met on an import block's id, arriving here as blast radius. One tainted object, two replacements, and only the first line says why.

The round trip itself is two commands and two plans, measured in labs/chapter16/lab5:

$ terraform taint aws_s3_bucket.site
Resource instance aws_s3_bucket.site has been marked as tainted.

$ terraform plan
  # aws_s3_bucket.site is tainted, so must be replaced
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.

$ terraform untaint aws_s3_bucket.site
Resource instance aws_s3_bucket.site has been successfully untainted.

$ terraform plan
No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.

Worth noticing what is missing from that transcript: taint prints no deprecation warning at all on v1.15.8, and exits zero. The command is deprecated in the documentation and silent at the terminal, which is how it keeps getting used.

OpenTofu — one word apart, and equally silent

Measured on OpenTofu 1.12.5: tofu taint is just as quiet, -replace renders identically as will be replaced, as requested, and the tainted plan line differs by a single word, is tainted, so it must be replaced. The strings come from the same file in both trees, internal/command/jsonformat/plan.go, which is where the fork shows: Terraform writes is tainted, so must be and OpenTofu writes is tainted, so it must be. Behaviour is identical; a grep for the Terraform wording will miss every OpenTofu run.

That is why terraform untaint survives the deprecation. It answers a question -replace cannot, which is Terraform thinks this is damaged and I disagree. And you do not have to re-taint to change your mind back: if you later decide it was degraded after all, apply -replace= schedules the rebuild directly.

items.title: -target: a subgraph, not a filter
items.text:
-target reads like a filter. Name a resource, act on that resource, leave the rest of the configuration alone. It is not a filter, and the difference is the whole reason the flag is dangerous: it selects a subgraph, and the selection closes over the dependency edges in one direction only. HashiCorp's Target resources tutorial states the direction in a single sentence:

"Resource targeting updates resources that the target depends on, but not resources that depend on it."

Everything the target needs comes along, whether you named it or not. Everything that needs the target is left stale.

Three buckets with one object in each are enough to watch that closure run, because every edge is between resources whose instances line up index for index. The configuration is committed at labs/chapter16/section9/target-graph/:

variable "generation" {
  type    = string
  default = "a"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "shard" {
  count  = 3
  bucket = "ch16-targetgraph-${count.index}-${var.generation}"
}

resource "aws_s3_object" "obj" {
  count   = 3
  bucket  = aws_s3_bucket.shard[count.index].id
  key     = "payload"
  content = "x"
}

Apply it once, then flip generation. That renames all three buckets, which forces all three replacements, and each object goes with its bucket. Plan the same change four ways:

tflocal apply -auto-approve                                       # generation = "a"
tflocal plan -var generation=b                                    # the whole graph
tflocal plan -var generation=b -target 'aws_s3_bucket.shard[0]'   # one upstream instance
tflocal plan -var generation=b -target aws_s3_object.obj          # the downstream resource
tflocal plan -var generation=b -target 'aws_s3_object.obj[1]'     # one downstream instance

Measured on v1.15.8:

Plan Result What the target dragged in no -target 6 to add, 0 to change, 6 to destroy everything -target 'aws_s3_bucket.shard[0]' 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy the bucket alone, leaving the object inside it pointed at a bucket about to be destroyed -target aws_s3_object.obj 6 to add, 0 to change, 6 to destroy three objects plus the three buckets they depend on -target 'aws_s3_object.obj[1]' 4 to add, 0 to change, 4 to destroy one object plus all three buckets

Row three is the upstream closure doing its job: targeting the objects reached the buckets nobody asked for, and reproduced the untargeted plan exactly. Row two is the same rule seen from the other end, and it is the row that costs you something, because a bucket replaced out from under an untargeted object is a graph half-applied.

Row four is the one worth staring at. Targeting one object instance planned the replacement of all three buckets:

  # aws_s3_bucket.shard[0] must be replaced
  # aws_s3_bucket.shard[1] must be replaced
  # aws_s3_bucket.shard[2] must be replaced
  # aws_s3_object.obj[1] must be replaced

Plan: 4 to add, 0 to change, 4 to destroy.

That is section 3's addressing grammar meeting the graph. Terraform builds edges between resource nodes and expands instances underneath them, so obj[1] → shard[1] is not an edge it holds; obj → shard is. The upstream closure of one instance is therefore the whole upstream resource, and an instance-level -target buys instance precision on the target itself and none at all above it. If the point of the flag was to shrink the blast radius, an instance address can widen it instead.

The stale half can fail the apply outright

Leaving downstream out is not only bookkeeping. Apply that fourth plan and the remote objects enforce the edge Terraform was told to skip. shard[1], whose object was in the target set, is emptied and replaced. shard[0] and shard[2] still hold the objects that were not, and S3 refuses to delete a bucket with contents:

aws_s3_object.obj[1]: Destroying... [id=ch16-targetgraph-1-a/payload]
aws_s3_bucket.shard[1]: Destroying... [id=ch16-targetgraph-1-a]
aws_s3_bucket.shard[1]: Creation complete after 1s [id=ch16-targetgraph-1-b]

Error: deleting S3 Bucket (ch16-targetgraph-2-a): operation error S3: DeleteBucket,
https response error StatusCode: 409, api error BucketNotEmpty: The bucket you tried
to delete is not empty.

Error: deleting S3 Bucket (ch16-targetgraph-0-a): operation error S3: DeleteBucket,
https response error StatusCode: 409, api error BucketNotEmpty: The bucket you tried
to delete is not empty.

One of three buckets moved to the new generation, two did not, and the run exits non-zero partway through. The repair is the untargeted apply, which cost 2 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy and returned the directory to an empty plan.

Two warnings guard all of this, they say different things, and the second one only appears if you apply. Two buckets that depend on nothing are enough to produce both, committed at labs/chapter16/section9/targeting/:

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "one" {
  bucket = "ch16-targetwarn-one"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "two" {
  bucket = "ch16-targetwarn-two"
}

tflocal plan -target aws_s3_bucket.one                  # one warning
tflocal apply -auto-approve -target aws_s3_bucket.one   # the same warning, then a second
tflocal plan                                            # what the targeted run deferred

Measured on v1.15.8:

Warning: Resource targeting is in effect

You are creating a plan with the -target option, which means that the result
of this plan may not represent all of the changes requested by the current
configuration.

The -target option is not for routine use, and is provided only for
exceptional situations such as recovering from errors or mistakes, or when
Terraform specifically suggests to use it as part of an error message.

Warning: Applied changes may be incomplete

The plan was created with the -target option in effect, so some changes
requested in the configuration may have been ignored and the output values
may not be fully updated. Run the following command to verify that no other
changes are pending:
    terraform plan

Note that the -target option is not suitable for routine use, and is provided
only for exceptional situations such as recovering from errors or mistakes,
or when Terraform specifically suggests to use it as part of an error
message.

The first says the plan is partial; the second says your infrastructure now is, and hands you the command that measures by how much. In that lab the follow-up plan answers aws_s3_bucket.two will be created, 1 to add: the deferred half, still waiting.

Both warnings name the same short list of legitimate uses, and the last item on it is the one that matters. "Or when Terraform specifically suggests to use it as part of an error message" is the one case where reaching for the flag is following instructions rather than improvising. The rest of the list is failures — a botched apply, a provider bug, a state that stopped matching reality — and none of them is a workflow.

The same sentence, one word apart

The apply-time note says "not suitable for routine use". The plan-time warning drops one word and says "not for routine use". Same list of legitimate uses either way, so a grep or a log filter matching one wording silently misses the other.

A targeted apply that does succeed leaves state internally inconsistent rather than corrupt, which is the harder failure to notice. Nothing in the file is malformed; the values simply describe different moments. One bucket named from a variable, and a second named after the first, is the smallest configuration that shows it, committed at labs/chapter16/section9/target-desync/:

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "source" {
  bucket = "ch16-desync-source-${var.generation}"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "mirror" {
  bucket = "mirror-of-${aws_s3_bucket.source.bucket}"
}

output "source_bucket" {
  value = aws_s3_bucket.source.bucket
}

output "mirror_bucket" {
  value = aws_s3_bucket.mirror.bucket
}

tflocal apply -auto-approve                                                 # generation = "a"
tflocal apply -auto-approve -var generation=b -target aws_s3_bucket.source

Measured on v1.15.8. The untargeted plan for that change is 2 to add, 0 to change, 2 to destroy; the targeted apply does half of it and reports:

Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 1 destroyed.

Outputs:

mirror_bucket = "mirror-of-ch16-desync-source-a"
source_bucket = "ch16-desync-source-b"

Two outputs, one live infrastructure, and they disagree about the name of the same bucket. Both are correctly recorded. source_bucket reads the resource that was targeted and did change; mirror_bucket reads the one that was not. The emulator now holds a bucket called mirror-of-ch16-desync-source-a named after a bucket that no longer exists, and nothing in state is wrong about it.

So the standing rule after any targeted run is an untargeted apply. Here it reported the deferred 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy and converged. Notice what the targeted run did not do: it did not reduce the work. Two replacements were owed before it and one is owed after it, and until that second apply lands, anything reading these outputs is reading two different moments as though they were one.

OpenTofu — -exclude is the inverse, and the two families never mix

OpenTofu 1.9 added -exclude, the deny-list form, and 1.10 added -target-file and -exclude-file. When one resource is broken and you want to apply everything else, enumerating every other resource with -target is far worse than one -exclude.

The two close in opposite directions, which the 1.9 changelog states in one line: "While -target specifies the objects to include and skips everything not needed for the selected objects, -exclude instead specifies objects to skip. OpenTofu will exclude the selected objects and everything that depends on them." The same three-bucket configuration, copied to labs/chapter16/section9/target-exclude/ and measured on OpenTofu 1.12.5, gives the mirror image of the table above:

Plan Result What the exclusion took with it -exclude 'aws_s3_bucket.shard[0]' 2 to add, 0 to change, 2 to destroy that bucket and all three objects, downstream -exclude aws_s3_object.obj 3 to add, 0 to change, 3 to destroy the objects only, since nothing depends on them -exclude 'aws_s3_object.obj[1]' 5 to add, 0 to change, 5 to destroy that one instance

Row one is the resource-granularity rule again, mirrored: excluding a single bucket instance dropped the entire obj resource from the plan, because the edge runs obj → shard. Between the two flags you can close over either half of an edge, which is what -target alone cannot do.

Any target-side option combined with any exclude-side option fails at argument parsing, before planning begins:

Error: Invalid combination of arguments

The target and exclude planning options are mutually-exclusive. Each plan
must use either only the target options or only the exclude options.

Measured on 1.12.5; the string lives in internal/command/arguments/extended.go. The message quoted above is 1.10's: at 1.9 the same collision answered -target and -exclude flags cannot be used together. Please remove one of the flags, guarding only the two direct flags, and 1.10 both widened the check to the two families and rewrote the text. Another string not worth matching on. The consequence for recovery work is that you cannot express "everything except X, but only within module Y" in one run. Terraform has neither flag, so this is an OpenTofu-only escape hatch and an OpenTofu-only constraint.

items.title: 10. The CLI family, and the backup rule that has five holes
items.text:
terraform state is eight subcommands on v1.15.8. Two rules are claimed for the family as a whole, both stated on its index page and, with one exception, on none of the individual command pages. The first is that every subcommand that modifies state is forced to write a backup file. The second is that the subcommands work against a remote backend exactly as they do against a local one, backups included. This section is mostly about how much of the first rule survives contact with v1.15.8, and about the fact that the second one does not. The exception is state replace-provider, whose own page repeats the backup rule — "This command will output a backup copy of the state prior to saving any changes. The backup cannot be disabled. Due to the destructive nature of this command, backups are required." — on the command that is not the most destructive in the family.

Subcommand Writes state? Preview? Prompt? state list no — — state show no — — state identities no — — state mv yes -dry-run only no state rm yes -dry-run only no state replace-provider yes yes, always yes state pull no — — state push yes none available no

The family hub omits two of its own subcommands

The terraform state reference lists six subcommands. state push is not among them, although it exists, has its own reference page, and sits in the sidebar next to state pull, which is listed. It is documented under Disaster Recovery instead. A reader navigating by the terraform state index will never learn that the one subcommand that overwrites a whole state file exists.

state identities is worse off: it has no reference page at all. https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/state/identities returns 404, the index does not list it, and a web search restricted to developer.hashicorp.com turns up no page for it. It has nonetheless been registered in commands.go since v1.12.0, the release that introduced resource identities, and it prints the identities that section 6's import blocks match on — which makes it the natural thing to reach for when an identity argument is not matching what you expect. Nothing is at risk, since it only reads. Its one requirement is -json, and there is no human-readable form:

terraform state identities -json

Run in labs/chapter16/section10/backups/ after its apply, that prints the identity of each tracked bucket:

{
  "aws_s3_bucket.renamed": {
    "account_id": "",
    "bucket": "ch16-s10-a",
    "region": "us-east-1"
  }
}

Without the flag it refuses:

The `terraform state identities` command requires the `-json` flag.

OpenTofu — seven operations under ten names, and no state identities

Measured on OpenTofu 1.12.5, which registers ten names for seven operations, against Terraform's eight names for eight. tofu state identities does not exist; asking for it prints the family's usage text rather than an error, because cmd/tofu/commands.go registers no such subcommand and the string identities does not appear in that file at all. What is missing is the command, not the feature: OpenTofu 1.12 has resource identities — states.ResourceInstanceObject carries an Identity, import blocks accept an identity argument, and the changelog announces it — so the data exists and there is simply no subcommand that prints it.

In the other direction OpenTofu registers three aliases Terraform does not have — state ls, state move and state remove, alongside list, mv and rm. Both spellings work and do the same thing:

tofu state ls                                          # same as tofu state list
tofu state move terraform_data.r terraform_data.q      # same as tofu state mv

terraform state ls prints the usage text instead. So a script written against tofu does not necessarily run under terraform, even where both engines implement the operation.

OpenTofu's hub has no subcommand list to be wrong. Where HashiCorp's index prints six of eight, website/docs/cli/commands/state/index.mdx at v1.12.5 says only "Please click a subcommand to the left for more information" — which is the workaround this section recommends to Terraform readers, adopted as the documentation itself. Nothing is omitted, because nothing is enumerated.

Everything else in this section holds on both, including the documentation bug. OpenTofu's hub carries the same remote-state paragraph, identical but for the product name — "backups are still written to disk and the CLI usage is the same as if it were local state" — and the same forced-backup rule, both inherited at the fork. The code they describe is the same shape too: internal/command/state_meta.go applies the backup path behind the identical *statemgr.Filesystem type assertion on both engines, and the S3 measurement below reproduces under tofu exactly, with no backup file and -backup refused in the identical words.

items.title: Approval defaults are backwards from the risk
items.text:
Take three of the state-writing commands this chapter has used and line up how each handles confirmation. Measured in labs/chapter16/section10/backups/ on v1.15.8:

Command Preview? Prompt? state replace-provider Yes, unconditionally — lists every affected address Yes, and with no terminal attached it aborts: Error asking for approval: EOF state mv Only if you ask, with -dry-run No — it rewrites bindings immediately refresh No No, and there is no flag to ask for one — refresh has no -auto-approve, because it has no approval step to skip

state mv and state rm do both have a preview; it is simply off unless you ask for it. The web page documents the flag but describes it with state rm's wording — "Report all of the resource instances that match the given address without actually “forgetting” any of them" — on the command that moves rather than forgets, so state mv -help is where you find out what it actually does. It costs one flag and one extra run:

terraform state mv -dry-run terraform_data.r terraform_data.q   # Would move "terraform_data.r" to "terraform_data.q"
terraform state rm -dry-run terraform_data.r                    # Would remove terraform_data.r

Those two are run in labs/chapter16/section10/same-second/, which is the directory that holds a terraform_data.r. Measured on v1.15.8: state is untouched afterwards — state list still shows terraform_data.r — and a dry run writes no backup either, since nothing was modified. state push and replace-provider have no such flag — DryRun appears in neither command's source at that tag — which for replace-provider does not matter, because its preview is unconditional, and for push means the wholesale overwrite is the one operation you cannot rehearse.

The command that merely rewrites a source string asks first. The one that rebinds objects to new addresses does not, unless you remember the flag. The one that can drop every tracked object on bad credentials has no way to be made to ask. Remember which way round that is, and remember that replace-provider is the one that will hang a CI job unless you pass -auto-approve.

The EOF abort is worth seeing once, because it is what a CI runner gets. Redirect stdin from nothing and the command prints its full preview, then dies at the prompt:

terraform state replace-provider hashicorp/aws registry.acme.corp/acme/aws < /dev/null

PowerShell has no < redirection — '<' operator is reserved for future use — so pipe an empty stream in instead, which closes stdin the same way:

$null | terraform state replace-provider hashicorp/aws registry.acme.corp/acme/aws

Either form produces the same run:

  ~ Updating provider:
    - registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws
    + registry.acme.corp/acme/aws

Changing 1 resources:

  aws_s3_bucket.renamed

Do you want to make these changes?
Only 'yes' will be accepted to continue.

Enter a value:
Error asking for approval: EOF

Exit status 1, and state untouched. The preview is printed on stdout and the error on stderr, so a job that only captures one of the two streams gets either a change list that never happened or an EOF with no indication of what it was about to change.

items.title: replace-provider is the one you cannot aim
items.text:
terraform state replace-provider hashicorp/aws registry.acme.corp/acme/aws

There is no address argument, so the unit of operation is every resource bound to that provider source. It is the only subcommand that edits state in place with a scope you cannot narrow: state rm refuses to run without one (Error: Required argument missing / At least one address is required.), state mv takes exactly two, and state list's addresses are optional only because it reads. The one other address-free writer is state push, whose scope is larger still — it replaces the entire file rather than editing part of it. The real uses are a registry namespace change, a vendored fork, or a move to a private mirror under a different source address — cases where the plugin is the same but the address recorded in state no longer matches what required_providers resolves.

OpenTofu — replace-provider is not how you migrate to OpenTofu, but it is how you migrate back

Moving Terraform → OpenTofu needs no replace-provider at all. A state written by Terraform records registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws, and OpenTofu reconciles that itself: internal/tofumigrate at v1.12.5 says it "can be used to update the in-memory view of the state to use registry.opentofu.org provider addresses", and it runs on init, on every local plan and apply, and on state show. The stored state is not edited — the translation is applied to a copy each time state is loaded — so there is nothing for you to rewrite.

The one lever is an explicit pin. With random = {} in required_providers the in-memory address becomes registry.opentofu.org/hashicorp/random; with source = "registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/random" spelled out in full, OpenTofu keeps the terraform.io address, taking the configuration as a deliberate choice of registry.

The reverse direction is the case that needs this command. Terraform has no matching translation — the string opentofu.org does not appear anywhere under internal/ at v1.15.8 — so a state whose entries were written as registry.opentofu.org/hashicorp/aws means nothing to it. That is a genuine all-or-nothing rebind, and state replace-provider is the tool for it.

items.title: The forced backup, and where it does not reach
items.text:
"Note that backups for state modification can not be disabled. Due to the sensitivity of the state file, Terraform forces every state modification command to write a backup file. You'll have to remove these files manually if you don't want to keep them around."

Worth running rather than reading, and the configuration is committed at labs/chapter16/section10/backups/. Two buckets on the local backend, one to move and one to remove:

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "a" {
  bucket = "ch16-s10-a"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "b" {
  bucket = "ch16-s10-b"
}

tflocal apply -auto-approve
terraform state mv aws_s3_bucket.a aws_s3_bucket.renamed
terraform state rm aws_s3_bucket.b
ls terraform.tfstate.*.backup                 # one file per operation

Measured on v1.15.8, that run left two:

terraform.tfstate.1787497615.backup
terraform.tfstate.1787497619.backup

The file is terraform.tfstate.<unix-timestamp>.backup, and none of them overwrites the local backend's own single-slot terraform.tfstate.backup. They accumulate, one full copy of a sensitive file per operation, and nothing prunes them.

-backup replaces the automatic file rather than adding to it

On the local backend -backup is accepted and honoured. What the docs do not say is that choosing a path substitutes for the timestamped one — you do not get both. Two runs of the same move in labs/chapter16/section10/same-second/, measured on v1.15.8:

terraform state mv -backup mine.backup terraform_data.r terraform_data.q   # leaves: mine.backup
terraform state mv terraform_data.r terraform_data.q                       # leaves: terraform.tfstate.1787499036.backup

state_meta.go only synthesises the timestamped name when backupPath is unset, so naming one takes over the single backup slot. Point -backup at a fixed filename inside a loop and each iteration overwrites the last — the same failure as the same-second collision below, made deliberate.

Four paths where the guarantee does not hold at all

The forced backup is a property of the local backend, not of the terraform state command family and not of the act of writing state. state_meta.go builds the timestamped path unconditionally and then only applies it behind a type assertion — if lb, ok := realState.(*statemgr.Filesystem); ok — under a comment claiming the backend "should always be" local. Everything below follows from where that assertion fails.

terraform state push writes no backup, on any backend. Verified on v1.15.8 and confirmed in the source at that tag: internal/command/state_push.go has no backup handling, where state_mv.go threads a backup path through. The most destructive command in the family keeps no copy of what it replaced. In the lab above, state pull → bump serial → state push moved the state from serial 5 to 6 and left the backup listing unchanged at two files.

On a remote backend, no terraform state subcommand writes a backup at all. This is the one the docs get backwards, and it has its own callout below.

removed and moved blocks go through apply, not through these commands, so the timestamped backup never applies to the path this chapter otherwise recommends. On the local backend an apply does write the single-slot terraform.tfstate.backup, which the next apply overwrites, so the protection is exactly one step deep; on a remote backend there is none. That is precisely why the manual-state section index gives its instruction unconditionally: "Make sure to keep backups of your state data if you choose to manually modify state."

terraform untaint modifies state and takes the lock, but it is not a state subcommand. Its -backup is grouped with -state and -state-out as a legacy, local-backend-only option, so an untaint against a remote backend writes state with no automatic backup — measured in labs/chapter16/section10/remote/, a taint followed by an untaint against the S3 backend leaves no backup file on disk.

On a remote backend the forced backup does not happen at all

"The Terraform state subcommands all work with remote state just as if it was local state. Reads and writes may take longer than normal as each read and each write do a full network roundtrip. Otherwise, backups are still written to disk and the CLI usage is the same as if it were local state."

That last clause is false on v1.15.8. The configuration is committed at labs/chapter16/section10/remote/ — one terraform_data resource, so the measurement is about the backend and nothing else, and the directory needs no provider:

terraform init -backend-config config.s3.tfbackend
terraform apply -auto-approve
terraform state mv terraform_data.r terraform_data.moved
find . -name '*.backup'                 # prints nothing

Move "terraform_data.r" to "terraform_data.moved"
Successfully moved 1 object(s).

No backup file is written — not beside the configuration, not under .terraform/, not anywhere. state rm behaves the same way. The reason is the type assertion quoted above: with an S3 backend the state manager is a remote.State, never a *statemgr.Filesystem, so SetBackupPath is simply never called.

Asking for one explicitly does not help either, because -backup is rejected on any backend but the local one:

terraform state mv -backup mine.backup terraform_data.moved terraform_data.r

╷
│ Error: Invalid command line options: -backup
│ 
│ Command line options -backup and -backup-out are legacy options that
│ operate on a local state file only. You must specify a local state file
│ with the -state option or switch to the local backend.
╵

So on the backend every team in Chapter 15 was told to adopt, the sentence "backups for state modification can not be disabled" describes a backup that is never taken. Read the two documentation sentences together and they promise the opposite of what happens. Before any state mv or state rm against a remote backend, take the backup yourself:

terraform state pull > pre-op.tfstate

Give it a name the local backend does not use, and a distinct one per operation, since nothing will stop the next pull overwriting it.

Then treat that file the way Chapter 15 says to treat state: it is a complete plaintext copy, and now it is on your disk rather than in the bucket.

The fifth hole: the timestamp is in whole seconds

Where a backup is written, the next one can still destroy it. The backup path is built with time.Now().UTC().Unix(), which has one-second resolution. Two terraform state commands that land in the same second therefore write to the same filename, and the second overwrites the first.

labs/chapter16/section10/same-second/ is one terraform_data resource and two chained moves, which is all it takes. It needs no provider and no emulator:

terraform apply -auto-approve
terraform state mv terraform_data.r terraform_data.step1 && terraform state mv terraform_data.step1 terraform_data.step2
ls terraform.tfstate.*.backup

Both moves on one line on purpose: a backslash continuation works in bash and not in PowerShell, while && is a pipeline chain operator in PowerShell 7 as well, so the line above runs the same way on both shells.

This is a race, not a rule, so the useful result is the series rather than a single run. Eight runs from scratch on v1.15.8, counting the backup files left behind: 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. Seven of the eight collided. The one that did not is the run whose two moves happened to straddle a second boundary.

On a collision, the surviving file holds step1 — the state after the first move. The original terraform_data.r snapshot is gone, and it was the only one worth keeping. A shell loop or a migration script that issues several state mv calls in a row is exactly the shape that hits this, and it is also exactly the shape whose author is relying on the backups.

items.title: Hand-editing, and the one legitimate way to do it
items.text:
Editing terraform.tfstate in a text editor is the method of last resort. HashiCorp's Manage Terraform state with the HCP Terraform API tutorial is unusually direct about both halves of that — why you might have to, and why you should not want to. On the first: "Although Terraform takes steps to prevent state errors, your state file can get corrupted due to partial apply operations or incorrectly running terraform import or terraform taint." On the second, stated mid-exercise while walking you through doing it: "We discourage directly editing state files. In production environments, you should only use this method as a last resort." What you give up is Terraform's validation and repeatability. JSON is unforgiving, and a slip can drop a resource so Terraform recreates something that already exists.

If you genuinely must hand-edit state

Work through terraform state pull → edit → terraform state push, never on the backend's object directly. Then:

  • keep a separate backup before you start, under a filename the local backend does not use;
  • run the result through a JSON validator;
  • diff it against the backup to see exactly what you changed;
  • increment serial by 1, so the push passes the safety checks instead of needing -force. statemgr.CheckValidImport rejects a push whose serial is lower than the destination's, and also one that carries the same serial with different content. Leaving serial alone therefore fails as surely as decrementing it, and measured on v1.15.8 the message says so plainly: Failed to write state: cannot overwrite existing state with serial 1 with a different state that has the same serial.

HashiCorp's terraform state push reference requires state files to be UTF-8 without a byte order mark, and gives Windows readers one line of advice for getting there: "use Set-Content to automatically encode files in UTF-8 format. For example, run terraform state push | Set-Content terraform.tfstate." The example is state pull's with the wrong verb pasted in, and it cannot do anything: push requires a PATH argument, so the command fails with Error: Required argument missing, and it writes nothing to stdout even when it succeeds. Nothing is lost — Set-Content on an empty pipeline leaves the target file untouched, verified — but nothing is gained either. The advice underneath it is real, and it is version-dependent, and the page does not say which PowerShell it means. Measured here, writing {"a":"é"} and reading the bytes back:

piped into Set-Content redirected with > PowerShell 7.6.5 UTF-8, no BOM ✅ — é is C3 A9 UTF-8, no BOM ✅ — é is C3 A9 Windows PowerShell 5.1 no BOM, but ANSI — é becomes E9, not C3 A9 ⚠️ UTF-16LE with a FF FE BOM ❌

On 7 the advice is redundant, because both forms already produce what Terraform wants. On 5.1 it only avoids the BOM, and it mangles every non-ASCII byte in the state — a tag, a description, a bucket name. That is worse than the failure it prevents, because nothing stops it. -Encoding UTF8 does not rescue it either: 5.1 writes UTF-8 with a BOM, EF BB BF on the front. The reliable form there, verified:

[System.IO.File]::WriteAllText($path, $text, (New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding $false))

The mangled push succeeds, and the damage surfaces as drift

This is worth running once, because the failure has no error in it. labs/chapter16/section10/ansi-push/ is one terraform_data resource whose input carries two accented characters, and a mkansi.ps1 that round-trips the pulled state through 5.1's Set-Content exactly as the docs advise, bumping serial on the way:

resource "terraform_data" "r" {
  input = "café-naïve"
}

terraform apply -auto-approve
terraform state pull > pulled.json
powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File mkansi.ps1
terraform state push ansi.json

The script reports what the encoding did — utf8 e-acute present: False, 0xE9 present: True — and then the push exits 0 and prints nothing, which is what success looks like for this command. The state on the backend now holds raw E9 and EF bytes where it held C3 A9 and C3 AF. Read it back:

# terraform_data.r:
resource "terraform_data" "r" {
    id     = "bf5170f9-eca2-c5d3-dee7-3e0f8e5374ab"
    input  = "caf?-na?ve"
    output = "caf?-na?ve"
}

Terraform never complains about the invalid UTF-8. It substitutes replacement characters and carries on, so the corruption shows up one command later as drift against a configuration nobody edited:

  # terraform_data.r will be updated in-place
  ~ resource "terraform_data" "r" {
        id     = "bf5170f9-eca2-c5d3-dee7-3e0f8e5374ab"
      ~ input  = "caf?-na?ve" -> "café-naïve"
      ~ output = "caf?-na?ve" -> (known after apply)
    }

Plan: 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.

Here the drift is harmless and the next apply repairs it, because terraform_data holds the value in state and nowhere else. Against a real provider the same bytes are an object's name or tag, so the plan proposes rewriting a remote object to fix damage that a text encoding did to the record of it.

Section 8's framing places this precisely: the state is wrong and the world is right, which is the one combination none of its three answers fits.

-refresh-only is the wrong reflex, and it makes the damage permanent. Reaching for it looks right — re-read the objects, repair the record — and it reports success:

Terraform has checked that the real remote objects still match the result of
your most recent changes, and found no differences.

Apply complete! Resources: 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.

Nothing was repaired. The following plan still proposes the same in-place update. What did change is the bytes: the state held a raw E9 before the refresh and holds EF BF BD afterwards — the UTF-8 encoding of U+FFFD. Terraform read the invalid byte as a replacement character and then wrote that character back out properly, so the lossy substitution is now recorded as a real, valid, wrong character.

Not every state write does this, and the split is exactly the chapter's subject. Three runs, each building a fresh corrupted state and then applying one command to it:

Command The é byte afterwards terraform state push E9 — raw, as written terraform state mv E9 — preserved terraform plan E9 — nothing persisted terraform apply -refresh-only EF BF BD — normalised

The reason is visible in the source at v1.15.8. An instance's attributes live in state as AttrsJSON, a raw []byte, and state_mv.go moves the instance by assignment — rs.Instances[addrTo.Resource.Key] = is — without ever looking inside it, so the bytes survive untouched. A plan or apply instead decodes that JSON into a cty value and re-encodes it with ctyjson.Marshal on the way back to state, and the decode is where an invalid byte becomes U+FFFD. That is the same boundary the rest of this section draws for backups, seen from another side: the state family treats state as a file, and everything else treats it as data.

The repair is to redo the push with the encoding fixed — terraform state pull, re-encode, bump serial, push again — and to do it before anything else writes state. Applying works too, at the cost of rewriting infrastructure that was never wrong.

There is also a clean copy on disk, briefly, and it is the backup this section has spent its length disparaging. Straight after the bad push, the local backend's single-slot terraform.tfstate.backup still holds C3 A9, because it was written by the last ordinary apply and that apply predates the corruption. The timestamped backup a subsequent state mv forces holds E9 — it faithfully preserves state that was already wrong. Measured:

terraform.tfstate.1787501615.backup -> caf E9      # the forced one: already corrupt
terraform.tfstate.backup            -> caf C3 A9   # the local backend's: still good

The window is one state-writing apply wide. Running -refresh-only closes it: the same command that normalises the live state to EF BF BD also overwrites terraform.tfstate.backup with the E9 version, so the reflex that seals the damage destroys the only clean copy in the same step. Copy that file somewhere else before you try anything.

The ? above are the book's rendering of U+FFFD; a terminal shows its own replacement glyph.

items.title: 11. Recovery: when state and the backend disagree
items.text:
The Disaster Recovery section is three sentences and three commands, and it exists for one scenario: "an accident when performing other state manipulation actions". It is what all those forced backups are for.

1. Unlock, if a run died holding the lock.

"You may need to unlock Terraform when a terraform apply or other process unexpectedly terminates before Terraform can release its lock on the state backend. Unlocking Terraform overrides protections that prevent two processes from modifying state at the same time. We do not recommend unlocking until you determine what caused the lock to get stuck."

Diagnose first, unlock second. Chapter 15 covered force-unlock and the LOCK_ID nonce it demands, which is the structural enforcement of that sequencing: you can only get the ID from the error Terraform printed, so there is no blind-unlock form.

2. Read with terraform state pull, remembering it upgrades the format on the way out.

3. Write with terraform state push.

items.title: What state push will and will not accept
items.text:
Two safety checks, both reproduced on v1.15.8:

Attempt Result Push lineage bbbb… over lineage aaaa… cannot import state with lineage "bbbb…" over unrelated state with lineage "aaaa…" — exit 1 Push serial 2 over serial 5 cannot import state with serial 2 over newer state with serial 5 — exit 1 Either, with -force Silent success, exit 0. The destination went from serial 5 to serial 2, a downgrade applied without a word.

A successful push prints nothing. The only signal is the exit status.

Three cases where the checks never run, and no flag is needed to bypass them

Found in statemgr.CheckValidImport at tag v1.15.8, after the checks failed to fire on a first test:

  1. The destination state is empty. "It's always okay to overwrite an empty state, regardless of its lineage/serial." A state file with no resources counts.
  2. The destination is a legacy state with no lineage.
  3. Same lineage, same serial, identical content is allowed. Same lineage and serial with different content is the one remaining error.

The practical form of the first: pushing into a workspace whose state has been emptied, say by a destroy or by an earlier bad push, is completely unguarded. The checks protect state that has something in it.

Chapter 15 covered the other recovery case, errored.tfstate, where the apply succeeded but persisting state to the backend failed. The rule there is worth restating because it is the one people get wrong under pressure: push the file, do not re-run apply first.

items.title: 🧪 Lab
items.text:
Six configurations, one operation each, in the order the chapter teaches them. Everything below was run end to end against the emulator on Terraform v1.15.8 with AWS provider v6.61.0, plus OpenTofu 1.12.5 for the last part. The configurations are committed at labs/chapter16/.

Start the emulator:

docker compose -f labs/docker-compose.yml up -d      # start the emulator on :4566
curl -s http://localhost:4566/_floci/health          # wait until the services read "running"

Set the lab environment once per shell:

source "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/labs/lab-env.sh"

. "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/labs/lab-env.ps1"

Emulation is not AWS

A green apply here proves your HCL and your workflow, not AWS fidelity. The emulator implements the S3 API well enough for every operation in this chapter, and it is not a substitute for validating a load-bearing configuration against real free-tier AWS. That matters more in this chapter than in most, because import IDs and identity attributes are provider implementation details and a composite ID format can differ between provider versions even against real AWS.

items.title: Lab 1 — adopt a bucket nobody told Terraform about
items.text:
Create something unmanaged, the way it happens in real life:

awslocal s3api create-bucket --bucket ch16-legacy-notes
awslocal s3api put-bucket-tagging --bucket ch16-legacy-notes \
  --tagging 'TagSet=[{Key=owner,Value=platform-team},{Key=managed_by,Value=nobody}]'
awslocal s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket ch16-legacy-notes \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

In labs/chapter16/lab1, imports.tf holds an import block and nothing else. Generate a draft:

tflocal init
tflocal plan -generate-config-out generated.tf

Read generated.tf. Every argument it emits is either required, a default, or computed. Now do the experiment the chapter describes: save it, then replace it with a minimal block naming only bucket, and plan again. You should see 1 to import, 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy and a ~ tags block that removes both tags. Add the tags argument back and the plan becomes 1 to import, 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

tflocal apply
tflocal state list          # aws_s3_bucket.legacy
tflocal plan                # No changes — the import block is idempotent

Try re-running the generation with the file still present, to see Error: Target generated file already exists.

items.title: Lab 2 — rename, and migrate count to for_each
items.text:
labs/chapter16/lab2 starts with aws_s3_bucket.notes and a two-instance aws_s3_bucket.archive under count.

tflocal init && tflocal apply

Rename the label from notes to team_notes and plan without a moved block. Read the # (because aws_s3_bucket.notes is not in configuration) line and the 1 to add, 1 to destroy counters.

Before fixing it, prove section 1's claim for yourself. Save that plan, then delete the notes block entirely and save a second one:

tflocal plan -no-color > renamed.txt      # with the label renamed
# now delete the resource block instead, and:
tflocal plan -no-color > deleted.txt
diff deleted.txt renamed.txt

Compare-Object (Get-Content deleted.txt) (Get-Content renamed.txt)

Measured here, Compare-Object reports 44 differing rows: 43 on the renamed side, which are the + create legend entry and the create block, and 1 on the deleted side, which is its counter line. The destroy block, reason line included, is identical in both and appears nowhere in the output.

Then add:

moved {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.notes
  to   = aws_s3_bucket.team_notes
}

and confirm has moved to with 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

For the second half, convert archive from count to for_each with the bucket names left unchanged, plan it bare to see 2 to add, 2 to destroy, then add one moved block per index and watch the same plan go empty.

items.title: Lab 3 — forget a bucket, then take it back
items.text:
labs/chapter16/lab3 adopts ch16-handover rather than creating it, so make it first and let Terraform import it:

awslocal s3api create-bucket --bucket ch16-handover
awslocal s3api create-bucket --bucket ch16-shard-a       # keytest.tf adopts these two
awslocal s3api create-bucket --bucket ch16-shard-b
tflocal init
tflocal apply -auto-approve                              # Resources: 3 imported

Now replace the resource block with a bare removed block and plan. Do not apply: the plan says 1 to destroy, which is the whole point of the exercise.

Add the lifecycle block, plan again, and look closely at three things: the empty symbol legend, the lone ., and the Warning: Some objects will no longer be managed by Terraform. Then apply and verify:

tflocal state list                                    # handover is gone, the shard pair is not
awslocal s3 ls | grep ch16-handover                   # still there

Plan once more with the removed block still in the file. It is No changes., which is the measurement behind the retention guidance: a block whose from finds nothing in state is inert.

Take it back with a resource block plus an import block, and confirm Resources: 1 imported. Delete the removed block as you do it. Leave it in and the plan is Error: Removed resource still exists, which is labs/chapter16/section5/retained-block on its own.

keytest.tf in the same directory adds a for_each resource. Point a removed block at one instance to see Error: Resource instance keys not allowed, then use terraform state rm on the bare address and watch it take out both instances with no prompt at all.

items.title: Lab 4 — split one configuration into two
items.text:
labs/chapter16/lab4/source holds two buckets, and ch16-split-customer-data is moving to lab4/dest.

cd labs/chapter16/lab4/source
tflocal init && tflocal apply
tflocal state pull > customer-split.backup.tfstate    # not terraform.tfstate.backup
tflocal state show aws_s3_bucket.customer_data        # find the id

Replace the resource block with removed and destroy = false, apply, then in dest/ add the resource block plus an import block and apply there. Finish with the step that is the actual deliverable:

cd ../dest && tflocal plan     # No changes.
cd ../source && tflocal plan   # No changes.

Two empty plans is the proof. Anything else means one side still believes something the other does not.

items.title: Lab 5 — manufacture drift and answer it three ways
items.text:
labs/chapter16/lab5 creates a bucket tagged owner = platform-team. Change it behind Terraform's back:

awslocal s3api put-bucket-tagging --bucket ch16-drift-site \
  --tagging 'TagSet=[{Key=owner,Value=oncall-hotfix}]'

Then run all three answers in turn and read the differences:

tflocal plan -refresh-only     # "has changed" — past tense, no action proposed
tflocal plan                   # "will be updated in-place" — the revert
tflocal apply -refresh-only    # accept it into state; note the counters say 0/0/0

To see that the counters are lying, read serial before and after the refresh-only apply:

tflocal state pull | python -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['serial'])"

It went 1 → 2 in the measurement above while the apply reported 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed. Finish by editing the configuration to say oncall-hotfix, which is the durable form of adopting drift, and confirming the plan is empty.

items.title: Lab 6 — the same forget under OpenTofu
items.text:
labs/chapter16/opentofu is one bucket with lifecycle { destroy = false } on the resource itself. Run it with tofu:

TF_CMD=tofu tflocal init
TF_CMD=tofu tflocal apply
TF_CMD=tofu tflocal destroy

Two things to notice. The removed-block plan under OpenTofu prints . forget in the symbol legend and counts 1 to forget as a fifth counter, where Terraform prints an empty legend and 0 to destroy. And the resource-level destroy = false, which Terraform 1.15.8 rejects as an unsupported argument, makes tofu destroy forget rather than delete and then exit non-zero with Destroy was successful but left behind forgotten instances.

items.title: Clean up
items.text:
tflocal destroy     # in each lab directory

Every lab's destroy is worth running deliberately rather than skipping, because in labs 1 and 3 it deletes a bucket Terraform did not create. That is section 6's commitment, arriving.

The section3/ and section4/ directories that the earlier sections follow along with need a word of their own. Several never apply anything, since their whole purpose is an error at validate or plan time, and section3/bare-address/ ends with a state rm that leaves two buckets nothing tracks, so destroy there has nothing to act on and the cleanup is awslocal s3 rb. Each directory's README says which case it is.

items.title: Common pitfalls
items.text:
• Writing a bare removed block when you meant to forget. It destroys the object. lifecycle { destroy = false } is the whole operation, and the block's own documentation still opens by describing the safe behaviour as the default.
  • Getting the moved direction backwards. to is the address in your configuration now; from is the one that has gone. Reversed, the plan does not run at all: from names something configuration still declares, and Terraform answers Moved object still exists.
  • Declaring both resources during a moved migration. Terraform rejects it. The rename is the edit to the existing block's label.
  • Deleting moved blocks too early. The question is whether any state anywhere still holds the old address, not how long ago the change was. Published modules keep theirs forever, and chain them.
  • Deleting removed blocks too early. The same question, and a worse answer. Any state that still holds the address and no longer sees the block plans a plain destroy, with nothing recreated afterwards. HashiCorp calls keeping the block optional, which is true of the state you already applied and of no other.
  • Importing with a minimal resource block. Every argument you omit is silently the schema default. Measured here, that stripped two tags from a bucket on the very apply that adopted it.
  • Reading 1 to import and stopping. Read the other three counters. 1 to import, 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy means Terraform is going to adopt the object and then replace it.
  • Treating generated configuration as finished. It emits defaults and computed attributes, it is experimental, and a failed generation still leaves the file behind so the retry fails for a different reason.
  • Using terraform refresh. It is apply -refresh-only -auto-approve with an auto-approve you cannot switch off, and misconfigured credentials turn it into a state-wipe with no prompt.
  • Believing the counters on a refresh-only or forget plan. They count infrastructure actions. State was written anyway; check serial.
  • Reaching for -target to reduce blast radius. It selects upstream only, computes dependencies per resource rather than per instance, and leaves state internally inconsistent until you run an untargeted apply.
  • Trusting the forced backup. It is a property of the local backend, not of the terraform state family: on a remote backend no subcommand writes one and -backup is refused outright. state push writes none on any backend, untaint on a remote backend writes none, the removed/moved path goes through apply and gets only the single-slot terraform.tfstate.backup locally, and two operations in the same second share one filename.
  • Backing up to terraform.tfstate.backup. That is the local backend's own filename, and you will overwrite its copy with yours — which section 10 shows is sometimes the only uncorrupted copy you have.
  • Reaching for -refresh-only to repair a bad state file. It repairs nothing, reports "found no differences", permanently normalises invalid bytes into U+FFFD, and overwrites the one clean backup on its way past. Fix the file and push it instead.
  • Splitting a state without checking both plans afterwards. An empty plan on one side proves nothing.

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
1. Take any two-resource configuration you have applied. Rename one resource and plan. Now add a moved block and plan again. Write down which line in the first plan told you it was a rename rather than a deletion, and explain why Terraform could not tell.
  2. Create an S3 bucket in the emulator with two tags and a non-default setting. Adopt it with a hand-written resource block naming only the bucket name. Predict the plan's four counters before you run it, then run it.
  3. Repeat exercise 2 with -generate-config-out. Prune the generated file to a clean plan and list every line you deleted, sorted into "default", "computed" and "genuinely redundant".
  4. Convert a count-based resource to for_each on a live state. Do it wrong first, with no moved blocks, and record what the plan proposes to destroy. Then do it right.
  5. Forget a resource with removed and destroy = false, then bring it back. Write down the two artefacts that had to change on the way out and on the way in, and explain why one direction needs an import and the other does not.
  6. Manufacture drift, then answer it three ways in three separate runs: revert, adopt into state, and adopt into configuration. Record the serial before and after each. Which of the three leaves the next plan empty?
  7. Split a two-resource configuration into two directories using removed and import. Then break the migration deliberately: skip the import in the destination and run its plan. What does it propose, and why is that the most dangerous plan in this chapter?
  8. Run the same removed and destroy = false plan under terraform and under tofu. List every difference in the output, and say which tool's version you would rather have in a pull request.

items.title: Summary
items.text:
State operations exist because an address is an identity, and identities change for reasons that have nothing to do with the infrastructure they name.

  • Terraform loses the binding when you rename a resource, move it to another module, or change its provider. Usually destroy-and-recreate is the right answer; this chapter is for when it is not.
  • # (because X is not in configuration) is the universal diagnostic. It means state holds an address configuration does not claim, and it looks identical whether you deleted, renamed, or forgot to commit a file.
  • Prefer configuration to the CLI, for three separate reasons. moved renames state before the plan is computed. A block ships to every consumer where a command does not. And a block makes the rename part of the same apply, so there is no window in which a coworker's plan proposes a destroy.
  • moved renames without destroying, migrates count to for_each one index at a time, cascades over a whole module call, and preserves identity, not configuration. A zero-destroy plan can still be a three-change plan.
  • removed forgets without destroying, but only with lifecycle { destroy = false }. Bare, it destroys. It plans as a lone . under an empty symbol legend and 0 to destroy, it refuses instance keys, and the only way back is an import.
  • import needs two things, the block and a resource block at the same address, and its hard part is the configuration rather than the ID. Name exactly the arguments whose values differ from the provider's defaults. Read all four counters, not just 1 to import. Generation is a draft and is still experimental.
  • Splitting a state is removed plus import across two configurations, verified by an empty plan on both sides. state mv -state-out is the legacy route and the only one that crosses a state boundary in a single command.
  • Drift is detected by every ordinary plan. -refresh-only reports it in the past tense and lets you accept it with a prompt; terraform refresh is the same operation with the prompt permanently disabled, and with bad credentials it removes every tracked object without asking. There are three legitimate answers, revert, adopt and ignore, and choosing is your job rather than Terraform's.
  • The counters count infrastructure actions. Measured: apply -refresh-only reported 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed while serial went 1 → 2. OpenTofu is honest about the forget case and reports 1 to forget; Terraform is not.
  • -replace for a degraded object, -target only for recovery. Targeting walks upstream only and computes dependencies per resource, so instance-level targeting buys no precision at all.
  • The forced backup belongs to the local backend, not to the terraform state family. On a remote backend no subcommand writes one and -backup is refused outright, which is the opposite of what the docs promise. state push writes none anywhere, the removed/moved path goes through apply and gets only the single-slot terraform.tfstate.backup locally, and two operations inside one second share a filename. Take the copy yourself with state pull before remote state surgery.

items.title: What's next
items.text:
You can now bring unmanaged infrastructure under Terraform, rearrange what you already manage without destroying it, and repair state when it and reality disagree. Chapter 17 goes back to the thing every one of these operations quietly depends on: provider configuration, including the aliases the import block takes, the meta-arguments that pass providers into modules, and how a provider gets its credentials in the first place.

Two threads from this chapter continue later. Refactoring at scale — the module-split shim, the migration sequencing, and what to do when a rename spans dozens of consumers — is Chapter 25. Deciding how many state files you should have, which is the structural answer to most of the operations here, is Chapter 24.

items.title: Learning outcomes
items.text:
By the end you can:

  • Say what a provider configuration is: a global, root-module-only object that resources are bound to statically, and a running process on the other end of a gRPC connection.
  • Give a provider more than one configuration with alias, and recognise the implied empty default that appears the moment you alias every block.
  • Choose a configuration with provider on a resource and with the providers map on a module, and explain why one is singular and the other is plural.
  • Deploy the same resource to two regions two ways: aliased providers, and the AWS provider's per-resource region argument. Migrate between them with an empty plan.
  • Cross an account boundary with assume_role, and name both halves of the permission that makes it work.
  • State why a reusable module must contain no provider block, using the lifecycle reason rather than the count one.
  • Pin providers where pinning belongs, read a constraint intersection, and say when terraform init needs -upgrade.
  • Explain what a provider configuration costs, and when an alias is the wrong answer.
  • Use OpenTofu's provider for_each, and structure it so a retirement can actually be destroyed.

items.title: 1. One provider block is one region and one account
items.text:
Every worked configuration in this book so far has had exactly one provider "aws" block, and that block is where three things were quietly decided: which region resources land in, which account they land in, and which credentials do the landing. Every one of those blocks set a region and nothing else, so the account and the credentials came from the provider's default credential lookup rather than from the configuration.

provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
}

Chapter 5 put a second, aliased block on the page and deferred its mechanics to this chapter.

provider "aws" {                 # second config, tagged with an alias
  alias  = "eu"
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

Nothing has needed to change any of those three mid-configuration.

Real work does. Four cases, and none of them is exotic:

  • A read replica or a backup bucket has to sit in a different region from the thing it protects. Putting both in the same region defeats the point.
  • CloudFront will only attach a TLS certificate that lives in us-east-1, no matter where the rest of the stack runs. That is ACM's requirement as CloudFront states it, not a Terraform one.
  • Account-wide detective controls such as GuardDuty are meant to run in every supported region, not just the ones you deploy to. AWS recommends enabling it everywhere precisely so that it reports activity in the regions you never use.
  • Staging and production live in separate accounts, because that is the boundary that actually stops a mistake in one from reaching the other.

The mechanism for all four is the same, and it is small: a provider can have more than one configuration, and every resource is bound to exactly one of them. Setting that up takes one argument. The rest of this chapter is about the consequences, which are where the difficulty lives. Provider configurations are global rather than scoped, where nearly everything else in the language belongs to the module that declares it. They must outlive every object they created, and the binding between a resource and its configuration is static, which quietly rules out some things you will reach for.

There is also a newer answer that did not exist when most of the advice about this topic was written. Since AWS provider 6.0, most AWS resources take a region argument of their own, and a great many configurations that used to need aliases no longer do. In 6.61.0 the provider ships that argument on 1,526 of its 1,709 managed resource types. Section 5 measures both routes side by side.

items.title: 2. What a provider configuration actually is
items.text:
Chapter 2 and Chapter 5 established the split: required_providers declares a provider so Terraform can install it, and a provider block configures it.

# terraform.tf — DECLARE: which provider, which version
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
  required_version = ">= 1.2"
}

# providers.tf — CONFIGURE: how to connect
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
}

This chapter needs four more facts about the second half.

items.title: It is global, and it lives in the root module
items.text:
Most things in Terraform are scoped. A variable belongs to a module. An output belongs to a module. A resource address is relative to the module that declares it. Provider configurations break that pattern. HashiCorp's Providers Within Modules page states it directly:

"Provider configurations, unlike most other concepts in Terraform, are global to an entire Terraform configuration and can be shared across module boundaries. Provider configurations can be defined only in a root Terraform module."

Two rules:

  • Definitions go in the root module only.
  • What they define can be shared across the whole tree.

The second rule is a capability rather than a default. A child module automatically receives the default configuration and nothing else, so an aliased one reaches it only when the caller passes it in. Section 8 covers that boundary.

“Root module” means the directory you run the command in

The root module is wherever terraform apply is invoked, or wherever -chdir sends it. It is not a special file or a special name. A module becomes a child module when something calls it with a module block. The same directory can be a root module on Monday and a child module on Tuesday, and the provider rule follows that role rather than the files. This is why a no-code module in HCP Terraform is allowed to declare providers: HCP generates a workspace where that module is the root.

items.title: It is a process
items.text:
Chapter 5 described the plugin model. It matters again here for a reason that is purely operational. Terraform core is one binary, each provider is a separate binary, and they talk over gRPC on a local connection. A provider configuration is what gets a plugin process started and handed its settings.

So the number of provider configurations is not a stylistic detail. It is a count of processes, each opening its own connections to a remote API. The unit is the configuration rather than the block, and the two come apart in both directions:

  • A process with no block. A configuration you never wrote still starts one the moment something uses it. That is the implied empty default, which the last part of this section covers.
  • A block with no process. A provider block nothing refers to is pruned out of the graph before it is ever configured. The trace log states it outright: pruning unused provider["registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws"].unused.

Section 10 puts a measured number on what happens when that count gets large.

items.title: Its arguments are evaluated early
items.text:
A provider block may use expressions, but only over values that are known before anything is applied. Input variables are fine, and so is a local, as long as what the local itself resolves to is known that early. A computed attribute of a resource is not. Terraform has to configure a provider before it can create anything with it, so a provider argument that depends on a resource's output is a circular request.

“Early” here means before apply, not during init

Terraform uses early evaluation for something narrower: the configuration loading that happens during terraform init, where a module's source and version are resolved. A variable used in either of those must carry const = true, which is Chapter 13's subject. Provider arguments are not resolved that early. They are evaluated when Terraform builds the plan, by which point every root variable is known, so const is not required on a variable a provider block reads. Adding it costs something: a const variable with no default has to be supplied to init as well as to plan.

provider "aws" {
  region = var.region        # fine: a variable is known at plan time
}

provider "kubernetes" {
  host = aws_eks_cluster.main.endpoint   # a trap, even where it appears to work
}

The second shape does sometimes work, which is worse than if it never did. The Kubernetes provider's own documentation says not to do it: interpolating credentials from resources created in the same module "will lead to intermittent and unpredictable errors which are hard to debug and diagnose."

labs/chapter17/section2/early-eval/ reproduces the intermittency locally, with random standing in for EKS. The dependency is the same shape as the Kubernetes one, and it runs without a cluster:

resource "random_shuffle" "pick" {
  input        = ["us-east-1", "us-west-2"]
  result_count = 1
}

provider "aws" {                                # line 27
  region     = random_shuffle.pick.result[0]
  access_key = "test"
  secret_key = "test"
}

resource "aws_iam_role" "r" {
  name               = "ch17-early-eval"
  assume_role_policy = jsonencode({ Version = "2012-10-17", Statement = [] })
}

terraform validate reports Success! The configuration is valid. From clean state the plan then fails, and the error blames the wrong thing:

Error: invalid AWS Region: 

  with provider["registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws"],
  on main.tf line 27, in provider "aws":
  27: provider "aws" {

The value arrived empty, so the complaint is about the region rather than about the reference that produced it.

The reference resolves against state rather than against the file, so whether the identical configuration works is only a question of whether the dependency's attribute is already known when the plan is built:

  • Not in state yet. Unknown, and the provider is configured with an empty string. This is the first run, and it is also every fresh clone, new workspace and empty CI runner after it.
  • In state, unchanged. A plain known string. Apply that one resource on its own and the same file plans clean: Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. That clean run is what makes the shape look supportable.
  • In state, but being replaced. Unknown again. Add -replace random_shuffle.pick to that clean plan and the identical error returns on a workspace that has been working: Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy. followed by Error: invalid AWS Region:.

The third case is the one that costs a day. Nothing about the configuration changed, the workspace has applied successfully for months, and a forced replacement upstream is enough to make the provider unconfigurable again.

The supported answer needs no paid product. Split the work into two configurations applied in sequence, and let the second read the first's outputs through a terraform_remote_state data source or a provider data source, which is Chapter 15's subject. Two smaller open-source moves shrink the problem without removing it:

  • Take the credentials out of the interpolation. The Kubernetes provider's exec block calls a helper such as aws eks get-token while the provider is being configured, so no token has to come from a resource attribute. Its documentation warns against combining exec with token or client_certificate, because "there is no guarantee about which credential will actually be used." The host still has to come from somewhere, so this halves the problem rather than ending it.
  • Sequence inside one configuration with -target. This section's own lab does exactly that to get past the failing plan. It is recovery, not a design, and Chapter 3 says why.

What open source does not have is the deferral itself. HCP Terraform's Stacks defer provider initialisation until such values exist, which is a real fix on a different configuration surface rather than a switch you turn on. Chapter 27 covers Stacks. Terraform's own deferral machinery is compiled in but closed off: terraform plan -allow-deferral on the released 1.15.8 binary answers The -allow-deferral flag is only valid in experimental builds of Terraform.

An orchestrator does not close that gap, and it is worth knowing why before reaching for one. Terragrunt automates the split rather than removing it: dependency blocks put its units in a DAG, and its documentation is explicit that run --all apply "will not attempt to deploy the config until all the units referenced in dependency blocks have been applied". A downstream unit therefore reads outputs that have already been applied, which is the two-configuration answer with the sequencing done for you. What it cannot do is plan a unit whose dependency does not exist yet, so it offers mock_outputs — placeholder values — and warns that you "might not want to use the defaults for a plan operation because the plan doesn't give you any indication of what is actually going to be created". For a provider argument that means planning against a fabricated endpoint. Terrakube, the open-source HCP Terraform alternative, is the platform half rather than this one: its templates sequence steps within a single workspace, and its documentation describes no ordering between workspaces. Terragrunt as an orchestrator is a topic of its own, and this book reaches it under large-scale state and repository architecture rather than here.

OpenTofu — -exclude, and a deferral that was deliberately withdrawn

OpenTofu decided against provider deferral rather than lacking it. Release 1.11.4: "Providers are not configured anymore with DeferralAllowed capability of OpenTofu since having that created unwanted behaviour from some providers." The capability still exists in the plugin protocol; what changed is that OpenTofu stopped advertising it. A separate note, quoted below, gives the underlying complaint: providers that report they cannot plan because of unknown values, when planning would in fact have succeeded.

What it offers instead is -exclude, the inverse of -target: name the resources to leave out rather than the ones to build. Measured on OpenTofu 1.12.5, tofu plan -help documents -exclude=resource; on Terraform 1.15.8 the flag does not exist, in plan -help or in the source. OpenTofu withdrew its automatic suggestion of the flag in 1.11.2 while keeping the technique: "Using -exclude still a valid workaround for these problems even though OpenTofu cannot accurately detect when it's useful to make that suggestion." The same release made planning with unknown provider configuration work again for the helm and kubernetes providers, "as long as the configuration is carefully written to avoid the plan phase actually depending on those values."

items.title: There is always a default configuration
items.text:
